Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. In the 2.5 release, Google says its robotic AI is getting tantalizingly close to completing real-world tasks as well as humans do. In fact, some Gemini robots were able to get actual work done in Mercedes-Benz factories, and the team is preparing for a day when robots operate alongside humans with an open source safety benchmark.
DeepMind’s physical AI platform has several computational layers between user input and robotic action. There’s the vision-language model piece, which is Gemini Embodied Reasoning. Essentially, it takes your instructions and uses live video to plan how the robot can accomplish the task. The other main component is the vision-language-action (VLA) that actually generates robot actions, like moving an actuator—that’s Gemini Robotics, which has been bumped to version 2.5.
DeepMind says that Gemini Robotics 2.5 is much better at tasks that require a high degree of dexterity. The model was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, as you would see in a laboratory. Google also showed that Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot with Gemini Robotics 2.5 can now tie a bow with its five-fingered hands, a notable feat, because deformable objects (like ribbon) are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate.
Overall, Gemini Robotics 2.5 manages a 30 to 100 percent higher success rate compared to the last version. It’s also 20 to 30 percent faster. But that’s based on laboratory testing. Google partnered with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz to see how capable this AI is when faced with the uncertainty of the world outside robotics labs. The Gemini-powered Apollo 2 robots kitted automotive parts in a few European factories, reaching a 96 percent success rate.
That’s an impressive showing compared to previous robotic AI systems, but it’s still probably not enough for a company like Mercedes-Benz. A human doing that sort of repetitive task will get it right virtually every time, and DeepMind director Kanishka Rao notes that closing that last 4 percent gap will be a “steep road.”

In early November, a screenshot spread purportedly showing that Vice President JD Vance posted a message on X saying he was trying to find a way to avoid being the person who swears in Michigan's Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed.
People shared the alleged post, which does not contain a date, on X and Facebook. It reads:
I'm looking at every legal option to avoid being the one who swears Abdul El-Sayed into office. After the level of disrespect he's shown me he cant seriously expect me to stand there and do him that honor.
The claim circulated after El-Sayed defeated his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, on Election Day.
As president of the Senate, as per the Constitution, the incumbent vice president swears-in senators when a new Congress convenes, meaning Vance is set to swear El-Sayed in on Jan. 3, 2027.
In short, the screenshot shows a fake X post that is not on Vance's verified account. The image appears to originate from Idisobey, a Facebook page known for posting fabricated social media posts and false claims, one of which Snopes has previously debunked.
A manager of the account posted the fake screengrab on Nov. 7 (screenshotted).
We contacted the page's manager to ask why they had created the fake post without a disclaimer about its inauthenticity or possible satirical intent. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Searching Vance's X page for posts mentioning El-Sayed returns only one result, as of this writing. That post, dated Oct. 27, does not match the one in the fake screenshot. Instead, it includes a video of the vice president speaking at a rally in Michigan, and text that reads, "Let's send Abdul packing and tell him we don't want people who hate our country in the US Senate."
A reverse image search of the screengrab on Google only returns examples of users sharing the fake post in November, along with some calling out that it is fabricated. A similar reverse image search on Tin Eye returned no results.
Likewise, a Google search for verbatim keywords from the fabricated post returns no evidence of Vance ever producing such a comment (archived).
The screenshot spread following the Democratic Party's major victories in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections. Vance backed Rogers in the Michigan race and lobbed insults and criticisms at El-Sayed throughout the campaign.
In El-Sayed's victory speech, he directed a remark at Vance when he said (from 9:00 onward), "JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in, in January," referring to the Oath of Senators, referenced above, that specifies the president of the Senate — the U.S. vice president — will administer the oath of office to those who were elected.
Fake posts by politicians and public figures is a trope Snopes regularly addresses. For example, we previously debunked a claim that tech mogul Elon Musk said Teslas could not be used to dodge a military draft, and a rumor that Vance posted a memorial to an expensive couch lost in the 2025 Texas floods.

BSE 
Sensex
 has risen by a whopping 8,600 points in the last ten trading sessions - an increase of 11.8%! That’s a remarkable feat for a stock market that has been out of favour by most standards globally this year.
Sensex and 
Nifty
 are back at their highest levels since 27 February, which was the last trading day before the US-Iran war began on 28 February.
There has been a sudden turnaround in sentiment since late October and Indian equities have seen a series of upgrades in the last few days from global brokerages as well.
What’s brought this about? And importantly, what should your strategy be as an investor? Which sectors will be in focus going forward? We ask experts:
The reasons behind the rally
The recovery in Indian equities has been driven by easing geopolitical concerns, a sharp correction in crude oil prices, a notable reversal in FII flows and decent corporate earnings reported in the second quarter. The US-midterm blow for the Trump administration has strengthened hopes of a swift end to the war with Iran.
The crude prices dropped sharply and with easing geopolitical tension the war premium in crude is likely to go down. This is particularly positive for India as it eases inflationary pressures, supports the rupee and improves the current account position.
Additionally, global investors are reassessing their exposure to expensive US technology and artificial intelligence stocks and diversifying towards emerging markets, including India.
Brent crude prices have fallen sharply
Resilient domestic economic activity and improving corporate earnings have further supported investor sentiment.
There are also hopes that the government may announce relief from long-term capital gains tax in the coming months, another positive that is drawing foreign investors’ interest.
VK Vijayakumar, Chief Investment strategist, Geojit Investments Limited lists important reasons:
1. Weakening of the AI trade after the US mid-term elections. This is positive for India which is a non-AI trade.
2. The impressive Q2 results which have come much better than expected. The near 24 % earnings growth of Nifty 50 companies is a 12-quarter high.
3. The above two factors have turned FIIs aggressive buyers in India with a buy figure of Rs 53,170 crore in November, so far. The rally is being led by largecaps which are fairly valued.
The sustainability
Some experts suggest the possibility of pullbacks of 3-5% as the market digests oil, Fed and geopolitical news. They advise staggering flow of fresh money over the next few months.
Somil Mehta, Head of Retail Research at Mirae Asset Sharekhan says that the sustainability of this rally will depend on whether corporate earnings improve and global uncertainties continue to ease. Any fresh rise in crude oil prices or geopolitical tensions could lead to volatility.
But, experts believe the medium-term outlook remains constructive, but some consolidation and intermittent volatility cannot be ruled out after the sharp recovery.
“One needs to understand that the market has seen two years and time correction and hence we would not be surprised if benchmark indices soon hit their record highs. The valuations have become more reasonable following the earlier correction backed by double digit EPS growth over next 2-3 years,” explains Sunny Agrawal, Head - Fundamental Research at SBI Securities.
What should you do?
The next big question in the minds of investors is: is it time to reassess and adjust their investment strategy? Does their portfolio require a fresh look and if yes, what are the money pockets to invest in?
According to experts, in the short term, investors should avoid chasing the rally and use market volatility to gradually accumulate quality stocks.
Sunny Agrawal says that investors holding underperforming companies with weak outlooks may use this opportunity to exit, while quality stocks should be retained.
“The focus should remain on quality-led rebalancing rather than aggressive portfolio restructuring. Investors should consider reducing exposure to expensive stocks where valuations have outpaced earnings, increasing allocation towards quality businesses with sustainable growth prospects, and diversifying excessive sector concentration,” he tells TOI.
According to him, the next phase of wealth creation is likely to be driven more by company-specific earnings growth than by a broad-based market re-rating.
“We prefer businesses delivering sustainable 15–20% earnings growth at reasonable valuations, backed by strong balance sheets and credible management execution,” he says.
SBI Securities’ expert recommends maintaining a largecap-oriented portfolio while selectively increasing exposure to quality midcaps and smallcaps.
“Long-term investors should focus on businesses benefiting from structural growth opportunities, particularly domestic capex, manufacturing, consumption, electrification and infrastructure development etc,” he says.
“Largecaps offer relatively valuation supported by earnings visibility and stability, while midcaps provide opportunities for higher earnings growth and alpha generation. Smallcaps should be approached cautiously, focusing on companies with consistent revenue growth, ROCE above 15%, manageable debt, strong cash flows and sound corporate governance,” he adds.
Tanvi Kanchan observes that on days when the Sensex rallied 2-2.5%, the smallcap index barely moved or in fact even fell!
“Large-caps offer the best combination of reasonable valuations and earnings visibility. Investors with a long term equity portfolio can look at allocation to large caps in 50%-55% which becomes the core of the portfolio,” she tells TOI.
“Midcaps offer selective opportunities where earnings growth is strong, smallcaps, one would be cautious. They have lagged this rally, valuations in many pockets are still stretched relative to earnings, and they are the most vulnerable if foreign flows reverse. A good MF allocation can include large and midcap categories to balance between two composite market caps,” she advises.
And finally, what sectors should investors focus on?
From a sector perspective, Somil Mehta, Head of Retail Research at Mirae Asset Sharekhan remains positive on banking, automobiles, healthcare, infrastructure and select consumer companies.
Tanvi Kanchan recommends financials, especially large private banks, autos, which just posted record October sales, and aviation and select consumption names where input costs fall with oil, and a contrarian position in Indian IT, which is drawing renewed interest as an alternative to global AI hardware stocks, though volatility there will stay high.
Sunny Agrawal of SBI Securities advises focus on auto, banks, capital market themes (wealth management, exchanges, stock broking, intermediaries), capital goods, specialty metals and metal products, consumption, electrical equipment, wires and cables, and industrial automation remain attractive, supported by the investment cycle in infrastructure, electrification, and digital capacity.
“Defence and aerospace manufacturing also offer long-term opportunities, although valuations warrant monitoring. Pharmaceuticals and select auto component manufacturers are other preferred areas. Investors should remain selective in chemicals, FMCG, and real estate, where earnings visibility and valuations vary across companies,” he says.
Tanvi Kanchan concludes by saying that in the long term, the case for Indian equities is intact, and arguably stronger than it was in February.
Corporate earnings are recovering, valuations are more reasonable than in 2024, and India has shown it can attract foreign capital even in a volatile world.
“Investors should keep SIPs running regardless of market levels. This is exactly when discipline pays, because the investors who stopped SIPs in March, at the bottom, missed this recovery. So yes, it is a good time to review portfolios, but not to make dramatic changes. Readjust towards quality, rebalance where allocation has drifted, keep some liquidity for corrections for averaging inflows,” she says.
(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market, or any other asset classes or personal finance management tips given by experts and analysts are their own. These opinions do not represent the views of The Times of India.)

Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he'd lost coverage
Eli McCreary of Omaha, Neb., said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn't insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.
McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.
"You're required to do work to stay on," McCreary said a representative told him. "And you haven't fulfilled your work requirement."
For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
"I don't understand what job I can get," McCreary said. "I can't walk. I can hardly breathe. I can't move around. What job am I going to get?"
McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation's largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. "I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month," he said.
Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary's experience. In an emailed statement, she said that "CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources."
Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states are set to do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear if they will be successful, because Trump could veto it.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen said in December that state officials "certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform." Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.
"We're excited to be able to be the first to make it happen," the Republican governor said.
Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn't respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska's Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout "has been very successful." He pointed to state data showing 86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.
Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.
The high price of cutting benefits
About 70,000 adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they're working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.
To deploy the law's Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska's health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.
Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states, which outsource the work to companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska's health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.
The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.
One of the companies has praised Nebraska's implementation of work requirements. A post on Public Consulting Group's website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux.
"I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement," Michaux said, crediting the firm's "incredible relationship" with the state.
Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department "uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets."
Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don't know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have gotten inaccurate information. In December, Pillen said the state "won't be adding workforce" to implement the work requirements, a decision those advocates have criticized. Pillen in July also instituted a government-wide hiring freeze.
Nebraska listed at least half a dozen contractors costing more than $250,000 each, including one person whose compensation exceeds $1.8 million, the documents show. Nebraska submitted the records to federal Medicaid regulators as part of a routine process to secure federal money. Powell said the funding requests "may not reflect actual expenditures."
Sarah Maresh, a program director with the social justice advocacy nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed, said the amounts were "shocking."
"When you put in complicated policies like this, there are large corporations making money behind the scenes," Maresh said. "This just further confirms that it's happening in Nebraska quietly."
Confusion and longer wait times
The Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other changes shepherded by Republicans will curtail insurance gains that came from the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. The GOP tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade, adds reporting requirements and restrictions that make it harder for people to stay enrolled.
As of early July, most denials related to the work requirements among Nebraska adults applying for Medicaid were due to unsubmitted paperwork, according to internal documents from Nebraska's health department that KFF Health News obtained through a public records request. The state wrote this was "expected."
State data shows that average wait times at a Nebraska health department call center nearly doubled between May and July, going from about 13 minutes to 26 minutes, before declining in August. In interviews, advocates for Medicaid enrollees said they've encountered people who have waited on the phone for hours.
Nebraska received more than 101,000 calls in August, a 66% jump from May.
"If people are working, they just don't have time to be sitting on the phone to go through all of this stuff," said Kenny McMorris, CEO of the Charles Drew Health Center, a federally qualified health center in North Omaha. He said roughly half of Charles Drew's 13,385 patients are on Medicaid, and of those, 42% are subject to the work requirements.
"You can leverage the technology, but you still got to have people there to help," McMorris said.
Then there are experiences the official data may not catch, like what happened to McCreary — saddled with figuring out what happened with his Medicaid benefits amid a health crisis, and whether it was even true that he had to work to keep them.
McCreary had heard about the Medicaid work requirements but didn't know they might apply to him. Powell confirmed McCreary was eligible for Medicaid because of the ACA — putting him in the population subject to work requirements.
His ordeal underscores the fallout from being caught in confusing government systems and silos that aren't obvious to the public.
"This cancer ain't going to stop just because I ain't got insurance," he said. "It's going to keep working on me."
When he received the call from the hospital about his coverage, "I was really in despair," McCreary said. Eventually, he said, he called for help.
Nebraska's health department runs AccessNebraska, a call center for help with safety net benefits such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps. But the number McCreary recalls dialing ended up not being AccessNebraska — it was for a different call center, one for SNAP accounts that Nebraska outsources to a private company. Powell said the state has no record of McCreary calling the health department.
McCreary said the worker didn't have a good explanation for why the Medicaid work requirements would apply to him. Before his health deteriorated, McCreary worked as a driver for an asphalt services company. He said he worked "until I couldn't do the job anymore."
"I really had hoped to work longer," he said. "I kind of enjoyed that job."
Attorneys and policy professionals who work with people on Medicaid and other public benefit programs said that McCreary's substance use treatment, lasting four months starting in November 2025, and other health conditions should have exempted him.
The federal law outlines categories of exemptions, such as being too sick to work. People who are considered too ill include those who have a serious medical condition or a substance use disorder.
Nebraska's health department said it sent tens of thousands of letters, text messages and emails to inform enrollees about the new requirements. According to state documents, Nebraska said it would "implement enhancements" to its computer system and online portal, including allowing people to submit documents online and having "clear, plain-language" enrollee notices. McCreary, however, doesn't have an account on Nebraska Medicaid's online portal, preferring to handle things over the phone or in person.
He also said it's possible he missed letters from Nebraska Medicaid about his coverage.
"I don't know if it's my fault or not," McCreary said.
The Cornhusker State's experience could be a harbinger of things to come. Next year, work requirements will apply to millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states.
The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.
"We definitely had fun"
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid changes are the most complicated in years — changes that government benefit experts say will strain and exacerbate long-standing problems with state technology systems for health benefits.
"It's already a shaky system, and now you've added more burdens on top of that," said Gelila Selassie, director of health advocacy for the nonprofit Justice in Aging.
Nebraska and federal officials, as well as consultants advising the state, detailed the difficulties and successes with the state's May 1 launch during an August panel discussion at a national conference in Oregon.
"They said, 'We're going to go live May 1.' To which CMS said, 'Oh, my God!'" Brent Weaver, an official who specializes in Medicaid IT at the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said about Nebraska.
Nebraska officials knew "they weren't as agile as they probably would have liked to have been," Weaver said, "but they didn't let that stop them."
"If they fail, we looked at it as a failure," he added in comments that broadly praised the state's approach.
CMS did not answer questions from KFF Health News about Nebraska's rollout and Weaver's remarks.
In Nebraska, a group of 60 people held hours-long meetings three days a week that were "very exhausting," Michaux, of Public Consulting Group, said during a different session at the conference.
"Our calendars were cleared, and that was the focus," Michaux said.
Because CMS had not yet issued regulations outlining key details such as how people could get exemptions — it would do so June 1 — Nebraska officials said they had to rely on the law's broad language to make initial decisions.
"We had to get comfortable being uncomfortable," Jacob Kawamoto, a deputy director at Nebraska's Medicaid division, said at the conference.
Public Consulting Group said it worked with the state to develop new guidance and "process guides" — materials for Nebraska eligibility workers with instructions on how to process Medicaid applications or renewals. Training materials for Nebraska caseworkers reviewed by KFF Health News refer to those guides.
"The training was very robust, and the process guides were very robust," Michaux said.
Maresh disagreed with that characterization. "There are gaps" in the state's training materials, she said, and caseworkers "are confused" about work requirements.
Public Consulting Group also helped the state institute changes to Nebraska's Medicaid IT system, according to the company. "We are preparing for future updates and enhancements," Michaux said.
In response to questions, Public Consulting Group spokesperson Alyssa Brown said the company "has supported Nebraska Medicaid via a broad range of consulting services since 2019, including work on federal and state compliance initiatives." She said Michaux "discussed" the process guides at the conference but Nebraska developed them. Similarly, Brown said the company did not develop training.
Federal taxpayers will largely bear the costs of implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid policies in Nebraska and elsewhere. Congress allocated $200 million in one-time funding to states. Under federal regulations, the U.S. government picks up most of the tab for state IT system changes, paying as much as 90% of the cost.
"Even though it was not so easy," Michaux said at the conference, "we definitely had fun standing up the Medicaid work requirement program."
Public Consulting Group's employees, Brown told KFF Health News, are "passionate about public service and helping our clients improve the lives of the people they serve."
Dropping Medicaid enrollment
As of August, roughly 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied benefits because of Medicaid work requirements. Most denials were because people did not respond to requests for information.
Nebraska's total Medicaid enrollment has declined by roughly 4,600 people since May, a drop of 1.4%, according to an August report.
As for McCreary, the Nebraska health department's Powell maintained he experienced "no lapses in coverage" and said he was disenrolled from Medicaid after turning 65. Despite what McCreary said he was told, Powell said Medicaid work requirements weren't the reason: He aged out of Medicaid and into Medicare before they could be applied to him.
Selassie, from the nonprofit Justice in Aging, said McCreary's care shouldn't have been disrupted.
McCreary is now enrolled in Medicare, and Medicaid covers some of his health costs. He was able to reschedule his canceled appointments.
"The cancer has grown so much," he said.
He had surgery in early November to remove his right kidney.
KFF Health News correspondent Samantha Liss contributed to this report.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

The sound of firecrackers filling the air is not far away as Deepavali draws closer. But the excitement of bursting firecrackers comes with a word of caution from ophthalmologists as they warn that a moment of carelessness can cause eye injuries ranging from minor abrasions to severe ocular trauma.
M. Elangovan, director, Regional Institute of Ophthalmology and Government Ophthalmic Hospital (RIO-GOH), Chennai, said that there are different types of crackers. “Bursting types (explosive crackers) will produce irregular, small and forcible particles in all directions and are the most dangerous. These particles can travel at such a velocity that they could hit or penetrate any soft surface. Then, there is direct heat injury caused by crackers such as sparklers that can cause scar formations in the cornea or conjunctiva due to the heat generated. Sudden and close exposure to bright light-emitting crackers can also cause bleaching or temporary blackout due to the impact on the rod and cone cells in the retina,” he explained.

Dipke gets exemption from in-person appearance before magistrate on medical grounds
The SEM at Mandir Marg police station allowed the exemption on Tuesday after Abhijeet Dipke’s counsel cited medical grounds for his absence.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has been granted an exemption from appearing in-person before the special executive magistrate (SEM) regarding the preventive inquiry against him.
The SEM at Mandir Marg police station allowed the exemption on Tuesday after Dipke’s counsel, Abhik Chimni, cited medical grounds for his absence. The matter has been posted for December 2 for further proceedings.
During the proceedings, Chimni was also provided copies of the “kalandra” (preventive police report) and other legal documents that the Delhi Police relied on to issue Dipke a show-cause notice, asking him to furnish a bond for maintaining peace.
ALSO READ: CJP’s Abhijeet Dipke says he spent night at airport on way back from Kochi protest
This development comes weeks after Dipke was granted conditional bail by an SEM following his arrest over an alleged breach of a peace bond he furnished earlier. One principal condition imposed on him was that he must ensure no breach of peace on his part for a period of one year.
Dipke was detained on October 16 while heading towards Connaught Place for a protest march called by the CJP under the banner of ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’. The march was called despite a Delhi Police notice asking him not to participate, citing prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
He was subsequently arrested on October 17 for allegedly violating a peace bond furnished on October 10. He was later released on a conditional bail bond by the special executive magistrate. The bond was intended to secure an undertaking from him to maintain peace and prevent any disturbance to public order for a year.

Breast cancer begins long before the lump: why diet and lifestyle matter
While genetic predisposition is one factor, a majority of breast cancers develop in women with no family history: metabolic health and physical inactivity play a role too, and it is important for women to know about these factors
Students seen taking part in a ‘Pink Umbrella’ walk to create awareness on breast cancer. Image used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: VELANKANNI RAJ B
Last month, celebrated as Breast Cancer Awareness Month, reminded us, as it does every year, about the importance of mammograms, early diagnosis, and advances in treatment. These messages save lives and deserve continued attention. However, there is another conversation that often receives far less attention: the role of food, physical activity, obesity, diabetes, physical activity, and metabolic health in breast cancer.
In my oncology clinic, patients are often surprised when I bring up these topics. They say, “Doctor, I knew breast cancer was related to family history. I didn’t know that lifestyle diseases such as diabetes and obesity had anything to do with it.”

Spain's first general strike in 14 years demands solutions to housing crisis
BARCELONA, Spain — Less than three weeks before a national election that could catapult the far right to power, millions of Spain's workers are striking on Wednesday to demand that the government remedy the nation's housing crisis.
The general strike — Spain's first in 14 years — is causing delays in the public transport system and slowing down factories across the eurozone's fourth-largest economy. Many schools and universities reportedly closed or are working at minimal capacity. In the capital, Madrid, this adds to an ongoing strike started by teachers nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions.
In Barcelona, the country's second-largest city, public transport was at a standstill or facing long delays in the morning rush hour. In Madrid, which saw heavy rains in the morning, city buses were the hardest affected. Unions have called for Madrid workers to gather and march through the city center later Wednesday. Marches and gatherings are also planned in Barcelona and other cities.
The two main unions calling for the strike, UGT and CCOO, said in a statement that there was widespread participation, "with significant work stoppages in strategic sectors" — 90% in the automotive and port sectors, 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection, and 75% in the energy sector.
"It's extremely important to remind people that we, the workers — who are also renters or who also pay mortgages — are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill," Sandra Mora, spokesperson for the Tenants' Union, told the national radio, RNE.
Minor incidents were reported in the first hours of the strike, including roadblocks — some with burning tires — in Barcelona, and scuffles between picketers and police near the country's main wholesale market on Madrid's outskirts.
Earlier, at the stroke of midnight on Wednesday, striking workers set off fireworks as they gathered in public squares in Barcelona.
Workers and activists want more government action on housing
Wednesday's walkout has brought together workers, activists, politicians and ordinary Spaniards around the same interests — accessible housing. The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters.
"There is one issue that is dividing the country: the struggle to access housing," said Unai Sordo, secretary general of CCOO, on Cadena Ser radio.
Public anger over housing reached a boiling point following the nationally televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last month. The subsequent death of Maricarmen, as the woman became known, caused even more indignation and solidified her as a symbol of Spaniards who feel they pay too much in rent and can't even dream of homeownership.
Housing activists leveraged the uproar over Maricarmen's eviction to call for the general strike. They soon won the backing of the UGT and CCOO unions.
The housing activists want several measures, including the elimination of tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation and protection for renters in the form of automatic renewals of leases.
The UGT and CCOO unions are demanding more government intervention in the housing market and a new minimum wage agreement through talks with the business owners' association.
Spain's left hopes to put focus back on housing
The nationwide protests over the eviction of Maricarmen propelled Spain's government to push through emergency measures to limit evictions and help tenants, but right-wing parties in the Parliament refused to ratify them on the grounds they would provoke a flight of properties from the rental market.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez responded by doubling down politically and called the election on Oct. 5, hoping to earn four more years in power for his left-wing coalition.
But then came a brutal high-speed train collision — Spain's second deadly rail disaster of the year. That collision, which killed 69 people, has dominated Spanish news and created a drag on Sánchez's campaign just when he had hoped to build momentum.
The strike — with its official slogan "Salaries. Housing. Prices." — is an opportunity for Sánchez's Socialists and the other parties on the Left that he will need to remain in power, analyst Oriol Bartomeus said.
"The Socialists need for the strike to be a success and for there not to be any violence so that the election campaign can swing back to being about housing," Bartomeus, a professor of political science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, told The Associated Press.
On Thursday, the government will again try to have a reduced interim Parliament ratify the two housing decrees that the full lower chamber rejected last month.
Sánchez posted a long video on social media this week, in which he lauded the prior social policies like the 40-hour work week and national health insurance that were the fruit of the workers' movement and the right to strike.
"It wasn't easy, but they changed Spain," Sánchez said, while warning that right-wing parties would bring austerity and underfunded social services.
Verónica Martínez, spokesperson for Sumar, the junior member of the government, separately said "the Left needs the workers of this country to mobilize. Rights are first won on the streets and then later in the institution."
The right could benefit if the strike turns ugly
The traditional conservative Popular Party and the far-right Vox are against any government intervention in the housing market other than incentivizing construction of new homes.
They also both argue that the unions are trying to help Sánchez stay in office, with months of polling showing voters leaning toward the Right.
"This strike is not a general strike; it is an electoral strike," Popular Party spokesperson Miguel Tellado said Tuesday.
If the strike descends into violence, right-wing parties, which already have joined forces to govern in some Spanish regions, could benefit, Bartomeus said.
Spain, like other European countries, often has peaceful public protests that radical groups take advantage of to clash with police and destroy property.
"The Popular Party and Vox both want the strike to be a flop and to end in scenes of burning dumpsters and shattered shop windows," said Bartomeus, so that the next morning, "they can say, 'This is chaos and we are coming to establish order.'"

Gurugram bans coal, wood-fired tandoors at hotels and eateries under revised GRAP norms to curb pollution
Under the revised provisions of the GRAP issued by the CAQM, only equipment powered by electricity, gas, or other approved clean fuels may now be used.
District Magistrate and Gurugram Deputy Commissioner Uttam Singh has issued orders to prohibit the use of coal and wood as fuel in tandoors at all hotels, restaurants, and open-air eateries across the district in an effort to combat air pollution.
Under the revised provisions of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) issued by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), only equipment powered by electricity, gas, or other approved clean fuels may now be used in these establishments. This order is effective immediately, an official said.

According to an official statement, the district magistrate has directed the Municipal Corporation of Gurugram, the Municipal Corporation of Manesar, the relevant officials of the Haryana State Pollution Control Board, and other concerned departments to ensure strict compliance with these orders.
All sub-divisional magistrates will also coordinate with the respective municipal bodies and enforcement agencies to ensure the effective implementation of these orders.

The district magistrate has requested that officials conduct regular inspections, take action against any violations, and submit daily reports detailing inspections, violations, and actions taken.
He has also appealed to the general public and the operators of business establishments to cooperate with the administration in this campaign to reduce air pollution.
Operators of hotels, restaurants, and eateries must strictly refrain from using prohibited fuels and ensure that only equipment utilising approved, clean-burning fuels is used in their establishments.

On Nov. 6, after Republicans lost the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, purported footage of U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., spread in which he was unresponsive when a reporter asked for his reaction to the GOP's losses and whether he thought "Republicans would get anything done in the lame-duck session."
In the clip, McConnell, seated in a wheelchair, stared ahead, blinking a few times while someone (possibly an aide) spoke to the reporter off-camera. McConnell briefly glanced at the reporter.
Posts on X (archived), Facebook and YouTube sharing the video questioned the state of McConnell's health. (The senator had been hospitalized for several months earlier in 2026.)
The footage, which appeared on Newsmax show "Frontline" on Nov. 6, is authentic and was taken by Newsmax reporter Kilmeny Duchardt on Capitol Hill. There is no visible manipulation with artificial intelligence or other digital editing tools. As such, we rate this claim as true.
Snopes reached out to McConnell's staff to learn more about his health and his reaction in the video. We will update this post if we learn more.
On Nov. 6, "Frontline" host Carl Higbie shared the clip of McConnell on his show. The footage is available on Newsmax as well as YouTube.
Off screen, someone interrupted Duchardt, who said, "OK, no problem," suggesting she was interacting with the senator's aide.
Higbie reacted to the video saying, "That can't be legal, he's a vegetable!" He asked Theo Wold, a former assistant attorney general under President Donald Trump, for his reaction. Wold said:
This isn't just an ideological conflict for the soul of the Republican Party now, it is a generational one. We are tired of the geriatric gerontocracy ruling the conservative movement … the idea that [Republican Sen. Thom Tillis] and these folks now want to negotiate on things like amnesty with the Democrats. Look, you can't negotiate with a tiger when your face is inside of its mouth, OK? And what we need now are fighters who are not wheelchair-bound, but who can actually stand on their own two feet.
Over the years, Snopes readers have frequently asked us if the senator is dead or dying. Snopes has reported on many rumors about McConnell's health, including investigating a claim the U.S. government paid for his polio treatment.

It would be naive to think that getting listed on quick commerce platforms is half the battle won. If anything, that’s where the real battle begins. Building sales velocity, keeping products in stock, managing sky-high platform costs, and, believe it or not, we have barely peered into the abyss. Gramiyaa, a premium cold-pressed edible oil brand, learnt this the hard way when it boarded the quick commerce bandwagon through Blinkit in 2024. The first hurdle was affordability. When Gramiyaa finally made it onto quick commerce platforms, it found itself paying nearly twice the commission its national competitors paid. For a small brand already operating on razor-thin margins, that was a steep price to pay just to get a foot in the door. On top of that, the brand had to set aside a hefty advertising budget, only to burn through it while learning the ropes and figuring out how to make the channel work. After weathering several battles, including pricing wars between platforms, Gramiyaa has managed to turn the tables. Today, quick commerce is its largest revenue contributor, accounting for 35% of its ₹5 Cr monthly recurring revenue (MRR). So, how did Gramiyaa navigate these hurdles and turn quick commerce from a costly gamble into its biggest revenue driver? In an exclusive conversation for The Quick Commerce Code by Inc42 and Nitro Commerce, Gramiyaa cofounder Mohamed Yaseen shed light on what worked for the brand, how it managed to bring down platform commissions, and the dos and don’ts for emerging D2C brands looking to crack quick commerce. Why Gramiyaa Had To Look Beyond Its D2C Playbook Founded by three friends, Mohamed Yaseen, Naveenrajamaran RL and Sibi Manivannan, Gramiyaa’s journey began in 2018 as a local offline business. Manivannan’s grandfather ran an oil mill, and Manivannan wanted to breathe new life into the family business, which sold unbranded oil in PET bottles through five to six retail shops in Chennai. While these shops brought in ₹15-20 Lakh a month, high rents and operating costs ate into the earnings. Besides, each store could only cater to customers in its immediate neighbourhood, leaving little room for growth. “We had a very stable audience, but were not moving anywhere in terms of growth,” Yaseen told Inc42. In 2022, Yaseen and Naveenrajamaran RL joined Manivannan, and the three decided to build a new company. Gramiyaa was born. The founders initially took the D2C route, selling through their own website and setting up small warehouses across four metros to deliver orders within a day. They also looked beyond India, tapping distributors that catered to the Indian diaspora in the US, to take their products overseas. This gave the company a small but high-margin revenue stream. “However, this was not enough, even though we were doing quite well from our website,” Yaseen said. As a brand selling only cold-pressed oils, Gramiyaa could attract only so many customers to its own website. To reach a wider audience, the founders decided to list their products on Amazon in November 2022. But this came with an unexpected trade-off. Instead of bringing in only new customers, Amazon began eating into Gramiyaa's existing D2C sales. Customers who previously bought from its website started ordering through the marketplace, where the brand earned less on every sale. With its own website offering limited room for growth and Amazon eating into margins, the founders began looking for another avenue to scale, and quick commerce seemed like the obvious next step. The High Cost Of Breaking Into Quick Commerce The founders were convinced that quick commerce was a channel they could no longer afford to ignore. But wanting to get on board and actually making it happen were two different things. For nearly a year, the Gramiyaa founders remained hesitant. The reason? Blinkit and Instamart's steep commissions. With the brand operating on a razor-thin profit margin of just 2-3%, the cost of entering quick commerce was simply too much. “This was one year of anxiety and worry. We wanted to do this but couldn’t,” Yaseen recalled. According to him, if a national cooking oil brand paid a commission of X to a quick commerce channel, a premium oil from a national brand paid about 1.5X. And Gramiyaa, a small and unproven brand, had to pay twice as much. However, Yaseen argues that quick commerce is not necessarily more expensive than other distribution channels. Consider a product selling for ₹400, where the brand needs to retain ₹300. The remaining ₹100 goes towards platform margins and advertising on quick commerce. In traditional retail, a similar amount could be absorbed by distributor margins, retailer commissions and the cost of maintaining a sales team. The bigger challenge for smaller brands, therefore, is not just the cost of distribution, but having enough capital to absorb these expenses before the channel starts generating meaningful sales. The advertising commitment made the decision even harder. According to Yaseen, brands entering quick commerce with three to four SKUs may be expected to spend ₹5–10 Lakh a month on advertising, even before they have established consistent demand. For a business like Gramiyaa, which was operating on margins of just 2–3% at the time, committing such capital without any assurance of sales was a significant risk. The decision was eventually made, and the brand got listed on Blinkit in 2024. But after the listing, the channel remained loss-making for nearly six months. According to Yaseen, most brands that do reasonably well on quick commerce barely break even or lose money for six months to a year, and Gramiyaa was no exception. “Brands without the capital to absorb this often pause or shut down their quick commerce operations. Thankfully, we had raised funding by the time we went in,” said Yaseen. For Gramiyaa, the commissions came down once it proved that demand was pulling customers toward the platforms. When its sales grew from ₹5 Lakh a month to ₹10-15 Lakh and repeat purchases showed that some customers would switch apps, the platforms began treating it more like a large brand. “Our margins eventually moved gradually closer to what national brands paid,” Yaseen said. The One-City, One-SKU Strategy Behind Gramiyaa's Growth On ecommerce platforms like Amazon, Gramiyaa could ship products to customers anywhere in India from a central warehouse. How well a product ranked depended on how many people clicked on its listing and went on to buy it. Where those customers lived hardly mattered. Quick commerce, however, is a different ball game altogether. Here, what matters is how quickly a product is sold in a particular neighbourhood. The challenge becomes clearer at the dark-store level. A slow-moving product may get just one unit of inventory in a particular store. Once a customer buys it, the product can remain unavailable for the next 24–48 hours until it is replenished. Unless the product consistently sells in that locality, platforms have little reason to increase the inventory allocated to it. This creates a difficult cycle for smaller brands. Limited inventory leads to frequent stockouts, but without sustained sales velocity, securing additional inventory becomes equally difficult. Yaseen’s rule is that a brand with full confidence in a product in one city should launch there alone, rather than spread across four cities where it is only fairly sure. Within that city, the product has to sell quickly in at least half the dark stores before platforms begin stocking it more deeply. “Velocity is everything,” Yaseen said, adding that it was the hardest shift for Gramiyaa’s team. Its ecommerce managers were used to optimise listings and found it difficult to plan around availability in each locality. Yaseen took charge of the channel himself and pushed the team to learn how supermarkets and general trade distributors manage stock in each area. “I believe supermarkets have more in common with running a kirana counter than with running an Amazon listing,” said Yaseen. To understand where its products were selling and where they weren't, Gramiyaa began tracking performance city by city. An intern manually checked pin codes to see where its products appeared in search results and whether they were in stock. Today, the brand uses tools such as Nitro Commerce to track these metrics, with Yaseen checking the dashboard every morning. The exercise revealed two trends: In some areas, platforms weren't stocking Gramiyaa's products at all. In other areas, demand was strong enough for products to sell out quickly Armed with these data points, the brand began pushing platforms to stock more units wherever demand was high. The same data-driven approach helped Gramiyaa optimise advertising spend. Yaseen realised that the company was sometimes paying to promote products that were already ranking well organically on quick commerce apps. By tracking organic and paid share of voice at the SKU and city level, the team began redirecting advertising budgets towards products and locations where additional visibility could make a difference. This allowed Gramiyaa to make better use of its marketing budget rather than spending indiscriminately across products that were already generating sales. Over time, product availability became one of Gramiyaa's most important metrics. The brand now targets 90% on-shelf availability (OSA) and typically achieves 85-90%. According to Yaseen, even the category leader manages only 92-93% in its best month. And this is where Yaseen sees an opportunity for smaller brands. “When a leading brand runs out of stock, customers often turn to alternatives. If Gramiyaa is available at that moment and its product meets their expectations, it has a chance to win over a new customer,” the cofounder said. The Big Trade-Off: Pricing, Assortment And Availability Gramiyaa’s best-selling product on quick commerce is groundnut oil, and its best-selling size is one litre. At one point, it also listed half-litre bottles, a size only a few brands bet on. Yaseen expected it to work as a cheaper trial pack. At first, the half-litre pack made up 30% of groundnut oil sales. The team expected that share to fade, but it held. Today, the smaller half-litre packs account for about 15% of total sales volume, which is roughly 30% of its customers. This revealed an insight that its young and conscious customers cook occasionally, and others plan their groceries monthly, buy large packs on Amazon, and only use quick commerce when they run out a few days early. Adding smaller pack sizes seemed like a good way to attract more customers, but it came with a trade-off. Dark stores have limited shelf space and stock for each brand. If Gramiyaa stocked both half-litre and one-litre bottles, its inventory would be split between the two sizes. A competitor selling only one-litre bottles could stock more units of that size and stay available for longer. Yaseen decided to prioritise the larger pack, even if it meant losing customers who preferred smaller quantities. “If you’re the 20% of customers who won’t buy my brand without the half-litre, I will let go of you. But the 80% who buy my one-litre, I want it repeatedly available for them,” he said, advising new brands to start with a single SKU and choose a product category where larger brands have left a gap. Not every product decision worked out for Gramiyaa. Of the four oil products the brand introduced on quick commerce, one failed to gain traction because it could not be priced competitively. Yaseen acknowledged that the company had pushed ahead with a product despite knowing it was overpriced and not particularly suited to its core customer base in southern India. The experience reinforced that expanding an assortment does not necessarily translate into higher sales, especially when dark-store inventory is limited, and a poorly performing SKU can tie up resources better allocated to bestselling products. Pricing was another headache for Gramiyaa. Yaseen shared that platforms were changing the selling price of their products to match competitors. For example, if Instamart offered a discount on one of its SKUs, Blinkit was just going ahead to match that price for the next 20 days to recover its margins. At times, as Yaseen shared, platforms also asked Gramiyaa to cover the price difference. “We get caught between two giants fighting to acquire customers,” Yaseen said. These price fluctuations caused significant losses for Gramiyaa in its early months on quick commerce. It took the company nearly five to six months of negotiations to bring platform margins closer to each other and push back against pricing changes and penalties that were beyond its control. The pressure was compounded by competition from much larger FMCG players. Yaseen credits Tata with helping popularise the cold-pressed oil category, but its aggressive push has also intensified price competition. For a smaller brand like Gramiyaa, competing on discounts against national players with deeper pockets was never going to be a sustainable strategy. Yaseen believes that while a popular product such as groundnut oil can help a brand establish itself on quick commerce, its longer-term position will depend on building a presence in more differentiated categories. For Gramiyaa, this makes products such as coconut and sesame oil important, particularly in segments where larger FMCG companies may not be competing as aggressively. Today, Yaseen shared, Gramiyaa does not need to rely heavily on discounts to drive sales. At ₹350-750, a single one-litre bottle is expensive enough to qualify for a platform's free delivery threshold. The purchasing behaviour also works in Gramiyaa's favour. According to Yaseen, its customers typically reorder every 40–45 days and buy an average of 1.3-1.4 products per order, while ₹350 is an effective price point for the brand on quick commerce. Unlike lower-ticket products that may depend on being added to a larger grocery basket, a single bottle of Gramiyaa's oil can account for a substantial portion of the order value. Combined with repeat demand, this gives the brand an advantage in building consistent sales velocity. Gramiyaa's Next Quick Commerce Test Gramiyaa reported ₹18 Cr in revenue in FY25, which grew 61.1% to ₹29 Cr in FY26, with quick commerce the largest channel at 35%, or about ₹10.15 Cr. But this growth has come at the expense of profit. According to Yaseen, the brand was profitable in FY25. As of now, remaining profitable is the least of its concerns, as the company expects to burn for brand visibility and new channels. Recently, Gramiyaa raised ₹21 Cr as part of its ongoing Series A fundraise led by Optiscape Network Holdings, Homegrown Ventures, Campus Fund and others. The funds would be used to fuel its expansion in Tier II markets. For Gramiyaa, the next phase of quick commerce growth lies beyond India's metros. Yaseen believes the channel's appeal in Tier II cities is somewhat different from that in larger markets. Rather than simply promising delivery within minutes, quick-commerce platforms are increasingly offering consumers access to products that may not be readily available at their neighbourhood kirana stores. For a premium cold-pressed oil brand with limited offline distribution in these markets, that creates an opportunity to reach customers who might otherwise struggle to find its products locally. The company expects quick commerce to remain its largest revenue channel as it expands into these markets. However, Yaseen acknowledges that the next phase will depend on how successfully platforms penetrate smaller cities, particularly as growth in established metro markets begins to moderate. However, when asked about platforms prioritising their own labels over D2C brands, Yaseen does not see much competition there, as the brand operates in the premium category, selling to customers who prefer quality over price. But for founders considering the channel, Yaseen's advice is to wait. “Quick commerce should be built only after a brand has a core business on its website or an ecommerce platform like Amazon. They need to know their hero products, figure out pricing, and have strong liquidity from another channel or cash flow,” the cofounder stated, outlining the imperatives for newer brands stuck at the bottom of the pyramid. Gramiyaa avoided this trap, but the harder test of holding its position in Tier II cities is yet to come. Can it sustain demand in markets where premium purchases often take a backseat to essential spending?

You can’t blame people for shopping at Amazon during the holiday season, especially if they are Prime members (yay, two-day shipping). Unless you have qualms about buying from the retailer, Amazon’s Black Friday deals start on November 19—much sooner than the traditional day after Thanksgiving. But the company has already discounted many items ahead of its own sale, including things we’ve tested and recommend. You should wait for potentially bigger discounts during Black Friday, but if your wallet is itching, here are a few products that caught our attention.

Amazon Early Black Friday Tech Deals

This is the lowest price on Amazon; however, it has dropped to this price before. Note that Walmart and Best Buy are also offering the XM6 at this sale price.

GNA power row: Satheesan says no formal agreement signed
Thiruvananthapuram, Amid an escalating political row over the state's move to purchase electricity, Keralam Chief Minister V D Satheesan on Wednesday said no agreement had been signed with the private GNA platform for power purchase and questioned how the government could withdraw from a deal that was never formally entered into.
Appearing to hold a transferred KSEB Managing Director responsible for the move to procure power through GNA, Satheesan said the Kerala State Electricity Board had written to him warning that the state could face prolonged power cuts from November if no decision was taken on purchasing power.
"Later, another team examined the situation and said there was no such problem," he said.
Satheesan said that there were also news reports criticising the time he was taking to come out with a decision and questioned whether these were attempts to make him hurriedly sign the agreement with GNA.
"No one can force me to take a decision hurriedly by such tactics," Satheesan said, adding that he was not sitting on the file, but was "studying" the matter.
He made the remarks while responding to allegations surrounding the government's proposed power purchase through the GNA platform.
Satheesan, speaking at a press conference here after a cabinet meeting chaired by him, referred to the new reports and remarks by Leader of Opposition in the state assembly Pinarayi Vijayan that the government withdrew from the agreement with GNA, and said there was no contract with the private platform to begin with.
"There was no contract, so where is the question of withdrawing from it," he contended.
Vijayan, a day ago, had claimed that the recent power crisis in the state was created "artificially" by the UDF government to purchase power from a private entity at huge rates, the burden of which consumers will have to bear.
He had also claimed that the government later decided against purchasing power from GNA due to serious questions raised by the opposition regarding irregularities in the power deal and the potential for financial losses to the exchequer.
The LoP had also accused the CM of keeping state Electricity Minister Sunny Joseph in the dark regarding the entire matter.
Refuting the claims, Satheesan said that the Electricity Department sent him a file saying the state can either purchase power from the Himachal Pradesh government at around ₹14 or from GNA at around ₹8 per unit.
He said that the file also mentioned that the power from Himachal Pradesh has gone to Rajasthan by October 18 at a rate of over ₹15 per unit and therefore, the only option before the government was GNA.
"GNA was the better option also in comparison. Then we decided to examine if there was a requirement to buy power currently. The Electricity Minister was right when he said there was no requirement currently. Therefore, we decided not to purchase it," the CM contended.
He also claimed that the power cut crisis experienced by the state was due to the lack of long term planning or any electricity purchase agreement by the previous LDF government.
He said that during the last 10 years, the then LDF government did nothing to increase the state's power generation or set up battery storage units.
"The power we generate during the daytime is from the solar panels set up on rooftops of people's homes. But there is no option to store it, unlike in other states," he contended.
Instead, the then government was more interested in short-term purchase of power, instead of entering into a long-term agreement.
"Purchase of power from outside had become a culture," he contended.
Satheesan also said that even he, like Joseph, came to know that the government was withdrawing from the contract with GNA.
Joseph had told reporters on Monday that he came to know through news reports that the government was withdrawing from the agreement with GNA.
"How can we withdraw when there was no contract?" Satheesan asked.
He said that the government was planning to purchase power from GNA only till March 2027 as the National Thermal Power Corporation has promised to provide electricity at the rate of ₹5.18 per unit from its Sinnar plant in Maharashtra from April onwards.
He said that the government will enter into an arrangement with NTPC and attempts to increase the power that can be got from there.
The CM also contended that Vijayan was making contradictory statements.
"He in a recent press conference said we should purchase power from Himachal Pradesh and not a private entity. Now in his statement a day ago, he said there is no need to buy electricity as there is no requirement. He is making contradictory statements. Someone is not briefing him properly," he said.
Satheesan assured that the UDF government will come out with a permanent solution by the end of the month to address the power crisis issue.
It would involve increasing the renewable power production in the state, which currently only generates 15 per cent of its requirement and purchases the rest, setting up battery storage units to store the electricity generated through solar panels during the daytime and entering into a long term power purchase agreement.
He further assured that the government will purchase power at the cheapest available rates.

'Sandpapergate': Nasser Hussain calls Australia ball-tampering scandal 'a complete mess' after Usman Khawaja claims
Michael Atherton says Cricket Australia "left questions unanswered" with initial handling of incident eight years ago and that the players "not having each other's backs" will cause most "disquiet" among fans; Australia play England in eight white-ball matches from Friday
Wednesday 11 November 2026 12:32, UK
Sky Sports' Nasser Hussain has called the Australia 'Sandpapergate' affair and its subsequent explosive fallout a "complete mess".
The 2018 ball-tampering scandal in South Africa, in which Australia's Cameron Bancroft was caught on camera trying to use sandpaper on the ball in order to make it swing, has been catapulted back into the spotlight following the release of Usman Khawaja's book.
Former Baggy Greens batter Khawaja, who played in that infamous Cape Town Test, claims the entire team knew about the scheme and not just those banned, in Bancroft, then-captain Steve Smith and David Warner, who was deemed the architect.

Khawaja also said he was not quizzed at the time by Cricket Australia despite sitting next to Bancroft in the Newlands dressing room and that he urged the team to come clean and take collective responsibility before being talked out of it by Smith.
Speaking on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, former England captain Hussain said: "I think it's a complete mess.
"Let's be honest, for the history of the game, people have been trying to work out what to do with cricket balls to make it swing more, whether it be mints, sweets, throwing the ball to the ground on the bounce, Vaseline, dirt in pocket, whatever it might be.
"[But] how a side thought it was okay to take sandpaper out, how no one before that in a meeting went, 'I don't think this is okay, I don't think we're doing the right thing', how they thought they were going to get away with it with all the cameras around [I don't know].
"Then to lie about it after and for Cricket Australia not to speak to every player, not to speak to Khawaja who was sitting next to Bancroft. It just feels like a right mess.
"The team, the baggy green, the mateship and all that stuff - that was what playing Australia was like, so for an Australian team to say, 'no, it's just those three' when it was never going to be just those three [is surprising]."
'Worst of both worlds from Cricket Australia'
Hussain's fellow analyst, Michael Atherton, is currently in Australia ahead of England's white-ball tour of the country, which begins with the first ODI in Perth on Friday (3.30am UK time).
Atherton will attend what he anticipates being a "circus" of a press conference on Thursday as Australia white-ball captain Mitchell Marsh - the only player to have figured in the Newlands Test in 2018 in the hosts' squad to tackle England - fronts up.
Usual ODI skipper Pat Cummins has been rested, along with Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, all three of whom were involved in the sandpaper Test and released a joint statement back in 2021, with spinner Nathan Lyon, denying prior knowledge of the plot.
Sky Sports pundit Atherton was critical of Cricket Australia's handling of the situation eight years ago, saying it was always "going to come back to haunt them".
Smith and Warrner were banned for a year after 'Sandpapergate' with Bancroft suspended for nine months.
Atherton, who does not see a need for a new investigation to be opened following Khawaja's claims, said: "It was almost like the sandpaper was the straw that broke the camel's back.
"It was on the back of the team having become, and Khawaja talks about it in his book, slightly out of control, a bit unlikable and with a kind of win-at-all costs mentality.
"Then it was the worst of both worlds.
"They handed down unbelievably heavy sanctions - I thought hard-to-justify sanctions - and left three players to take the rap. But it left questions unanswered, left the door open for it to come back to haunt them, which it is doing now.
"It was eight years ago and there will be a weariness around the story eventually, because it's all over every newspaper, podcast, whatever.
"But I do think the particular point about not having people's backs is the thing causing the most disquiet [in the Australia public] and will rumble on for a while yet."
Atherton: Cracks in the Australia team
Australia have also toiled on the field, losing 2-1 in South Africa in their first Test series in the country since the ball-tampering scandal, with the out-of-form Marnus Labuschagne now dropped for the impending home clashes with New Zealand.
Amid a relentless Test calendar that then features a five-match assignment in India, the day-night 150th anniversary Test against England in Melbourne in March, and an away Ashes series in June and July, Atherton feels the Baggy Greens are in a tough spot.
He added: "The schedule is brutal and unforgiving and already there's cracks in that team.
"It doesn't feel as though the team is robust enough to get through this period.
"This [the ball-tampering claims] is adding a little bit more fuel to the fire."
