One of the biggest reasons most people use WhatsApp, besides the fact that their friends or family are already on it, is that it is free to use. And since Meta owns it, free usually comes with a caveat. And that’s your data and how Meta tracks your WhatsApp chats. Although your chats are encrypted and Meta openly says it won’t use your data for advertising, you can talk to a friend on WhatsApp and still see relevant ads on other Meta platforms like Instagram instantly. Don’t you believe me? Just try it once.
Fortunately, WhatsApp also offers various privacy settings to keep your conversations private, prevent scams, and more. In this ultimate guide, we’ll cover all the privacy settings you need to enable on WhatsApp for maximum privacy. This guide includes all the methods, and I update it frequently and make changes if the features or flow change. Bookmark this page and revisit it anytime to keep your WhatsApp privacy settings up to date.
Table of Contents
WhatsApp Privacy Settings You Should Enable
Hide your Last Seen and Online status
If you care about your privacy and don’t want your people to know when you were online and when you last used the app, WhatsApp allows you to hide the last seen and online status completely
By default, WhatsApp shows the exact time when you last used the app and shows users when you are actually using the app
While these two features let others know when you use WhatsApp, they can also be a downside, especially if others are expecting an immediate reply when they see you online
Fortunately, WhatsApp lets you disable your last seen and completely hide your status. It also gives you more flexibility by letting you hide these from specific contacts, from your contacts, or disable them entirely for everyone.
Here is how to hide your last seen and online status on WhatsApp:
Open WhatsApp on your Android or iPhone and tap the You tab in the bottom-right corner, then tap Privacy.
Now scroll down and, under Who can see your personal info, tap Last seen and online. To hide it from everyone, select Nobody. To show it only to my contacts, select My contacts; to show it only to specific contacts, tap My contacts except.
Hide your profile photo, About, and Links from strangers
Like Last Seen and online status, WhatsApp also shows your profile picture and About to contacts. This also applies to contacts you have outside your network.
Fortunately, like Last Seen and Online Status, WhatsApp also lets you hide your profile photo and About info from strangers, specific contacts, or no one.
How to hide your profile and About from strangers
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, then tap on Privacy, and then tap on the Profile Picture option
Now you can hide your profile picture, About, and links. To hide it from everyone, set it to Nobody.
If you want to share with all your contacts, select My contacts. To share your profile picture only with specific contacts, tap My contacts except and select the contacts you want to hide your profile picture, About, and links from.
Control who can see and reshare your Status
WhatsApp’s status feature is slowly turning into Instagram Stories. You can now also reshare statuses on WhatsApp. However, unlike Last Seen, this feature is disabled by default.
If you accidentally enabled it and don’t want others to share your status, you can turn off sharing in the status privacy settings. From there, you can also turn off Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your WhatsApp status from being shared on other platforms.
How to turn off status sharing on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, and from here tap on the privacy option
Scroll down, tap Status, then turn off Allow sharing and set your status to be visible only to my contacts. You can also remove specific people by setting up exceptions for contacts, or you can share only with specific contacts. From the bottom, also disable Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your status from automatically sharing to Facebook and Instagram Stories.
Turn off read receipts
Even if you hide your online status and last seen on WhatsApp, read receipts can still show blue checkmarks when you read their messages. However, if you don’t want them to know you have read their messages and feel pressured to reply instantly, or if you want better privacy and to balance work and personal WhatsApp chats, you can disable read receipts.
Remember, if you disable it, you also cannot see whether they have read your messages. WhatsApp only shows grey ticks even if you read their messages.
Here is how to turn off read receipts on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture. Scroll down and tap Privacy. Scroll down again and turn off Read Receipts.
Stop strangers from adding you to groups
Another feature that WhatsApp turns on by default is the ability to let your contacts add you to any groups. This includes the number you have temporarily shared with users you don’t know, and once you add it to the group, your number will be shared with everyone in that group, which is a total privacy nightmare.
Fortunately, WhatsApp allows you to stop random people from adding you to groups.
How to stop people from adding you to random groups
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, then tap on the privacy option
Scroll down and tap on Groups, then select who can add you to groups. However, WhatsApp doesn’t let you set nobody as an option, but you can still do it by selecting My contacts except and selecting all contacts.
Silence calls from unknown numbers
Since WhatsApp primarily requires your phone number to create an account, once your number is exposed, anyone can contact you on WhatsApp. This is why many of us often receive spam business calls.
However, you can silence unknown calls so that you won’t get notified of random spam calls.
How to silence unknown callers on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp, tap on your profile picture, and tap on the privacy option
Now scroll down, tap on Calls, and enable the Silence unknown callers option
Make new chats disappear automatically
WhatsApp now supports disappearing messages, which deletes chats from both the sender and receiver after a set time. WhatsApp allows you to enable disappearing messages for individual chats or for the entire WhatsApp for up to 90 days
This is especially useful if you don’t want the other person to save your chats.
Since WhatsApp keeps your messages forever even if you delete your own copy, the other person’s phone still has everything.
When you turn on disappearing messages, WhatsApp also prevents the other person from taking a screenshot and reminds you when they try to save a specific chat.
How to enable disappearing messages on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, then tap Privacy. From here, tap on Default message timer and select how many days you want to set for WhatsApp. You can select up to 90 days or even 24 hours.
If you want to turn on disappearing messages for individual chats, open the new chat and tap on the three-dot menu on the top right corner of the screen, select disappearing messages, and select the timer
Keep WhatsApp photos out of your gallery
By default, WhatsApp saves all photos you receive to your media gallery, including sensitive and personal ones. Even if you lock WhatsApp, anyone can see the photos you received by opening your phone gallery. This also uses your data to automatically download them and increases your storage usage.
WhatsApp allows you to turn off automatic media download and also lets you stop showing media directly from your photos app
How to stop WhatsApp from automatically saving media
First, you can turn off automatic media downloads. To do that, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then scroll down and tap Storage and data.
From there, scroll down and tap Media auto-download, then select all three: when you are using mobile data, when you are connected to Wi-Fi, and when roaming. Then disable all download options, including photos, audio, video, and documents. This prevents files from auto-downloading on Wi-Fi, mobile data, or while roaming.
How to stop WhatsApp from showing media in your device gallery
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, scroll down, tap Chats, then under Chat settings, disable Media visibility.
Turn on two-step verification with a password
WhatsApp also supports two-step verification to prevent your account from getting hacked. While WhatsApp sends a six-digit SMS code for verification, someone with access to that code can log in to your WhatsApp account. However, you can set a second verification method, such as a password, to prevent anyone from accessing your WhatsApp.
Here is how having two-factor authentication adds better security for your WhatsApp account.
Here is how to set two-step verification with a password on WhatsApp
First, open your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, tap on account option, and tap on Password
Now create a new password. Tap Create password and create a new password.
Once you add two-factor authentication, remember to add a recovery email. This is especially useful if you lose your network; your email acts as a secondary verification method, where WhatsApp sends a code to your email instead of sending a verification SMS.
Create a passkey for phishing-proof login
WhatsApp also added support for passkeys; if you’re not sure what a passkey is, we have explained it in a detailed guide.
Passkeys use your fingerprint or Face ID for authentication instead of depending on SMS or passwords. Setting up passkeys lets you log in to your WhatsApp account using your device ID, which is unique to you.
But it also comes with downsides: if someone else has registered a Face ID or fingerprint, they can also log in to your WhatsApp account, so keep note of it.
How to enable passkeys for your WhatsApp account
To enable passkeys, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then tap Account. From here, under the Login and Security section, tap on Passkeys. Then follow the on-screen instructions to create a passkey.
Turn on security notifications
Next, enable security notifications on your WhatsApp account so WhatsApp notifies you if someone switches phones, reinstalls WhatsApp, or changes linked devices. This could also mean someone else accessed their WhatsApp account and signed in on a new device. Turn on security notifications and confirm with the other person why the security key changed.
How to enable security notifications on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp on your phone. Tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Account. Scroll down, tap Security notifications, and turn on the option that says Show security notifications on this device.
Check linked devices and log out unknown sessions
WhatsApp lets you link and use your account on multiple devices. However, this could also mean someone could link your account to their device without you knowing. So, if you are suspicious about your account activity, you can check linked devices and sign out of any you don’t recognize.
How to check linked devices and log out of unknown devices on your WhatsApp account
Lock WhatsApp with your Biometrics
WhatsApp includes a native app lock feature that lets you lock it with your fingerprint or a pattern. WhatsApp also lets you lock immediately or after a set time. WhatsApp also recently rolled out a new feature to lock WhatsApp Web chats. So, I have made a detailed guide on how to lock WhatsApp on WhatsApp Web. You can watch the video below or follow the detailed steps in this guide.
How to lock your WhatsApp account with your fingerprint or Face ID
Lock and hide your most private chats
WhatsApp also lets you lock individual chats, not just the app. This way, you can lock or hide your most private chats. Here is how.
However, Locked Chat uses your device’s biometrics to lock chats. And if you cannot unlock the chat for any reason, you cannot get those messages back. Your only option is to clear the messages and unlock the chat, which you can do by going to Settings > Privacy, tapping Chat Lock, and tapping Clear Chat Lock. To lock the chats, follow the guide below.
Open WhatsApp on your device and, if you want to lock multiple chats on the home screen, select the chats you want to lock, tap the three-dot menu, and tap Lock chat. You can also do it for individual chats right here only.
Turn on Advanced chat privacy for sensitive chats
While disappearing messages remove your chat after a set period, you can turn on Advanced Chat Privacy for chats with sensitive content. This stops the other user from sharing or exporting your chats, and the media used in the chat won’t be saved in that person’s gallery. It also blocks the new Meta AI used in the chat itself.
Here is how to turn on Advanced Chat Privacy on WhatsApp
Hide your IP address in calls
WhatsApp also supports voice calls. Direct calls can connect your phone to another person’s phone, which can reveal your IP address and, in turn, your location. However, WhatsApp allows you to hide your IP during calls. Here is how.
How to protect your IP address in calls
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Privacy. Then scroll down, tap on Advanced, and enable the option that says ” Protect IP address in calls.
Disable link previews
WhatsApp also supports link previews, which show a preview of the website content. However, to do that, your phone connects to your website and sends a request from your IP address.
So it can easily reveal your phone’s IP address to the website, along with your location. You can also turn off link previews, which prevents those fancy images websites use for spam calls.
How to disable link previews on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Scroll down and tap on Privacy. From here, scroll down again, tap Advanced, and enable Disable link previews.
Block floods of messages from unknown accounts
WhatsApp also introduced a new feature that blocks messages from unknown accounts. It blocks unknown accounts that send you high volumes of messages, which is especially useful if you receive frequent spam texts or your WhatsApp is being bombed with multiple messages.
How to block a flood of messages from unknown accounts
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Tap Privacy, then tap Advanced again, and turn on the option that says Block unknown account messages.
Encrypt your chat backup
WhatsApp relies on Google Drive for your WhatsApp backup and iCloud on iPhone. However, by default, your chat backup isn’t encrypted.
You can turn on end-to-end encrypted backup with a passkey, password, or 64-digit key so third-party servers, including Google, can’t read your backup.
Here is how to encrypt your chat backup on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Chats. From here, scroll down and tap Chat backup, then scroll down again and tap End-to-end encrypted backup.
Here, you can turn it on and then use your passkey. Remember, you’ll need this passkey whenever you back up your WhatsApp with this data. You can also use a password or a 64-digit key.
Limit what Meta AI can do with your data
Like any other app, Meta also offers AI features that let you summarise and read messages and also chat with Meta AI. However, because these AI chatbots can’t use your data publicly, Meta uses Private Processing features, which it says process your data privately for those AI features.
However, both of the AI features, including Private Processing features and web search, where Meta AI can search the web based on your queries, are turned off by default. If you turn them on, you can turn them off by default to prevent Meta AI from using your data, even though it is processed privately.
Here is how to turn off the private messaging feature and that switch on WhatsApp
Reserve a username to keep your number private
Recently, WhatsApp introduced usernames on the platform, so instead of your phone number, you can create and share a username and let others contact you through it.
However, your phone number still verifies your account, but for better privacy, you don’t need to reveal it when sharing your WhatsApp account with others. You can also restrict who can message you using your username through a secondary verification method. I have covered in detail how to find your WhatsApp username.
How to reserve a username on WhatsApp?
Use Strict account settings if you’re a high-risk target
If you are a journalist, activist, or public figure, Meta offers Strict Account Settings to help protect your account’s security and privacy. Here is a clear breakdown of the difference between standard settings and Strict Account Settings and how to enable strict account settings for your WhatsApp account.

Run the built-in Privacy Checkup
WhatsApp privacy settings can be confusing for beginners since the platform is used by people of all ages. However, WhatsApp also offers a built-in Privacy Checkup tool that provides a step-by-step process to help you enhance your WhatsApp account’s privacy.
It includes details such as choosing who can contact you, controlling your personal info, the ability to add more privacy to your chats, adding more protection to your account, and much more
This privacy checkup offers detailed, step-by-step instructions to help you enable important privacy settings. If you find any steps in this guide confusing, you can use this tool.

In November, a claim (archived) circulated online that the U.S. Air Force had held Maj. Jason Watson, an active-duty airman who publicly called for the impeachment of President Donald Trump, in solitary confinement for more than 80 days while he awaited court-martial.
CNN reported that the Air Force ordered Watson into "pre-trial confinement" on Aug. 18. Two days later, on Aug. 20, Watson's lawyer Christopher Mutimer told CNN that Watson was "basically in solitary confinement." He repeated this claim in early October, telling CNN (at 1:46, archived) that Watson was "still in solitary confinement."
One X user who claimed Watson remained in solitary confinement in early November — 84 days after the Air Force first ordered him into pretrial confinement — wrote:
Maj. Jason Watson has been in 24-hour solitary confinement for 80+ days & has reportedly lost 20 pounds, all before any trial. UN experts consider solitary beyond 15 days to be torture. He offered to resign, give up all his benefits, & the Air Force said no. Because he protested.
The claim also circulated on Facebook and Threads (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
Speaking to Snopes on Nov. 10, Mutimer confirmed Watson had been detained at Maryland's Calvert County Detention Center since Aug. 18 and described conditions that he said met generally understood definitions for solitary confinement.
Mutimer said Watson "is in a room by himself 22 to 23 hours a day. No one stays in there with him, he is not allowed to have any interaction. When he's let out it's to shower, make a phone call, get some time in the yard by himself." He described Watson's cell as a "pen" where "the light is on all the time."
The Air Force District of Washington, which the Air Force Press Office said handled questions about Watson, had not replied to a question from Snopes about whether it held Watson in solitary confinement at the time of this writing. Military.com reported that an Air Force spokesperson said on Oct. 14 that Watson had access to "exercise, the library, and personal hygiene items" in his pretrial confinement and that an agreement between the Air Force and Calvert County Detention Center required Watson to be held "separately" from convicted prisoners.
Mutimer corroborated the Air Force's October statement, saying in November, "Because he's an officer, he is in the military, that contract says he is not allowed to be with anybody who is not in the military."
Pending comment from the Air Force District of Washington on the conditions of Watson's confinement, we leave this claim unrated.
By November, the docket of the Air Force's military justice branch showed Watson was due for general court-martial in February. Mutimer said he would argue a petition for Watson's pretrial release on Nov. 17.
Mutimer also confirmed the claim some social media users made that Watson had attempted to resign after his July 1 arrest but said officials had denied his resignation and instead pressed ahead with the court-martial, a move that Mutimer described as "absolutely unheard of."
Tracking Watson's case
Capitol Police arrested Watson on July 1 on after he publicly called for Trump's impeachment while wearing his Air Force uniform. A live stream (at 50:56) of the arrest showed Watson standing on the Capitol steps in uniform while holding a sign that read "Impeach Convict Remove."
Watson said at a news conference earlier that day that he was calling for Trump to be impeached because he thought the president and Vice President JD Vance had governed in an unconstitutional way throughout their administration.
Watson highlighted the war in Iran, Elon Musk's sweeping cuts to federal government and the Department of Homeland Security's immigration crackdown and killings of protesters as "high crimes and misdemeanors" (at 28:28) for which "the president and vice president must be impeached, convicted, and removed."
The Air Force major repeated his call for Trump and Vance's removal while speaking to CNN's Erin Burnett (at 1:52) on Aug. 17. Burnett said (at 2:41) during the interview that the military had placed a "gag order" on Watson after his July 1 protest and that he was "under investigation."
According to a later CNN report, the Air Force took Watson into pretrial confinement days after he spoke to the network.
CNN reported that the Air Force charged Watson with 10 violations of three articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the military's legal framework, on Aug. 20. Mutimer reportedly spoke to Watson on that date and reported that he was "basically in solitary confinement."
On Sept. 29, The New York Times reported that an Air Force investigating officer had recommended Watson's case for general court-martial, the military's highest level of trial court.
According to the Judge Advocate General's Corps Department of the Air Force, which investigated and charged Watson, the major faced charges of four violations of articles 88, 92 and 133 of the UCMJ.
Article 88 (Page 34) of the UCMJ states that any commissioned officer who uses "contemptuous words" against certain public officials, which includes the president and vice president, should face a court-martial. Article 92 (Page 35) states that a person subject to the code that fails to obey an order or regulation can be subject to court-martial. Article 133 (Page 48) states that "Any commissioned officer, cadet, or midshipman who is convicted of conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman shall be punished as a court-martial may direct."
The code does not explicitly define what "conduct unbecoming an officer" means.
An Air Force spokesperson reportedly told Military.com in October that the Air Force had acted in accordance with the Rule for Court-Martial 305 when it took Watson into pretrial confinement in August. That rule says someone can be placed in pretrial confinement if there is probable cause they committed "an offense triable by court-martial."
That rule also says that someone taken into pretrial confinement can ask a military judge to review the "propriety" of the confinement, meaning whether it is appropriate. Mutimer said such a review for Watson would happen on Nov. 17.
According to the UCMJ's Article 13 (Page 5), it is prohibited to punish a service member awaiting trial. Any confinement before trial must not "be any more rigorous than the circumstances require to insure his presence, but he may be subjected to minor punishment during that period for infractions of discipline."
At the time of this writing, Watson had not been convicted or sentenced. Punishments for service members convicted by court-martial range from reprimands and salary reductions to dismissal or discharge.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated whether an active-duty soldier took part in an anti-immigration-enforcement protest.

The European Commission announced a sweeping set of updates to consumer law on Wednesday to protect European Union citizens from “harmful digital practices”—whether while online shopping, browsing social media, or doing their Duolingo lesson.
Within the package, the Commission unveiled its Digital Fairness Act to address harmful practices online. Proposed rules include banning dark patterns—practices which manipulate consumers into making decisions they would not otherwise make, such as falsely claiming a product is running low. They will also curb dynamic pricing by ticket retailers, like Ticketmaster; force influencers to disclose when they are being paid to promote a product; outrule personalized advertising and pricing targeting minors or taking advantage of sensitive data; make digital subscriptions easier to cancel; and give consumers a right to interact with human customer service.
The package “represents the most significant reform of EU consumer protection rules in more than 20 years” according to Michael McGrath, the EC Consumer Protection Commissioner, noting that existing consumer rules were developed before ecommerce, the attention economy, and use of personal data for marketing took off. “The digital fairness act will make sure the digital economy works for consumers and not against them,” he said at a press conference.
The bill will also enable all consumers to turn off addictive design features on digital services, such as autoplay of videos and streaks—including on apps like Strava and Duolingo.
Some of these patterns the EU has already restricted for children through its Kids Act, which in addition to banning under-13s from accessing social media and chatbots, targets addictive designs in those services. Some European rights groups have called for those protections to be extended to all consumers and, teasing the Digital Fairness Act in September’s State of the Union address, President Ursula von der Leyen said: “But it is not only minors who are at risk. Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone. That is why we need a wider framework.”
Some of the risks are also already regulated by the EU Digital Services Act. On Friday, the European Commission said ByteDance’s TikTok had breached those rules with the “rabbit hole effect” of its “For You” feed algorithm which personalizes content recommended to users. The tech regulator had previously found TikTok’s “addictive design” broke the rules by including features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, and push notifications, in addition to the algorithm. In July, it found Meta to be in breach of the act due to similar features on Instagram and Facebook. If confirmed, both companies may now face fines of up to 6 percent of worldwide annual turnover.
The new regulation is designed to fill the gaps between this, the Digital Markets Act, and August’s AI Act, says executive vice president Henna Virkkunen, “not duplicate this.” The package should simplify consumer protection rules across the bloc’s 27 members and be a “strong safety net in the digital world,” she adds.
The Commission aims to accelerate cross-border cooperation through strengthened enforcement rules. These would also give the regulator direct powers to investigate large-scale impact and fine firms up to 6 percent of their worldwide annual turnover. Non-EU companies would be required to appoint a local legal representative to cooperate with authorities.

Canadian family finds long-lost WW II baby in England after 81 years
DNA testing uncovered truth about secret buried for decades
Rod Anderson grew up in England always wondering who his father was.
He was born at the end of the Second World War to a British mother.
At 81 years old, he received a call out of the blue this year with news he never expected — his dad was actually a Canadian soldier.
"I was knocked down by it all. It was just such a shock," Rodney told CBC News.
"Still, you could knock me down with a feather. Even today."
Anderson learned the truth about a family secret buried for generations. He was one of thousands of babies born in England and other countries where Canadian troops and allied forces were stationed during the Second World War.
In the 1940s, mothers were blamed and shamed for these pregnancies out of wedlock. Children were given up for adoption. Families were torn apart. Some parents hid the truth until the day they died. 
"My grandmother, my mother, none of them said a word," Anderson said.
Rod Anderson when he was a baby in his mother Yvonne Anderson's arms. He was born in 1945. (Submitted by Dawn Anderson)
But little did Anderson know, a family on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean spent almost two decades searching for him, hoping it wasn't too late.
Now after a remarkable turn of events, Anderson has connected with family in Canada he never knew existed.
An 18-year search
Canadian Bethany Allen spent almost two decades searching for Rodney Anderson.
She said it all started with a "persistent" family rumour about her grandfather Charles Blakney that never went away.
"After the war, there were rumors that my grandfather had a child with a woman in England," said Allen. "Some people heard it. Some people were well aware of it. While others have never heard a whisper of it."
Blakney was married and had a baby girl in New Brunswick when he stepped aboard the HMT Andes to travel across the Atlantic to serve in England in 1942.
Charles Blakney in uniform with his Canadian wife and baby (Bethany Allen's mother). (Submitted by Linda Rowe)
His military records describe him as a "very soft spoken" and reliable solider. He served as a motor and driver mechanic with the New Brunswick Rangers until he returned home in 1945.
Rod Anderson was born in Farnham, England, that same year.
Allen requested her grandfather's divorce records from the archives in 2008. She says they contained the "mother lode of information." The documents confirmed the baby in England was indeed real.
"The moment that I saw it, I was so surprised because it was so obvious," said Allen. "It was so definitive … turned all the rumours into fact."
Bethany Allen in New Brunswick holding her grandfather's divorce records that confirmed he had a baby during the Second World War while stationed in the United Kingdom. (Pierre Fournier/CBC)
But the mystery was far from over. Allen had no idea who the baby was.
Before Allen's mother died, she asked her daughter to keep searching for her sibling overseas no matter what.
"My mother had always wanted to know that he had a good life and was happy," she said.
Suddenly this past spring, "everything changed very quickly" when she did a DNA test through the U.S.-based company Ancestry, Allen said.
The results pointed to Rod Anderson as her half-uncle.
"I was like, oh my god, there he is," said Allen. "Oh my god, his name is Rodney!"
'I thought this is a wind up'
That same day, she managed to track down Rod Anderson's daughter, Dawn Roberts, in England.
Roberts called her dad and asked if he was sitting down.
"She said I had a phone call from a lady in Canada who said that you're her long lost relative," Rod Anderson said.
"I thought this is a wind up. It has to be. But it wasn't. You can't believe what a shock it is to get that knowledge."
Anderson had once done his own DNA test. For 50 years he tried to find the man he always suspected was his father. But in a crushing blow years ago, the test results found they weren't related.
In the end, that DNA test was the key that connected him to his newfound family in Canada.
Second World War historian Jeff Noakes at the Canadian War Museum says the parents of wartime babies whose fathers were Canadian or allied soldiers often kept the details about these children hidden.
'Unbelievable amount of stigma'
There was an "unbelievable amount of stigma," he said, back in the 1940s around having children outside of marriage.
"Eighty years ago, there would have been a tremendous amount of shame for many people attached to this," Noakes said.
"The blame also fell disproportionately on women who were involved rather than the men."
A photo of Charles Blakney taken during a family gathering. (Submitted by Bethany Allen)
Noakes said there was so much public attention around it, Canadian military commander Lt.-Gen. Guy Simonds held a news conference in 1945 to defend his troops. Dutch newspapers had written editorials about an alleged decline in Dutch morality because of the Canadian soldiers stationed in the Netherlands.
Now, decades after these parents have died and there's far less stigma, some Canadian relatives are searching for these war babies before it's too late.
Toine van der Weerden lives in the Netherlands and helps families do the detective work needed to track down the truth.
"They are always happy when they find out," said van der Weerden.
"Everybody wants to know where they come from. Where you got those gestures from, where you got your posture from."
'You've got the same ears'
Since Anderson's revelation about his father, he's connected with his 77-year-old half-sister Barb Lowe in St. Thomas, Ont. They now talk every week.
They said they felt instantly connected the first time they spoke. They both like to laugh, share the same sense of humour and joke about the mischief they got into growing up.
Lowe said he reminds her of their father, who died in 1987.
"You've got the same ears," Lowe told him on one of their calls that CBC News filmed.
'Everything you do is a challenge, especially when you've got one arm and one eye. You have to conquer those challenges no matter how,' said Anderson. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)
Rodney joked she once called them big "elephant-like" ears.
Despite never knowing his biological father, Anderson was amazed to find out he takes after him.
Like father, like son
As a child, Anderson lost his eye and an arm in a rail accident.
In the 1960s, a government assessment found the only job he couldn't do because of his injuries was work as a mechanic.
In true Rod Anderson fashion, he proved them wrong and became one.
Rod Anderson's photos that show his work as a motor mechanic over the years. He eventually opened his own business. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)
It turns out, that's the exact job his Canadian father did for a living and during the war.
"That did surprise me. Isn't it strange?" Anderson said.
These newfound siblings can't quite believe they found each other before it's too late.
"I means the world," Lowe said. "My sister had passed away, my half-sister had passed away. And I finally found Rod. He's everything."
"Don't give up. You never know what the DNA can do."
Barb Lowe lives in St. Thomas, Ont., and said it means 'the world' to her that she's connected with her half-sibling Rod Anderson in England. She's photographed on a video call with Rod. They speak every week. (Yan Theoret/CBC)
But for this family, the mystery may not be over yet.
The divorce records that helped the Canadians find Anderson said his father had another baby in Britain during the war.
"There's still more mysteries to be had," said Allen while laughing. "There's still a search going on, and now we have two sides of the Atlantic trying to solve that mystery."
For now, Anderson's booked his plane ticket to New Brunswick this summer.
He's bringing his granddaughter Samantha Eldridge with him to finally meet the extended family he almost never knew.
"It'll make a difference to my children and their children and their children's children. It will go on," Anderson said.
"Never give up looking."

Islamabad, Nov 11: Pakistan’s incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan was taken to a government hospital for treatment of his eye condition, a media report said on Wednesday.
The 74-year-old founder of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has been incarcerated since 2023 and faces more than 100 cases, including corruption and charges related to inciting violence. He is lodged at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.
Khan has been undergoing treatment for his right eye since January this year after he complained of vision loss.
Khan was brought to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) for tests and follow-up treatment for his eye condition, Dawn reported, quoting a hospital official.
“Imran Ahmed Khan Niazi was brought from Adiala jail in Rawalpindi to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad during the night between November 10 and 11, 2026, for a medical check-up and follow-up eye treatment on the advice of his treating ophthalmologist,” a PIMS official said.
The hospital official added that, prior to the procedure, the former premier underwent a medical examination, including an ocular assessment.
“His vital parameters were found to be normal. He was clinically stable, and his general physical examination was unremarkable. After obtaining informed consent and following standard monitoring procedures, precautionary measures and clinical protocols, the ophthalmology team administered an intravitreal anti-VEGF injection,” the official said.
“He remained clinically stable before, during and after the procedure. He was discharged at around 2:30 am with the necessary instructions for further care and follow-up,” he said.
Khan's party PTI and his family insisted that he should be shifted to a private hospital for treatment, the government official insisted that his eyesight improved after treatment at the government facility.
The Supreme Court had ordered on August 18 to shift Khan to a private hospital for treatment, but he was instead taken to PIMS and returned to jail after various medical tests at the hospital.
Khan became prime minister in 2018 but lost the top job after a no-confidence vote in 2022.

In the Israeli legislative elections held in late October 2026, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, falling short of the 61-seat majority required to govern. The Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, alongside other opposition factions, won 48 seats. Notably, Arab-led parties made historic gains, winning 19 seats and becoming potential “kingmakers”. Following the vote, President Isaac Herzog formally accepted the results. He opened a two-day consultation window with party leaders to determine who is best positioned to assemble a stable coalition.
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament building.
Fact: The video does not show the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament. It shows a pro-Palestine activist replacing the German national flag with a Palestinian flag on a flagpole outside the Reichstag building, which houses the German Parliament (Bundestag), in Berlin on 08 November 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring visuals similar to those seen in the viral video. According to these reports, the incident took place outside the Reichstag building, which houses the German Parliament (Bundestag), in Berlin on Sunday, 08 November 2026.
The reports (here, here) state that a 22-year-old pro-Palestine activist climbed a 30-metre-high flagpole in front of the Reichstag building at around 11:30 am, removed the German national flag, and replaced it with a Palestinian flag.
The group ‘Peacefully Against Genocide‘ claimed responsibility for the incident, stating that the action was a protest against the German government’s pro-Israel policy and its silence on alleged human rights violations in Gaza.
According to a press release issued by Berlin Police on 08 November 2026, two people who allegedly assisted the 22-year-old activist were detained and later released after their identities were established. The Palestinian flag was subsequently removed with the assistance of the Berlin Fire Brigade. Police also launched an investigation into suspected offences, including insulting state symbols, damaging government property, trespassing, and violating Berlin’s assembly law.
To sum up, the viral video shows the Palestinian flag hoisted outside the German Parliament, not the Israeli Parliament.

After Michigan voters elected Democrat Abdul El-Sayed as senator in November 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that he had failed the background check required for classified Senate briefings.
One X user named Jonathan Gregory who shared the claim wrote that El-Sayed's alleged failure would exclude him from some meetings as a senator. The user wrote:
Abdul El Sayed has failed the background check required for classified Senate briefings. The denial blocks him from any session that involves sensitive national security information. Officials who conduct the clearances reported that the review did not meet the standards necessary for access to restricted materials. The failure leaves open the question of what specific issues prevented approval.
Senators who receive classified briefings must clear the same process before they can attend. El Sayed's rejection means he cannot participate in those meetings. The decision places him outside the normal flow of information that other members receive. Americans who expect every senator to qualify for the same briefings now see one individual excluded by the clearance system.
(@TrumpNews_Baby, accessed via X)
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to verify whether it was true.
The claim was false. El-Sayed could not have "failed" a background check "required for classified Senate briefings" because no such background check exists.
Congress members, including senators, are not required to pass a background check to gain security clearance and access classified material, according to a Congressional Research Service "Frequently Asked Questions" report about security clearances from 2023.
The U.S. Constitution, which lays out the requirements for senators, does not include a requirement for them to pass a background check to access classified information. According to Constitution Annotated, the Library of Congress' legal analysis and interpretation of the Constitution, the document has never allowed for changes to the requirements for a senator because that would undermine the legislative branch's investigative powers.
Additionally, federal law exempts members of Congress, including senators, from legislation that governs background checks and security clearances.
The false rumor may have originated as satire. Snopes previously linked another false claim about election fraud to Jonathan Gregory, who shared the first instance of the rumor about El-Sayed that we identified on X. Gregory labels himself as a comedian on his Facebook page, though his Instagram and X accounts don't display such a label. None of Gregory's profiles specifically mention the word "satire," though he has previously used the term near the very end of some of his posts — potentially as a way of hinting at the truth about his content.
We've published fact checks about other matters originating from Gregory's social media accounts, all of which involved false claims.
We contacted El-Sayed's campaign to ask if he had ever applied for, been granted or denied government security clearance before becoming a senator-elect. We also asked the national intelligence director's office whether it had ever granted or denied security clearance to El-Sayed in the past. We await replies to our questions.
Congress investigative powers allow members access to classified information
Members of Congress are implicitly allowed to access classified information because the U.S. Constitution gives the legislative branch investigative powers to inform laws and ensure they are being carried out. In practice, carrying out these investigations can mean that members of Congress need to access classified material, and the Information Security Oversight Office, which is responsible for the policy and oversight of the U.S. government's security classification system, wrote in 2001 that this is generally allowed (PDF Page 66).
It is important to note, however, that though El-Sayed and any other member of Congress bypass the normal procedure for getting security clearance, that does not give them unlimited access to classified information.
For example, the ISOO wrote in 2001 that though members of Congress were exempt from background checks and filling out the government's classified information nondisclosure agreement, they were not exempt from the "'need-to-know' requirement" (PDF Page 66).
For example, the office wrote (PDF Page 66) that members of Congress, "are not inherently authorized to receive all classified information, but agencies provide access as is necessary for Congress to perform its legislative functions."
Subject to election certification by state officials, the 120th Congress, which will include El-Sayed as one of two senators from Michigan, will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027.
For further reading, Snopes frequently investigates rumors relating to El-Sayed.

A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen, a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Researchers have been searching for a drug to lower Lp(a)
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence.
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
What went wrong?
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz, a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal, a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron, a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson, a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

Spain holds state funeral for 69 killed in high-speed rail crash
Relatives of the 69 people killed in a high-speed rail collision in Spain last month attended a state funeral Tuesday
TOLEDO, Spain -- Relatives of the 69 people killed in a high-speed rail collision in Spain last month attended a state funeral on Tuesday with Spain's royals, almost two weeks after the crash.
The ceremony took place in the towering 13th-century Toledo Cathedral in central Spain.
The collision happened on Oct. 28 when a high-speed train slammed into another that was stationary on the Madrid-Seville line near Urda, around 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital.
It was the second deadly collision this year involving Spain’s extensive high-speed rail network, shattering Spaniards' trust in the transit system that is regarded as one of the country's crowning achievements.
Under growing pressure, Transport Minister Óscar Puente stepped down last week. His resignation was followed by that of Luis Pedro Marco, who was head of Spain's railway infrastructure operator.
Spain will hold a general election on Nov. 29, in which progressive Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is seeking reelection.
Sánchez did not attend Tuesday's funeral service.
A 16th-century sculpture of Christ was moved from the town of Urda to the cathedral in Toledo for the funeral service.
Residents of Urda placed 69 candles near the altar in honor of the victims. King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia sat near their families.
Sánchez has pledged an investigation and improvements to restore trust in the rail system that last year carried 45 million travelers, including millions of tourists.
Last week, the European Union's independent prosecutor said it had opened an investigation into possible fraud in the use of European funds allocated for safety upgrades and renovations on the same high-speed railway line on which both fatal crashes this year took place.
Rail travel in Spain was disrupted on Tuesday due to a train drivers' strike. A general strike on Wednesday is expected to cause further disruptions to public transit, and shutter or slow down businesses, factories and shops across Spain.

4 grizzly bears linked by DNA to deadly attack on mother and daughter in Canada
Canadian wildlife officials say four grizzly bears captured in western Canada were responsible for killing a mother and her adult daughter earlier this month in what investigators believe was a rare predatory attack
VANCOUVER, British Columbia -- Four grizzly bears captured in western Canada were responsible for killing a mother and her adult daughter this month in what investigators believe was a rare predatory attack, wildlife officials said Tuesday.
DNA tests conclusively linked a female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the deaths of Jenny Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said. All four bears were killed to protect the public.
“Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare,” Inspector Jeff Tyre told an online briefing.
“That is to say, we don’t know how it started, but we know how it ended.”
The women’s remains were found about 150 meters (490 feet) apart near a trail outside Bella Coola, a remote community about 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) north of Vancouver.
Family members raised the alarm after Reed missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister. Searchers found her mother’s remains first, then discovered Reed’s remains in a bear cache, where bears store food.
Tyre said the bears were not involved in a separate grizzly attack last November on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area. Eleven people were injured, including two critically.
The latest killings have shaken the Nuxalk Nation community, which is still recovering from last year’s attack. Local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew, and police escorted children to school.
“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” said Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, the Nuxalk Nation’s elected chief councilor.
He said community support services would remain available as long as needed.
Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks cannot be rehabilitated or relocated because they pose an extreme risk to public safety.

NASA has unveiled a new experimental vehicle, the X-70 Fractal, although many of its features remain a mystery. The agency describes it as a research platform designed to conduct advanced aeronautical tests, but so far it has released only computer-generated images and some technical specifications regarding its capabilities.
Despite the secrecy, it is possible to get some idea of what the new vehicle is like. First of all, it’s not a spacecraft, meaning it is not designed to reach Earth’s orbit or operate outside the atmosphere. However, this crewed, subsonic aircraft is capable of flying far above commercial jets, reaching altitudes over 45,000 feet, well into the stratosphere. Other specs released include the plane’s max speed of Mach 0.75—about 575 miles per hour—and that it can travel nearly 1,700 miles in a single flight.
According to NASA, the X-70 Fractal will enable research into maneuver capabilities never before demonstrated in crewed aircraft, although the agency has not specified what types of maneuvers it intends to perform. The plane will also be capable of carrying up to one ton of experimental equipment and is expected to make its first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years.
One of the key features of the craft will be its modular design, allowing for the rapid installation and replacement of experimental equipment both inside and outside the aircraft. This is largely why it is referred to as an “experimental platform.” It will also feature reconfigurable flight control systems so that NASA can study different ways of steering an aircraft without having to develop a separate platform for each research project.
Although NASA is best known for its space missions, it’s long been dedicated to aeronautical research. That’s what the first A stands for. The agency also traces its origins to the creation of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, which was founded in 1915 and was folded into the newly formed NASA in 1958.
Since then, the space agency has developed numerous experimental aircraft to test technologies that range from supersonic flight and propulsion systems to new aerodynamic configurations. Not all of these prototypes go on to become operational aircraft, but the knowledge gained contributes to the development of future commercial and military aircraft as well as space vehicles.
Among its most recent projects is the X-59, developed in collaboration with aerospace and defense company Lockheed Martin to investigate ways to reduce the noise produced by supersonic aircraft. The X-70 Fractal will join this tradition of pioneers in the sky.
The development of these technologies also has a strategic dimension. In its budget documents for 2027, NASA identifies aeronautical research as a tool for maintaining US technological leadership in the face of growing international competition. The agency also plans to collaborate with the Department of Defense to advance new flight capabilities, although it has not yet announced any military applications for the X-70 Fractal.
During the unveiling of the new aircraft, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman noted that the project represents only one part of a new era for federal aeronautical research and hinted that more announcements are coming. For now, the agency has not provided details on what those initiatives might be, nor has it specified when it will release more information about the X-70 Fractal.

Army's key communication wing, vital from Kargil to Op Sindoor, gets new address
The Indian Army's strategic communication directorate will move from South Block to Shaurya Bhawan by the end of November, marking a new chapter in its four-decade evolution as the Army's key media liaison unit.
The Indian Army's Additional Directorate General of Strategic Communication (ADG Strat Comn) will soon move out of the iconic South Block and shift to the newly built Shaurya Bhawan in Delhi Cantonment. The relocation, part of a larger exercise to move all Army and Navy offices out of South Block, including the office of the Chief of the Army Staff, is expected to be completed by the end of this month.
The Defence Minister, the Chief of Defence Staff and the Defence Secretary had moved their offices to Kartavya Bhawan in March 2026.
The move will mark the end of a significant chapter in the directorate's history, which has evolved over four decades alongside major changes in the media landscape. Established in 1985 as a small Publicity Cell, the directorate began its journey when print media was the dominant platform and electronic media was only beginning to expand. It was later brought under the Military Operations Directorate.
During the 1990s, its responsibilities expanded as round-the-clock television news began shaping public opinion. The unit was renamed the Psy Ops Cell in 1994 and subsequently became the Army Liaison Cell in 1996. In 2004, it was upgraded to the Additional Directorate General of Public Information, reflecting the growing importance of online media alongside print and television.
Over the years, the directorate has established itself as one of the most trusted and reliable links between the Indian Army and the media. Journalists have relied on it for accurate, timely and credible information, particularly during major military operations.
Some of its biggest tests came during the Kargil conflict, the Surgical Strikes and Operation Sindoor, when it kept the media and the public updated on military developments. Its communication was marked by clarity and restraint, helping build public confidence in the armed forces during critical moments.
In 2020, the directorate was renamed ADG Strategic Communication and equipped with enhanced capabilities to address the demands of new-age media and the growing challenges posed by fake and synthetic news.
Despite the changes in its structure and responsibilities, its commitment to open and constructive engagement with the media has remained unchanged. It continues to be a key pillar of the Ministry of Defence's public relations set-up, with its present mandate centred on calibrated strategic communication, ensuring that the Army's position is accurately presented and protected against distortion.
The move to Shaurya Bhawan will provide the directorate with a modern base to carry forward this mandate. While South Block will remain an integral part of its institutional history, its focus at the new address will remain unchanged: to inform, engage and serve as a dependable bridge between the Indian Army and the media.

One killed in Indonesia helicopter crash during firefighting operation
- Published
One person has died after a helicopter crashed into a river in Indonesia during a mission to fight wildfires in South Kalimantan.
An Indonesian crew member was killed, while two others on board - an Australian and New Zealander - were "found safe" and taken to hospital for treatment, according to Indonesia's disaster mitigation agency.
Investigations into the accident are ongoing, the agency said on Sunday, adding that it could continue its firefighting operations.
For months, parts of Indonesia have been battling wildfires that have shrouded large swathes of South East Asia in toxic haze. The blazes in forests and peatlands are fuelled by a dry season that has been exacerbated by El Niño.
Videos posted by Indonesia's disaster authorities and circulating on social media show the helicopter hovering over the river with a helicopter bucket - a collapsible container typically used to douse water over fires - before it nosedives into the water.
Other videos show rescuers later reaching the partially submerged helicopter by boat.
The fallen chopper, a Super Puma H-225, was owned by a company that disaster authorities had contracted for the firefighting operations, a disaster official told AFP.
The incident comes days after another helicopter crashed in central Kalimantan during a firefighting operation, killing three crew members.
The military said on Saturday that they had managed to retrieve the helicopter's blackbox, which would help their investigations into the cause of the crash.
Despite intensive firefighting efforts, the wildfires in Indonesia this year have been especially difficult to tame due to drought conditions exacerbated by a stronger El Niño.
The raging wildfires sent toxic smog blanketing cities in Indonesia, turning the air amber and triggering a surge in respiratory illnesses in cities across the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra.
The haze also drifted to neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore, where it has triggered public health concerns.
Foreign governments have sent assistance to help with firefighting efforts, including Australia, which has deployed aircraft and 20 personnel including pilots and paramedics.

Some of the most impressive tech that Adobe showcases at its annual Max conference each year is the experimental features it’s developing, and the latest of those tools are being announced today: they can transform images into explorable 3D scenes, design AI characters by talking to them, and turn photo editing into a copy/paste process.
Adobe’s AI experiments let you walk around in photos and interview your characters
Here are some of the experimental ‘sneaks’ being showcased at Adobe Max.
The first (and weirdest, in my opinion) is Project Screen Test, which is designed to make AI-generated characters easier to develop and use for video content. Instead of just describing how the character should sound and behave in text prompts, the tool lets you talk to the character and direct them in an audition-like environment. You start by describing some base personality traits, such as “anxious, shy, awkward,” and giving the character a voice, either by selecting a preset, describing how it sounds in a prompt, or uploading sample audio for it to reference.
You can then expand its persona in further detail by conversing with the character as if you’re talking on FaceTime, outlining its backstory, temperament, goals, flaws, fears, movement quirks and more. Once you’re happy, the tool lets you generate animated screen tests with the character by describing an environment or scenario you want to put them in.
This is currently a standalone creative exercise, and it’s not clear how (or if) it could feature in any of Adobe’s existing AI video tools. The results provided a more identifiable and consistent personality compared to many soulless animated AI characters I’ve seen, but that’s the entire reason this exists — AI video generation provides far less creative control compared to traditional animation, where every aspect of a character is included with absolute intention.
There’s also Project Sight Span, which reframes photographs and images by turning them into a 3D environment that you can navigate through and reposition. The 3D space generates objects and backgrounds that are outside of the original frame, but feel like a natural part of the image, even if you’re turning to see what’s behind you. While the visuals in the 3D environment are pixelated and ill–defined, the resolution quality is restored when you select your chosen angle.
Sight Span works with any flat image, including photos, paintings, and illustrations, and can preserve and replicate artistic styles. Even repositioned tattoos and facial features in photographs remain surprisingly recognizable and true to the original reference. It’s a bit like a version of Apple’s Spatial Reframing feature on steroids: you can reposition more aggressively and change the shooting point entirely if you want, but it also feels far less deserving of being called a photo afterward.
Project Sound Bender is an AI audio mixing feature that lets you customize sound effects as if you’re clicking your cursor around a color wheel. It works by uploading a video clip and then describing your desired audio in a text prompt, such as “bubbling sci-fi cauldron noises.” Sound Bender then generates sound effects and automatically syncs it to the video, and provides a square sound canvas that lets you adjust the noises in real time. Each corner of the canvas will automatically assign a relevant AI-generated sound, such as dense gurgling with popping bubbles, rumbling boiling rocks, pitched bloops, and crackling electric fire. You can drag your cursor around the canvas to select which noises stand out the most, or customize each corner with different sound effects.
Adobe also showcased Project Rinse Repeat, which lets you copy edits and then automatically apply them to other objects or people in the same photo. For example, if you painstakingly airbrush out acne or blemishes on one person, Rinse Repeat will adapt your specific changes to anyone else in a group of people who need similar touchups. It can also be used to add shadows to products in marketing graphics, even if the objects are different shapes and sizes. Rinse Repeat is built around Photoshop, and the edits you apply to other subjects remain fully editable because the tool recreates them with native Photoshop tools.
These “sneaks” are tech previews of capabilities that might eventually be developed into tools for Adobe’s Creative Cloud apps or Firefly platform, so there’s no guarantee that they’ll graduate into being available features. Almost all of these projects are built around Adobe’s generative AI developments, however, and given AI tools now play a central role in the company’s growth strategy, it’s likely that at least some of the experiments will see an official launch. As wacky or fun as these AI experiments are, they’re also an omen. If they’re useful enough, that means AI may eventually replace the tools and stock libraries that creative professionals currently use, regardless of how complex their feelings are about the technology.
A notable theme across these sneaks is making complicated photo editing, filmmaking, and audio mixing workflows feel more accessible and intuitive, adapting them into something that’s more interactive and easy to use. In some cases the features almost seem like toys, but with the benefit of allowing you to make practical changes to creative projects.
“Making these interactions more intuitive is also about giving experienced creatives more precise control,” senior principle Adobe research scientist Gautham Mysore, told The Verge. “Sound Bender’s sonic exploration capability and Sight Span’s camera positioning are examples of how professionals could apply their judgment and refine a result more directly. That connection between creative intent and control is a big part of what we’re exploring.”

Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
- Published
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.
The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.
One man, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of doing the same from Iran.
Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford incident, which came to light when suspicious vans were reported near the base. Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident.
Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.
It accuses the trio of planning attacks in Europe that were carried out under the name of a purportedly new group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand - HAYI).
"Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK," the DOJ statement said. It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".
Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.
"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.
He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.
Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.
A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.
No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.
The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".
On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.
In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.
According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".
The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated.
"On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."
The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive.
"At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added.
It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police.

Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot.
The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason.
RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, to immediately suspend the manufacturing licences of drugs declared Not of Standard Quality (NSQ) on specified critical quality parameters.
The government said on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) that the proposed amendments seek to enable prompt regulatory intervention upon detection of substandard medicines, prevent their continued manufacture and distribution, and strengthen the mechanism for ensuring compliance with prescribed quality standards, in the interest of patient safety and public health.
Under the existing provisions of the Drugs Rules, 1945, suspension or cancellation of a manufacturing licence is preceded by the prescribed regulatory procedure, including issuance of a show-cause notice. This may result in a time gap between the declaration of a drug as NSQ and the initiation of regulatory action. During this period, the drug may remain in circulation, posing potential risks to public health and making effective recall more challenging.
To address this regulatory concern, the Ministry has proposed a provision for immediate suspension of the manufacturing licence of the drug by the Central Licensing Approving Authority or the State Licensing Authority upon receipt of a government analyst’s report declaring the drug as NSQ with respect to assay, dissolution, related substances, impurities or sterility.
“These parameters are critical to determining the quality of medicines. The proposed provision aims to ensure that instances of non-compliance involving these specified parameters are met with prompt regulatory action, thereby minimising potential risks to patients,’’ the Ministry said.
The proposed amendment provides for mandatory corrective measures before revocation of the suspension. The suspension shall continue until the manufacturer undertakes an effective root cause analysis to identify the reasons for the quality failure and implements appropriate Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) to the satisfaction of the licensing authority.
Suspension can be revoked after the requisite corrective and preventive measures are implemented and then verified by the licensing authority. This mechanism will ensure that identified quality deficiencies are adequately addressed and necessary safeguards are put in place to prevent their recurrence.
“To further strengthen regulatory coordination and facilitate timely action, consequential amendments have also been proposed to Form 13, relating to the test report of the Government Analyst. Under the proposed mechanism, the Government Analyst’s report would be endorsed to the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), the concerned State/UT Licensing Authority under whose jurisdiction the manufacturing site is located, as well as the manufacturer and marketer of the concerned drug,’’ the government said.
It added that the proposed arrangement is aimed at ensuring timely communication of NSQ findings to the relevant authorities and stakeholders, thereby facilitating coordinated regulatory action and strengthening accountability across the drug manufacturing and marketing chain.
The proposed amendments follow deliberations at the 65th meeting of the Drugs Consultative Committee, held on December 20, 2024, and recommendations of the 92nd meeting of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board, held on April 24, 2025.
The amendments are expected to strengthen post-marketing regulatory surveillance, facilitate timely action against substandard medicines, promote greater accountability among manufacturers and marketers, and reinforce public confidence in the quality of medicines available in the country.
The draft amendments have been notified for public consultation, inviting objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days from the date on which copies of the Gazette of India containing the draft rules are made available to the public.

A former Eli Lilly sales rep filed a lawsuit alleging that she was fired after complaining the company was promoting its Mounjaro diabetes drug to combat weight loss before receiving regulatory approval to do so.
Jennifer Mansion, who was hired as a senior territory manager in Dallas four years ago, claimed that she observed other Lilly sales reps promoting the diabetes drug as a salve for obesity. Mansion also contended that a physician touted Mounjaro as a weight loss option during a luncheon sponsored by the drugmaker, according to the suit filed in federal court in Texas.
Such promotions are known as off-label marketing in the pharmaceutical industry. The phrase refers to promoting a medicine for a usage that was not approved by the Food and Drug Administration. A physician may prescribe a medicine for an unapproved use, but a drugmaker is not permitted to market its drug for that purpose.
