Danielle Thumann Severs, Federal Communications Commission nominee, waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce, Science, & Transportation Committee on Tuesday, November 10, 2026.
Credit:
Getty Images | CQ Roll Call
Senate Democrats today opposed President Trump’s nominee for an open Federal Communications Commission seat, and criticized Republicans for moving to confirm a new commissioner during the period before Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027. Democrats also plan to use their majority next year to launch probes of FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.
“After the American people last week overwhelmingly rejected the MAGA agenda, there is no justification for this committee to advance partisan nominees during the lame-duck period,” Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) said today at the Commerce Committee’s nomination hearing for Danielle Thumann Severs, Trump’s pick to fill an empty commissioner’s seat.
Thumann Severs, an attorney and senior counsel to Carr, faced questions from Democrats about whether she supports Carr’s attacks on TV broadcasters.
“Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?” Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked the nominee.
Thumann Severs responded that she has not advised Carr on media-related topics and declined Luján’s request to identify any specific policy issues on which she disagrees with Carr.
“I don’t think Chairman Carr is going to be around more than another three or four months”
Luján predicted trouble for Carr when Democrats take the majority in both chambers of Congress. He seemed to suggest that Carr will quickly grow tired of having to testify in Congress multiple times a month under the Democratic majorities.
“I don’t think Chairman Carr is going to be around more than another three or four months because when we have the gavels in here, he will be here once a month,” Luján said. “And Mr. Carr, if you’re listening now, know you’re going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions, and you don’t have the protection of the gavel any longer.” Luján said Democrats will use “subpoena authorities that you have to respond to so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place.”
Markey accused Thumann Severs of evading questions about Carr threatening and taking actions against broadcasters on behalf of Trump. “Anyone seeking a seat on the Federal Communications Commission must be willing to stand up to such threats and to defend the First Amendment, and you’re not willing to do so here in your confirmation hearing,” Markey said.
Democrats similarly criticized Thumann Severs for not giving a clear answer on whether the FCC has authority to eliminate E-Rate, a $2 billion-a-year program that was created by Congress to connect students and library visitors to the Internet. Carr has proposed eliminating or scaling back the program. Thumann Severs said she helped Carr work on the E-Rate Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, which seeks public comment about the program and the FCC’s authority to change or eliminate it.
“I can’t prejudge the open proceeding [on E-Rate] at the FCC right now,” she said today.
“I am not comfortable with your answers today”
Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) criticized Thumann Severs’ answers. “If you’re confirmed, you’re going to be one of the votes that decides whether the FCC stays an independent regulator, or becomes an arm of the White House press office. We deserve to know where you stand, and I am not comfortable with your answers today,” Duckworth said.
Duckworth told Thumann Severs that the FCC cannot eliminate E-Rate without Congressional approval. “We never directed the FCC to eliminate the program and frankly, at a time when the price of gas, groceries, and utilities is skyrocketing, the last thing the FCC should be doing is making it harder for schools to stay connected,” Duckworth said.
The Senate Commerce, Science & Transportation Committee held today’s hearing for Thumann Severs and three other nominees for federal positions. Senators have until Thursday to submit additional questions for the record, and nominees will have until November 16 to respond.
Thumann Severs needs approval from the committee and then the full Senate to be confirmed to the FCC. Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is trying to get her approved before Republicans have to give up their Senate majority.
Thumann Severs would give Republicans an unusual 3-1 advantage on the FCC, which usually operates with a 3-2 split. Democrats criticized Republicans for not pairing her nomination with a Democratic one. The commission has only one Democrat, Anna Gomez, and she would have to leave at the end of 2027 if she is not given another term.
“For many decades, the Senate has paired commission nominees: A Republican and a Democrat moving together,” Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) said. “Congress established the FCC as an independent, bipartisan agency… a bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation, and I think also more fundamentally to protect a free and diverse press.”
Carr’s threat to ABC “were his words… not my words”
Because US law requires the FCC to have three commissioners for a quorum, Gomez’s “presence in the current 2-1 Republican majority is necessary for the FCC to conduct business,” Hickenlooper said. The Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority, but Hickenlooper predicted that Trump will fire Gomez to give Republicans a 3-0 stranglehold.
“If today’s nominee is confirmed, President Trump could then fire Commissioner Gomez and have an FCC with no Democratic voice at all,” Hickenlooper said.
Hickenlooper questioned whether Thumann Severs is sufficiently independent from Carr. “Ms. Thumann Severs, your career has largely been spent serving Brendan Carr,” Hickenlooper said. “[You are] currently Chairman Carr’s senior counsel; previously, you were legal advisor to Commissioner Carr. Your official duties include near-daily meetings with Chairman Carr and working to advance his agenda, amplify his messaging.”
Markey asked Thumann Severs if it was appropriate for Carr to use the FCC’s regulatory authority to pressure broadcasters into taking a comedian off the air. Markey was referring to an incident last year in which Carr threatened to revoke ABC broadcast TV licenses over remarks made by Kimmel, who was then suspended by ABC owner Disney.
“We can do this the easy way or the hard way,” Carr said at the time, adding that Disney must “take action” on Kimmel “or there’s going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.”
When asked about Carr’s comments today, Thumann Severs said, “Those were his words. They were not my words, and I have not advised him or worked with the chairman on these particular issues. I can say that if I were to be confirmed as commissioner, I would make all of my decisions [based on] the facts and the law and the record.”
FCC review of ABC station licenses
Senate Democrats tried to get Thumann Severs to discuss Carr’s decision to order an early review of ABC station licenses. “Do you think the FCC should revoke broadcasters’ licenses because the president does not like their coverage?” Duckworth asked.
Thumann Severs answered that the FCC “has a responsibility to fully investigate any complaint… and to evaluate that complaint on the merits. I don’t think a decision should be made purely based on someone’s discontent with the content being aired.”
Although the ABC license review is widely seen as retaliation against the network for its news coverage and other programming, Carr’s proceeding is ostensibly based on an allegation that Disney’s diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices are discriminatory.
“Based on publicly available material, which is all I have seen on that particular matter, the licenses were called for early renewal as part of an investigation into potential rule violations,” Thumann Severs said today.
Ted Cruz satisfied by nominee’s answers
Cruz mentioned the Carr FCC’s review of ABC licenses and noted that “ABC argues [the review] is actually in retaliation for the network’s programming.” Cruz also alleged that in Democratic administrations, “the FCC has previously used its public interest standard as a weapon against conservatives.”
“If you are confirmed, will you commit to basing licensing decisions on the law and the record and to not using the FCC’s authority to pressure or punish a broadcaster for protected speech?” Cruz asked the nominee. She answered, “Yes.”
Cruz then asked Thumann Severs if she supports the JAWBONE Act, a bill that Cruz introduced with Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) to enable lawsuits against federal officials who try to coerce broadcasters or tech platforms into restricting speech.
Thumann Severs answered that she supports the bill. “I think it’s incredibly important that federal officials not use their position… to coerce against protected speech,” she said.
Cruz seemed satisfied with her answers. While Democrats recognized that Republicans have the votes to advance the nomination, they spent much of the hearing criticizing Thumann Severs’ answers and the Republican plan to confirm her without a paired Democratic nominee.
“We should not be confirming a Republican nominee without also renominating and confirming Anna Gomez, the Democrat, and filling the other vacant Democratic seat,” Markey said. “There is a potential next year where there will be three Republicans and no Democrats on the Federal Communications Commission… that is wrong, and that is why I do not believe we should proceed with this nomination at this time.”
Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India, a country he visited many times on extended trips.
His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company.
Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.
Roy’s other books included A Brief History of Tea (2003), an authoritative account of the complex political and horticultural history of tea, and Outlaw (2010), which looked at the life of India’s “bandit queen” and politician Phoolan Devi, drawing on Roy’s friendship with her before her assassination in 2001. His last book, The Theft of India (2015), documented the rivalry between European colonial powers and the impact this had on Indians themselves.
Roy was born in Evesham, Worcestershire, to Marie (known as Min, nee Bland) and Wilson Moxham. Wilson, a baker, died when Roy was 11, after which Min, a shop worker, raised her three sons under straitened circumstances, often taking in lodgers to make ends meet.
After leaving Prince Henry’s grammar school in Evesham in the early 1960s, Roy put an advert in the Times newspaper that read: “Young man, good A-levels, seeks opportunity in Africa in tobacco or tea.” He received a reply offering him a job on a tea plantation in the British colony of Nyasaland (now Malawi), where, despite his youth, he became a supervisor in charge of 1,000 female tea pickers. Later he switched to selling agricultural machinery across east Africa, particularly in Kenya. In the mid-70s, after 13 years in Africa he returned to the UK, where he opened a gallery in Covent Garden, London, selling African art.
Following a period of squatting in Covent Garden, Roy became an early and longstanding member of the Seven Dials Housing Co-operative, living in one of their properties in that area for most of the rest of his life.
In 1978 he changed direction by studying book and paper conservation at Camberwell College of Arts, after which he worked as a conservator at the Canterbury Cathedral Archive, then at Senate House Library, University of London, where he remained until 2005.
While working, Roy had begun travelling regularly to India from 1992 onwards, and it was on those journeys that he began his three-year search for the Great Hedge. The book was hugely successful, often referenced by historians, writers and artists, and even inspired a Horrible Histories sketch.
After retiring in 2005, Roy lived in India for a number of months each year. His book about Devi, a champion of the Indian poor, came about after he wrote to her when she was in prison. When she was released they arranged a meeting, and became great friends.
Roy is survived by his two brothers, John and Jim, a nephew, three nieces and me.

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.
It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.
See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.
Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.
While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.
Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.
“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.
“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”
Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.
As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.
Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.
“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.
“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”
See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

Samsung Gallery now syncs with Google to back up your photos
The company ended Gallery's Microsoft OneDrive integration back in September.
If you've ever owned a Samsung phone, you've most likely seen your device prompt you to back up your media to OneDrive at least once in the past. Back in September, however, Samsung removed its Gallery app's ability to sync with Microsoft OneDrive. Well, the phonemaker was likely cooking up another partnership behind the scenes, because it has just announced that its Gallery app can now sync with your Google account.
In the past, if you wanted to back up your photos and videos to your Google storage on a Samsung phone, you've had to use Google Photos instead of (or in addition to) your device's native Gallery app. With this update, you can stick to Samsung's Gallery app if you want to.The feature is currently only available on select Galaxy devices running One UI 9, Samsung's latest custom Android interface, but the company says it will roll out to more devices in phases. To enable the feature, tap the Cloud icon in Gallery or go to Gallery Settings and switch on Sync photos and videos.
Since the feature syncs media files to your Google account, you'll be able to access them in the Gallery app of another Samsung Galaxy device. Simply log into the same account on your other device and enable sync on it, as well. You'll then be able to see previews of your synced photos and videos on that device. If you want to access the original files, just select and download them. In case you want to do the opposite and remove files from your phone or tablet after they've been synced to Google storage, you can use Samsung's other new feature. It offers a Free up space option in the Sync photos and videos settings, which deletes original files from your device while keeping thumbnails visible in the Gallery app.
It's worth noting that Gallery sync will take up storage space on your Google account. Each Google account comes with 5GB of free storage by default, which you can expand to 15GB if you verify a valid phone number. If you want or need more than that, since that storage is shared across Google's services, you'll have to purchase a Google One subscription that will set you back $2 per month for 100GB of storage or $3 for 200GB.

Employee stock options (ESOPs) have become a major talking point in India’s startup ecosystem this year, with questions around liquidity, employee wealth creation and the ability to monetise years of accumulated stock options taking centre stage. While Flipkart’s ESOP-related employee woes have been in the news all through this summer, digital commerce startup GoKwik has brought another dimension to the ESOP debate. GoKwik, which is backed by the likes of Z47 Partners, Peak XV Partners, RTP Global and Think Investments, has amended its existing ESOP Plan 2021, through the insertion of a new non-compete clause, naming nine companies that employees are barred from joining or associating with, if they want to retain their ESOP rights. The provision gives the startup the authority to revoke unvested and vested-but-unexercised employee stock options if employees (even those who have quit GoKwik) are found to have breached the restriction. Inc42 has seen a copy of the internal document in question which has caused consternation among current and former employees. The mail was also sent to former GoKwik employees who continue to hold options. The insertion of the clause has raised questions around employee mobility and the rights of existing ESOP holders, particularly as the new provision applies to options granted in the past as well as future stock options. The clause was communicated to employees in the month of August, amid a spate of senior-level exits. The exits include vice president Sneha Rao, Sharad Gupta, the senior director of product management for the Checkout business, and Siddhartha Bahl, head of product, among others. The policy lists Razorpay, Shiprocket, CRED, Cashfree Payments, BiteSpeed, Snapmint, WebEngage, Shopflo (acquired by Pine Labs), and Pine Labs as competing businesses. Under the provision, employees cannot accept employment with, render services to, advise, invest in or otherwise associate with these companies. If the company determines that an employee has breached the restriction, it can forfeit their unvested options as well as vested options that have not yet been exercised. The GoKwik ESOP Plan 2021 (“Plan”) allows GoKwik to cancel or forfeit both unvested and vested-but-unexercised options if the Board or Nomination and Remuneration Committee determines that an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach”. While unvested options are stock options that employees are not yet entitled to exercise, vested-but-unexercised options are those that employees are entitled to exercise but have not yet converted into shares. The provision does not affect ESOPs that have already been exercised. In effect, an employee joining a competing business could lose options that are yet to vest, as well as those that have already vested by have not been exercised. This means that even employees who completed the vesting period and earned the right to buy shares coils lose those options if the company determines that they have breached the competition restriction. However, options already exercised and converted into shares are not covered by this forfeiture provision. Importantly, the restriction applies to all grants, whether issued before or after its effective date, and continues to bind former employees holding vested options even after their employment ends. The restriction, however, is not indefinite. A special resolution passed by GoKwik shareholders at the company’s September, 2025 AGM provides that the competition related restriction will remain in force from the grant date until two years after an employee;s last date of employment or engagement with the company or its affiliates. In other words, the restriction applies throughout an employee’s tenure at GoKwik and continues for two years after their departure. During this period, joining or associating with a competing business could put their outstanding ESOPs at risk. The policy appears to carve out passive investments in publicly traded securities. It also allows the GoKwik Board to approve exceptions in writing, with employees required to write to the company for such deviations. The inclusion is significant because it directly links an employee’s association with named competitors to the potential loss of their stock options, including options that have already vested but remain unexercised. Questions sent to GoKwik didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story even after Inc42 extended the deadline for responses upon the company’s request. Instead, GoKwik issued a press release claiming former employees might get 9X average returns on their ESOPs and the startup has turned EBITDA positive in October 2026. But this press release does not mention any of the concerns that employees have brought up. Employees In Limbo “The sudden change in the ESOP policy was a shock. People who have quite a significant ESOP holding are all of a sudden in fear that they will lose it if they leave the company and try to join a better company. Now the names that they have mentioned are much superior companies that they would want to join as part of having a better career trajectory,” a former GoKwik employee told Inc42. Employees with significant ESOP holdings, particularly those who may consider moving to other companies in the same sector, are stuck in limbo. Sources in the company say they are weighing potential job opportunities against the potential loss from forfeiting their outstanding stock options. This is especially relevant for employees whose options have vested but have not been exercised, since the new clause explicitly includes vested-but-unexercised options within the scope of potential forfeiture. The forfeiture, however, is not automatic. The Board or the Nomination and Remuneration Committee has the discretion to determine whether an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach” and decide whether to cancel or forfeit their unvested and/or vested-but-unexercised options. Worryingly for employees, the provision is ambiguous about what kind of relationships are covered. For instance, it says that ESOPs may be revoked for employees who may “otherwise associate” with a competing business. This could cover relationships beyond direct employment, and the policy does not make the scope of this phrase immediately clear. The timing of the amendment is also notable against the backdrop of GoKwik’s growth ambitions and recent senior-level departures as well as layoffs. Founded in 2020 by Chirag Taneja, Vivek Bajpai, and Ankush Talwar, GoKwik is an ecommerce enablement startup that offers software tools to help online brands improve checkout, reduce order returns, automate customer engagement and increase sales. Earlier this year, Inc42 exclusively reported that GoKwik had laid off around 120 employees. The startup has to date raised $68 Mn in funding and counts investors including Peak XV Partners, Z47 Partners, RTP Global, and Think Investments, among others. In an interview with BW Disrupt, published in July 2025, cofounder and CEO Taneja said the company generated around ₹250 Cr in revenue in FY25. However, GoKwik Commerce Solutions Pvt Ltd’s financial disclosures show consolidated operating revenue of ₹146.2 Cr for FY25, and total consolidated revenue of approximately ₹163 Cr. GoKwik did not respond to questions about this discrepancy. Among the nine companies named in the policy, GoKwik directly competes with the likes of Shiprocket’s Fastrr, Razorpay’s Magic Checkout, Shopflo, and Cashfree’s One Click Checkout, while the remaining companies operate in adjacent or overlapping segments of ecommerce enablement, fintech, and merchant services ecosystem. Making Sense Of Non-Compete For ESOPs Non-compete restrictions are commonly included in employment agreements in India, although their enforceability is difficult to establish. However, explicitly naming competitors in an ESOP policy and linking an employee’s association with them to the cancellation of vested-but-unexercised options is unusual, according to Siddharth Manchanda, Partner at JSA Advocates & Solicitors. Manchanda further clarified that his comments reflected a general understanding of the law and should not be construed as an opinion on GoKwik. He also said that a restriction on an ESOP policy is unusual but its substance is not entirely new. Most ESOP policies, in his view, contain provisions that allow options to lapse if an employee breaches their employment agreement. Since employment agreements commonly include non-compete restrictions, companies may already have an indirect route to link an employee joining a competitor with the loss of ESOPs. However, companies do not typically go after employees solely for joining a competitor, unless the situation also involves allegations of confidentiality breaches, data theft or misuse of proprietary information. Under Rule 12(8)(f) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, unvested options ordinarily expire upon resignation or termination, while vested options can be exercised within the period specified by the ESOP scheme. The more consequential question, according to Manchanda, is whether a company can introduce additional grounds for forfeiture after employees have already received their options. While employers have discretion to set the grounds for cancellation when drafting an ESOP policy, changing those terms later to employees’ disadvantage could be legally questionable. In GoKwik’s case, the amendment applies to options that were already outstanding. As per another lawyer Inc42 spoke to, this change could be challenged from a legal standpoint, as amendments that adversely affect employees’ existing ESOP rights raise questions around their validity. He added that the enforceability of non-compete restrictions and the cancellation of ESOPs on that basis remains an unsettled issue that could be tested in legal dispute. ESOPs Turn Into A Governance Question The clause also raises a governance question that goes beyond enforceability. Plus, some clauses in the changed policy are ambiguous at best. Under the plan, it is the Board or its Nomination and Remuneration Committee that decides whether an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach”, a decision in which employees, and the former employees the clause continues to bind, have no part. ESOPs are a critical lever when it comes to attracting employees to early stage startups. They stand in for salary. An early stage startup can’t match what IT services giants, multinationals or global capability centres (GCCs) pay. Stock options fill the gap. The employee takes a lower monthly salary in exchange for a share of the upside in the future. At that stage the ESOP is part of the offer, not a perk. ESOPs are also seen as a retention tactic. Options vest over time and it ties in employees to the success of the business in the long run. Leaving early means giving up the options that haven’t vested or even leaving money on the table. And finally, ESOPs are one wealth creation instrument in the hands of employers. A total of 12 startups executed ESOP buybacks in 2025, paying ₹1,409 Cr ($158 Mn) to more than 9,200 employees. In 2024, 23 startups paid out ₹1,448 Cr to employees through buybacks. Even a minor change in the ESOP policy can lead to employees having to sacrifice an amount that can be equivalent to years of salary. GoKwik would not be the first startup to change ESOP terms after the options were granted. In December 2025, Unacademy cut the window its former employees had to exercise their vested options from 10 years to 30 days, while it was in M&A talks. Unacademy put the change on hold a month later, after a backlash from former employees. GoKwik’s claim of 9X average returns for former employees tells us what the options may be worth, but do employees get to keep them? GoKwik’s handling of the issue will be tested the first time an employee with vested options joins one of the nine companies it names, unless, like Unacademy, the ecommerce company decides to revisit this provision before then. Until that happens, every employee holding ESOPs, current or former, is left with the question: does a vested option actually belong to them even if it has been allocated on paper, or is it only theirs for as long as they stay away from the companies that GoKwik bars? The Abdullahs are facing the challenge of keeping the National Conference united amid mounting dissent.
NEW DELHI: Two years after sweeping to power on a promise to reclaim Jammu and Kashmir’s political identity and dignity, Omar Abdullah’s government is confronting the limits of governing a Union Territory with constrained powers.What began as a historic return to power in October 2024 has increasingly turned into a political and administrative tightrope. While 89-year-old National Conference patron Farooq Abdullah has stepped in to contain simmering discontent among MLAs left out of the cabinet expansion, an ideological rupture has emerged with the exit of Srinagar MP Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi, who has accused the party leadership of abandoning its core promises.Caught between disgruntled legislators seeking a greater share in government and a prominent party voice questioning its political compromises, the National Conference faces a twin challenge. The party has accused the BJP of exploiting its internal divisions to engineer an 'Operation Lotus' in Jammu and Kashmir. But is this an opposition attempt to destabilise the government, or does the turmoil point to a leadership crisis under Omar Abdullah?
The show of unity
The gates of the Abdullahs' Gupkar residence in Srinagar opened to a familiar political spectacle last week as yet another party leadership put up a show of strength amid growing discontent within its ranks.
Standing alongside 15 MLAs unhappy with the recent cabinet expansion, 89-year-old National Conference (NC) president Farooq Abdullah sought to project an image of an organisation firmly in control of its affairs."The baseless reports being spread that the National Conference is divided are completely false. This organisation is united, and those who think they can break this organisation should understand that it has never been broken and will never be broken," Farooq declared.He acknowledged that the legislators had genuine grievances and promised that some concerns would be addressed immediately, while others would be taken up gradually.But behind the show of unity, there's a bigger contradiction confronting Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah. The National Conference, which swept the 2024 assembly elections on the promise of reclaiming Kashmir's political identity, dignity and special status, is caught between the compromises of governing a Union Territory and the expectations of the constituency that brought it to power.The party is facing two distinct challenges. While a section of its MLAs is demanding a greater share in the government and a say in decision-making, one of its most prominent political voices, Srinagar MP Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi, has walked out accusing the leadership of abandoning the very promises on which it sought votes.
Farooq Abdullah dismisses reports of a split within the National Conference, asserting that the party remains united despite growing internal discontent.
The ideological rupture: Ruhullah's 'decree of freedom'
The fragility of the NC's united front was exposed three days before Farooq met with the disgruntled legislators.On November 3, at a gathering in Behisht-e-Zehra Park in Budgam marking the 26th death anniversary of his assassinated father, Aga Syed Mehdi, Ruhullah announced his resignation from both the National Conference and the Lok Sabha.In an 80-minute address, the Srinagar MP launched a scathing attack on Farooq and Omar Abdullah, accusing the leadership of abandoning its promises on Article 370, political prisoners and public relief.Describing his departure as a "decree of freedom", Ruhullah called the NC a "deceitful, corrupt organisation"."You told people that you were the guardians of their dignity. You said that if anyone touched that dignity, it would be like grabbing you by the collar. That dignity was buried on August 5, 2019. Tell me now, where is that dignity? Where is that autonomy?" he asked, targeting the party leadership.He accused the NC of seeking power on promises it had failed to fulfil and said he could no longer lend his name to what he described as political humiliation.On November 6, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla formally accepted his resignation, creating a vacancy in the Srinagar parliamentary constituency.Ruhullah's departure is more than an organisational setback for the NC. Elected to the Lok Sabha on the party's ticket in 2024, he had emerged as one of its most vocal faces on the question of Kashmir's political rights after the abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019.While Omar Abdullah has sought to pursue the restoration of statehood and special status through legislative and political channels, Ruhullah has demanded a more uncompromising approach. His exit gives him the opportunity to position himself as a voice of those who believe the NC has softened its stand after coming to power.He has hinted at launching a broader political movement rather than immediately forming a new party, saying he wants to bring together people committed to restoring the dignity and rights of Jammu and Kashmir.
Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi accused the NC leadership of abandoning its promises on Kashmir's dignity and autonomy after the abrogation of Article 370.
The NC, meanwhile, has questioned his own record, asking why he did not move a resolution or private member's bill in Parliament on special status or mobilise fellow MPs on the issue, despite having secured the support of more than 100 parliamentarians for an impeachment motion against an Allahabad High Court judge.The public exchange has exposed a larger ideological fault line: can the NC continue to claim ownership of the political struggle for Kashmir's rights while defending its record in government?
The arithmetic ceiling
While the ideological dissent has played out in public, the discontent within the legislative wing has centred on the distribution of power.The immediate trigger was the October 27 cabinet expansion, in which four new ministers were inducted, taking the council of ministers to its maximum permissible strength of nine.The restriction is rooted in Section 53 of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, which caps the council of ministers at 10% of the total membership of the Legislative Assembly. With 90 elected seats, the permissible strength is nine, including the chief minister.This creates a structural constraint for Omar Abdullah. Unlike a full-fledged state, where the constitutional ceiling for the council of ministers is 15% of the assembly's strength, Jammu and Kashmir's Union Territory framework leaves the CM with a smaller pool of ministerial positions to distribute.With all nine positions occupied, accommodating more aspirants would require dropping or replacing existing ministers.Several senior legislators, including six-time MLA Mubarak Gul, were reportedly unhappy at being left out. The discontent was not limited to ministerial berths. The legislators also raised concerns about administrative functioning, organisational decisions and what they described as the concentration of authority among a small group of leaders and advisers.A group of 18 aggrieved legislators had met a week before the Friday meeting. The subsequent gathering of 15 MLAs at Gupkar brought their grievances directly to Farooq and Omar Abdullah.The legislators reportedly sought a review of the cabinet, changes in the functioning of the CM's office and a mechanism to ensure that elected representatives have a greater say in government decisions.One of the legislators, Nazir Gurezi, sought to play down speculation about the emergence of a separate faction."A few days ago, we sat together at a place, and from there, social media hyped it up as if a separate faction had emerged from the National Conference. No separate faction or party has emerged," he said.Gurezi added that the legislators had placed their concerns before the CM and the party president, who had assured them that the issues would be addressed.For Omar Abdullah, however, the problem is not merely placating a group of unhappy MLAs. The cabinet expansion has exhausted the government's primary instrument of political accommodation. Any reshuffle could create fresh resentment among those who have already secured ministerial positions.Farooq's intervention may have prevented the discontent from turning into an open confrontation for now, but the leadership will have to find ways of accommodating senior legislators without triggering another round of dissatisfaction.
Omar Abdullah's Union Territory dilemma
The constraints facing Omar Abdullah go beyond cabinet arithmetic. They strike at the heart of the political contradiction of running an elected government in a Union Territory where the Lieutenant Governor and the Centre retain significant powers.Omar has repeatedly complained about the limits placed on his government, particularly in matters involving administration and the functioning of the bureaucracy.During the September 2026 assembly proceedings on a resolution seeking immediate restoration of full statehood, he revealed that the Law Secretary had written to the Speaker questioning whether the resolution should be discussed because the matter was sub judice. The chief secretary had also written to the Speaker.Omar, who also holds the law portfolio, expressed surprise at the communications."I am a law minister and I don't know that my law secretary is giving you an opinion. As a CM I don't know the chief secretary is writing to the Speaker against my resolution. I don't know on whose behalf it is being done," he said.He went on to question whether such a situation would arise in a full-fledged state."Would you think such a thing would happen in any State? This happens only in UT where a CM moves a resolution and the law secretary gives an opinion against it," he said.The episode illustrates the difficult position in which the chief minister finds himself. To deliver on everyday governance, including infrastructure, electricity, welfare schemes and administrative decisions, Omar has to work within the existing institutional arrangement. But the same arrangement limits his authority and has become a source of political frustration for his government.Every compromise with the Centre risks being interpreted by sections of the electorate as a dilution of the NC's political promises. Every confrontation, meanwhile, can further constrain the government's ability to function.The NC's August 19, 2024 manifesto had made restoration of Articles 370 and 35A a key promise. It also pledged to work towards restoration of statehood, repeal of the Public Safety Act and release of political prisoners.
CM Abdullah on statehood resolution.
The party subsequently sought to demonstrate its commitment through the assembly. On November 6, 2024, the House passed a resolution seeking restoration of special status, a move Ruhullah had initially welcomed.But two years after the abrogation of Article 370, the Centre has given no indication of reversing its decision. Statehood, too, remains unresolved, while the reservation policy has become another source of friction between the government and sections of the electorate.The NC has defended its record on reservations, saying its cabinet sub-committee has initiated changes but that the decisions are awaiting action from the Centre and the Lieutenant Governor's administration.Farooq Abdullah, after Friday's meeting, reiterated that the party would continue its fight for statehood and Articles 370 and 35A, taking the struggle to its "logical conclusion".
Political space opening up beyond NC
Ruhullah's exit could challenge the NC's claim to represent Kashmir's political aspirations. Having been elected on its ticket in 2024, he may now seek to occupy the political space he believes the party has vacated.The political implications will depend on whether Ruhullah can translate his criticism into an organised platform and attract support beyond his existing constituency. His resignation has already created a vacancy in Srinagar, and the eventual by-election could become an important test of the political space he hopes to occupy.The BJP has been quick to seize on the National Conference's internal troubles. On November 3, BJP national vice president Ram Madhav said Ruhullah's rally in Budgam had the blessings of "our people". The NC subsequently accused the BJP of attempting "Operation Lotus" in Kashmir, a charge the party has denied. For the BJP, the public friction within the ruling party offers an opportunity to question its cohesion and, more importantly, Omar Abdullah's leadership.The Congress, the NC's alliance partner, has taken a more cautious line. It has sought to play down the developments, attributing Ruhullah's departure to ideological differences while expressing confidence that the NC would resolve its internal disagreements.
But the strains within its ally also pose a political concern for the Congress, given its investment in the governing arrangement.For the Abdullahs, however, the challenge is that the two crises have unfolded back-to-back on different fronts.Farooq Abdullah's show of unity at Gupkar may have helped contain the immediate optics of the MLAs' rebellion. It does little, however, to answer the larger questions raised by Ruhullah's exit.The next few months will answer whether Omar Abdullah can hold his flock together and retain the public's trust at the same time.

How Hong Kong can double asset holdings: target world’s ‘patient’ capital, FSDC advises
City could double assets with just small portion of the more than US$100 trillion held by global pension funds and insurers, council advises
Assets under management in Hong Kong would double with the addition of just a small portion of the money global insurance and pension funds have to invest, according to a member of the Financial Development Services Council (FSDC).
Hong Kong should do more to attract this so-called patient capital – assets that insurance companies and pension funds invest for the long term, said the government think tank that promotes the city as an international financial centre, in a report on Wednesday.
Globally, pension funds had total assets of US$68 trillion at the end of last year, while global insurers had investment assets of US$42 trillion at the end of 2024, according to data from the FSDC.

Gurugram traffic policemen, homeguards to be transferred every 60 days after Diwali 'gift' demand leads to crackdown
Traffic personnel will be transferred through an automated system, zonal officers and traffic inspectors will be held accountable for staff's corrupt practices.
After a home guard was arrested for allegedly demanding "Diwali gifts" from a motorist in Gurugram, Police Commissioner Sibash Kabiraj has issued a series of instructions for traffic policemen and home guards to minimise the possibilities of irregularities while they perform their duties.
According to officials on Tuesday, random transfers will be carried out among the Gurugram traffic personnel every 60 days through an automated computerised system.
Zonal Officer (ZO) and Traffic Inspector (TI) will be held accountable if any traffic police personnel, home guard or special police officer is found involved in corrupt practices while performing traffic duty, they added.
The home guard incident took place on November 7, when a vlogger was travelling with his family in Gurugram. He was signalled by a home guard to pull over the car near Cyber Hub, and the latter repeatedly wished them "Happy Diwali".
Also read: Home guard held for demanding ‘Diwali gift’ from two car occupants in Gurugram
The accused home guard then allegedly began indirectly soliciting money or "gifts", saying it had been a "dry Diwali". When the vlogger said he did not have his wallet with him, the accused reportedly said, "So, none of the brothers sitting in the car has their wallets?"
Subsequently, a video of the incident surfaced on the internet.
An FIR was registered against the home guard at the DLF Phase-3 police station, and the accused was arrested.
According to the police on Tuesday, the police commissioner has also directed all deputy commissioners (DCsP) and assistant commissioners (ACsP) to conduct meetings with their subordinate officers and personnel up to the zonal level and issue strict instructions that any misconduct or corrupt practices while on duty will not be tolerated under any circumstances.

Further, the ACP-rank officers deployed in the Police Control Room have to ensure regular inspection and monitoring of all CCTV cameras so that the conduct of police personnel while on duty can be effectively monitored.
Instructions have also been issued to ensure that challan proceedings for traffic rule violations are carried out under the surveillance of body-worn Cameras, the police said.

A video is going viral on social media, where a young man is heard saying in Bangla, “We won’t allow any Hindutva aggression or Indian aggression in Jagannath University.”
The video wad shared by X handle Voice of BD Hindus (@HinduUnityBD) on November 7 with the claim that Muslim students of Jagannath University in Bangladesh had declared Diwali as a form of Hindutva aggression. (Archive)
🚨 BREAKING : Jamaat Student leaders at Jagannath University have declared Diwali a form of “Hindutva aggression” and “Indian aggression,”
announcing that they will not allow Diwali celebrations to take place on campus. But they can celebrate EID. A Hindu Zamindar Built Jagannath University.
— Voice Of BD Hindus 🇧🇩 (@HinduUnityBD) November 7, 2026
In the 25-second-long clip, the man states, “We won’t allow any Hindutva aggression or Indian aggression in Jagannath University. This university is situated in a country of 92% Muslims, and the university claims that it runs by nurturing the culture, ethics and heritage of the Muslims. If anyone wants to make things work differently, the people of Bangladesh will give a befitting reply. Inshallah”.
The video was also shared by X user Monica Verma with the claim that “Muslim Students in Bangladesh are calling Deepawali celebrations as “Hindu aggression” warning the Hindu students of consequences if they celebrate it.”
Muslim Students in Bangladesh are calling Deepawali celebrations as “Hindu aggression” warning the Hindu students of consequences if they celebrate it.
Indian as well as the global Media will never show you this side of the F*cked Up Bangladeshi Gen Z. https://t.co/wij366yQtp
— Monica Verma (@TrulyMonica) November 7, 2026
Several other prominent Indian social media users shared the same video with similar claims.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the claim, we conducted a reverse image search using key frames from the video in question.
This led us to a video published by Bangladesh-based media outlet ‘Desh Somoy News’. The video is identical to the one currently going viral and was published on October 16 in connection with the beef festival controversy at Jagannath University in Dhaka.
The controversy at Dhaka’s Jagannath University began on October 12, when students of the department of Islamic history and culture organised a beef feast near the university’s central temple. Hindu students objected to the proximity of the cooking arrangements to the temple and the alleged use of temple bricks to build a makeshift stove. Protests followed, triggering a wider dispute on campus.
On October 14, the university administration issued a notice prohibiting animal slaughter on campus, prompting further student protests.
Protesting against the administrative decision, students led by the Jagannath University Central Student’s Union organized a rally in the campus on October 14 itself, and held an impromptu press conference after the protest rally. The video in question is from that press conference.
Bangladesh-based online news portal Bd24report covered the press conference on its Facebook page on October 14. The live video is 17 minutes long, and from 5:13 minute mark, the press conference can be seen. At the 8:39-minute mark, the social work secretary of the Student’s Union, Mustafizur Rahaman, addresses the press. Rahaman is the same person seen speaking in the viral video.
Rahaman spoke from 8:50 till 10:56 minute mark, and the viral snippet is from 10:22 till 10:47. There was no mention of Diwali in the entire programme. The students spoke in protest against the University administration’s decision to ban animal slaughter within the campus.
Although the administration subsequently softened its position, students led by the Jagannath University Central Student’s Union slaughtered a cow on October 16 and organised a beef feast. The student’s union is run by Jamaat-e-Islami Bangladesh’s student wing Islami Chatra Shibir backed candidates.
On October 17, Bangladesh Khelafat Chatra Majlish held a similar feast, slaughtering a second cow and organising a Qawwali programme.
It is also important to note that Diwali celebrations and Kali Puja were organized on the Jagannath University campus this year. A pandal was set up for Kali Puja and students were seen creating ‘alpona’, a traditional Bengali art form drawn on floors, which is considered auspicious.
To sum up, a video related to the controversial beef festival on Dhaka’s Jagannath University campus in October is viral with the false claim that Jamaat student leaders objected to Diwali celebrations at the university. The statements made in the clip have got nothing to do with Diwali. Besides, Kali Puja was held on the campus like previous years.

Quick Answer
LastWave, Musify, Convx, Spotube, and SimpMusic are free open-source clients for YouTube Music and Spotify. They unlock premium perks without subscription fees or ad tracking, offering background playback, offline downloads, time-synced lyrics, lossless audio, and customized interfaces without locked controls.
Subscription prices are going through the roof. And when you stack multiple subscriptions together, it can put a big hole in your pocket. For listening to music, we usually depend on Spotify and YouTube Music. They are the default music streaming sources for millions across the globe. Though there are alternatives from which you can hear high-quality audio, they just can’t match the ease of popular apps. But you are bombarded with ads, and several features are locked behind a paywall unless you pay.
Thankfully, you don’t have to search the internet for free options. Developers around the world have built free apps that give you many of those perks. Below are five of the best, what each does well, and what to watch out for before installing.
Table of Contents
Why are open-source music apps worth a look?
To be clear, most of these apps are clients. This means that they don’t store any music themselves. They plug into a service like YouTube Music and show it in a cleaner, ad-free interface with extra features on top, which you’d usually get after paying for a premium subscription. For me, Spotify has been the go-to music streaming app, but slowly the app has become quite greedy.
After a few times, the next and previous song buttons get locked, and it asks you to pay to unlock them. I mean, what is wrong with companies today? Thankfully, I have now ditched Spotify and have picked one of the below open-source music options.
That has three practical effects:
- No ads and no subscription fees. Everything below is free.
- Most of these apps have no ad trackers or tracking SDKs.
- New features are constantly added, and some of them aren’t even available in paid apps.
The catch is that these apps rely on unofficial methods to fetch music, so they can break when YouTube or Spotify changes something. Treat them as great free alternatives, but not as rock-solid replacements. Let us take a look at the free alternatives.
Best free open-source music apps
LastWave
If you care about how your music sounds, LastWave is the one to install first. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. Most of us would care about the free music that we get with LastWave, but you will soon appreciate the quality of music that it offers. And since it is a YouTube Music client, you are getting access to almost every song that is available on YouTube.
The headline feature is lossless FLAC audio, up to 24-bit/192 kHz. When you press play, the song starts playing right away on the fastest available stream, and while you listen, the app fetches the lossless version in the background and switches over once it’s ready. On compatible phones and headphones, LastWave also plays the Dolby Atmos version of a song automatically. For those who own a USB DAC or a pair of IEMs, there’s a bit-perfect mode that sends raw, unprocessed audio straight to your device.
The app is packed with features that normally sit behind a subscription. The lyrics are synced word-by-word and pulled from sources like Apple Music, Musixmatch, and LRCLIB. There’s a 10-band equalizer with presets for thousands of headphone models, and smart playlists that build mixes from your listening history. Plus, you have the option to import playlists from Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube Music in seconds, and even sync your Spotify liked songs.
Musify
Not everyone wants a hundred settings and toggles. Some people just want to listen to their favorite music without having to deal with ads and a hundred pop-ups about purchasing the subscription between two songs. Musify is for people who just want to open an app, search for a song, and press play. It’s a lightweight Android app built around Material You, which means its colors automatically match your phone’s theme and wallpaper.
Using it is fairly easy. You search for songs, albums, artists, or playlists and start streaming over Wi-Fi or mobile data. If you want to save data or listen on a flight, you can download tracks and play them offline. It lets you create your own playlists, rename and reorder them, or import existing ones from online sources. The player shows lyrics so you can follow along. You can also control the quality of the audio.
There are no annoying banner ads, no audio ads, no sign-up, and no tracking inside the app, and the interface is translated into dozens of languages by the community. I found this to be a great choice for older phones, or for a parent or sibling who finds complicated apps annoying.
Convx
While most open source music apps work well, there are only a few that also feel nice to use. Convx comes in the second category. If you like iOS’s “Liquid Glass” design, then you would love Convx. It brings iPhone’s Liquid Glass design to Android, with frosted, see-through menus, floating controls, and album-inspired colors that change with whatever you are playing.
Under the pretty surface, Convx is a complete music player. You can browse and stream music, save songs for offline listening, build queues and playlists, set a sleep timer, change playback speed, and tweak the sound to your taste with an equalizer. What makes it stand out among the heavy hitters is its DJ-style playback. You also get automix, crossfade, and smooth transitions between one song and the next. Lyrics are synced word by word and come from several providers, plus it gets animated artwork.
Convx can play local files and even songs stored on a home server or NAS through SMB and WebDAV. You can choose the option to import your Spotify playlists, show what you’re playing on Discord, scrobble to Last.fm, recognize songs playing around you, and use Listen Together to sync playback with friends.
Spotube
Spotube is the veteran here, with over 46,000 stars on GitHub, and it works differently from the rest. Instead of being locked to one service like Spotify or YouTube, it runs on plugins. You choose your own music sources, metadata, and playlists through plugins made by the community, or if you’re good with it, you can write one yourself.
The biggest advantage is that it works everywhere. Spotube runs natively on Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. This means you can use the same app on your phone and your laptop. It’s small, fast, and light on data. You can import and sync playlists from popular music services or manage them locally. It gives time-synced lyrics from public lyric databases no matter which source you use. Offline downloads are supported, with proper metadata and ID.
Privacy is one of the biggest highlights of Spotube. It collects no telemetry and no user data. Installing it is also easy, because you can download it through winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, Homebrew, Flatpak, and F-Droid.
SimpMusic
SimpMusic is that one app that does everything. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android and desktop that borrows many of Spotify’s best ideas. You can play music from YouTube Music or regular YouTube without ads, and it gets you background playback. You can browse the home feed, charts, podcasts and moods, search everything on YouTube, cache songs for offline playback and use Android Auto.
SimpMusic Wrapped gives you a year-in-music recap just like Spotify’s. Then there is monthly recap playlists and listening charts that stay on your device. There are three Now Playing styles, including one that looks like Apple Music, and the lyrics are synced in 12 languages. You can even share lyrics as an image.
You can switch to 1080p video with subtitles, skip sponsor segments with SponsorBlock, see dislike counts with Return YouTube Dislike, and use a 10-band equalizer with AutoEq headphone profiles.
Which one should you pick?
If you care most about sound quality, I would suggest LastWave. If you want something simple, pick Musify. If design matters to you, try Convx. If you want plugins and an app that runs on every device you own, choose Spotube. If you want the most features in one place, install SimpMusic. The best part is that all five are free and can be installed side by side, so you can try a few and keep your favorite. You will get access to unlimited songs from the best sources in good quality. There’s a specific mantra drilled into government workers, military officers, and intelligence personnel during counterintelligence briefings: “If she’s a 10 and you’re a 5, she’s a spy!” Or, as the US Army’s Counterintelligence Command posted on Valentine’s Day: “It doesn’t take a mathematician to figure out ‘10 + 5 = honeytrap.’” The very beautiful woman who is suddenly interested in your very ordinary existence probably has ulterior motives, is the message.
Jensen Huang surely doesn’t live a typical life—he’s a centibillionaire, the swashbuckling CEO of Nvidia, one of the hottest and most geopolitically consequential companies of the 21st century. Surely he’s aware of the possibility that he’d cross paths with intelligence assets. In fact, it’s hard to think of many companies in the world that would be a higher priority target for foreign intelligence agencies.
All of that makes the stock-shaking news this week all the more surprising. How did Huang get embroiled in a spy scandal that mixes infidelity, international espionage, the Trump administration, and the economic behemoth of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry?
The story kicked off just before Halloween, with a six-byline story in The New York Times reporting that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Starting somewhere between 2024 and 2025, Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a one-time executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider known as Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies warned top US officials that they believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. So far, Nvidia’s board, which has launched its own investigation, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that’s far from the only concern.
As one would expect, China has denied any nefarious plot centered on Jensen Huang. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Monday said, “The narrative about so-called Chinese spies is entirely based on groundless speculation—it’s nothing more than slander and smearing.”
But according to reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times, US intelligence officials also claim that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was reporting to China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. On Monday, Megaspeed said on LinkedIn that US authorities found “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities." (There’s no indication so far that Alice Huang, a one-time Chinese state journalist, is an employee or “officer” of Chinese intelligence; she’s believed to be an “asset,” an outsider who aids an intelligence agency, sometimes for pay, sometimes not.)
China, though, has elevated economic espionage to a core pillar of its economic and military development, stealing the designs for everything from US fighter jets to solar panels and commercial paint recipes. “Honeypots” or “honey traps”—positioning an alluring operative to seduce or develop a relationship with a key target—are one of intelligence’s most infamous and well-established strategies. French officials have warned specifically about Chinese honeypots since at least 2011, when intelligence reports cited a pharmaceutical researcher who was seduced and then blackmailed by a Chinese spy operation.
Over the past quarter of a century, as Silicon Valley emerged as a center of political and economic power, it has become a key focus of Chinese intelligence. In one plot, a Chinese national named Fang Fang spent years trying to cozy up to Bay Area politicians, including then US Representative Eric Swalwell. (While intelligence officials at the time reportedly believed Fang to be an operative, law enforcement officials never brought any charges against her). When traveling to China, US business executives have become accustomed to leaving their regular phones and computers at home and using burner devices to prevent the installation of spyware or malware (as I did, when I traveled to China for WIRED in 2019 to report on Huawei). In 2012, when Leon Panetta was making his first trip to China as defense secretary, he and his team were advised to bathe and shower in the dark in the event his hotel room was bugged. Last year, the threat of honeypots prompted the US government to explicitly ban personnel working in China and Hong Kong from engaging in romantic or sexual relationships with Chinese citizens. More recently, US officials joined with allies to warn about China’s increasingly sophisticated “LinkedIn espionage”: using the business-focused social networking site to recruit and build relationships with unwitting executives.
Alice Huang’s Megaspeed, for its part, is a major Pacific region player in cloud services focused on the advanced computer chips that are the heart of Nvidia’s business. The Biden administration had sharply limited the export of cutting-edge chips globally to slow China’s development of AI, but Jensen Huang has successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen those restrictions.
Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Donald Trump denied having prior knowledge of Alice Huang’s potential espionage. “I didn’t hear about it then, but a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that,” Trump said. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’” On Tuesday, the Times reported that Marco Rubio had briefed Trump in May, right before Jensen Huang joined the President on Air Force One for a trip to China.
The veracity of Trump's claims will surely be investigated, especially in the context of the famous Watergate maxim: “What did the president know and when did he know it?” Nvidia’s CEO has been publicly linked to the Megaspeed executive since at least 2024 and Alice’s husband, Kang Weigh, has reportedly known Jensen since the 2010s. WIRED’s Lauren Goode reported on Monday that Jensen Huang, starting in 2025, hired Risa Heller’s crisis communications firm, which is well-versed in handling public sex scandals. This spring, secretary of state Marco Rubio evidently helped craft a classified memo inside the administration warning officials about Jensen Huang’s potentially compromising relationship.
Jensen Huang—who has developed an important reputation as AI’s #1 cheerleader at the frontier of AI labs—is now stuck in an awkward situation. Is he an idiot, unaware that his paramour might have been a foreign intelligence asset? Merely reckless with his own reputation, fiduciary responsibility to Nvidia, and the technological security of the United States? Or a witting accomplice to undermining US national security?
Regardless of the truth, Nvidia loses. Shareholders have ridden a roller-coaster that has seen Nvidia’s stock rise by about 600 percent over the past five years, becoming the world’s second-most valuable company. In the past month, the stock has plummeted by a quarter. The disaster for Nvidia is just beginning, it seems, as lawsuits loom, including by its own shareholders.
Similarly, the Trump administration is likely to face real questions from the newly Democratic congress: When were the president and other top officials briefed about this intelligence threat? What communication, if any, did they make to Nvidia and to whom? Should more have been done by US intelligence to block Alice Huang from having access to Nvidia and its CEO?
The fact that Megaspeed is a major customer of Nvidia makes everything more complicated. Indeed, reports have circulated for at least a year that the US was concerned that Megaspeed was diverting chips to Chinese intelligence agencies, an allegation that could have massive consequences for the global AI race. Bloomberg this week reported that Megaspeed's subsidiaries have purchased billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips and that an audit requested by the US government last year found that Megaspeed couldn’t initially account for some 50,000 chips it had purchased.
Meanwhile, Nvidia’s Huang and President Trump developed a uniquely close professional relationship. They’ve met multiple times as Huang has pushed to loosen Biden-era export controls, which Trump has repeatedly relaxed; Huang has donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project; while en route to Beijing earlier this year with a delegation of tech leaders, including Elon Musk and Tim Cook, Trump’s Air Force One actually made a special stop in Alaska to pick up Huang; Huang also attended a White House state dinner for Chinese president Xi Jinping and Trump, who in turn, awarded him a National Medal of Science earlier this fall.
The implication that Trump knew and did nothing for a year would make this one of the greatest counterintelligence failures of the past decade. There will be consequences: Across history, many have gone to prison for honeypot scandals; a former adviser was arrested just last year in a similar plot; though he was acquitted of committing economic espionage, he was convicted for making false statements to investigators.
Even in normal circumstances, corporate America’s tolerance of CEO misbehavior has shrunken dramatically. In recent years, CEOs at companies as varied as Nestlé, Kohl’s, BP, NBCUniversal, and the railroad Norfolk Southern have all resigned or been forced out after inappropriate relationships that violated company standards.
If Nvidia were any other company and Jensen Huang any other CEO, the facts of the scandal currently known would be enough to topple some heads. But Trump is still president, and November is only a third over. It’s not even clear that this will rank as the biggest scandal of the month—but it should.

What is the 'Dead Internet Theory' and should humanity be worried?
When spending time online today, do you ever get the feeling that digital life has become eerily less human? Perhaps social media posts seem a bit off, or you get the sneaking suspicion the customer service representative you are chatting with is actually a bot. If this sounds familiar, you aren't alone: a paradigm called the "dead internet theory" has been gaining momentum in the last several years, positing that the internet is increasingly dominated by non-human activity, including bots and AI-generated content.
Since the theory first started making the rounds on internet forums in the 2010s, AI has only gotten more powerful. In September 2026, OpenAI reported that it had found a solution to a famously difficult mathematics puzzle, the Navier-Stokes problem. Meanwhile, a 2026 report from cybersecurity group Thales found that automated traffic continues to overtake human activity online, with bots accounting for 53 percent of all web traffic, up from 51 percent the year before. And bots are now talking to each other without humans in the loop at all: In March, Meta acquired Moltbook — a social network on which AI chatbots communicate with one another, often discussing humans. So as the internet landscape potentially gets less human every day, what exactly is dead internet theory, where does it come from, and should we be worried?
What is the dead internet theory?
Dead Internet Theory — the idea that the majority of the internet is propelled by bots and other non-human agents – has been floating around for quite some time. It first emerged as a conspiracy theory on internet forums in the late 2010s, but gained a more concrete framework following a post in 2021 on online community Agora Road titled, "Dead Internet Theory: Most of the Internet Is Fake," which argued "the Internet feels empty and devoid of people." Followers of the theory argued that the internet "died" around 2016 when search engines and social media feeds started surfacing more AI-generated content.
The popularity of chatbots and AI-generated content has only further expanded since then. In 2024, only 33 percent of Americans said they had used chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot, a study from Pew Research found. By 2026, that number had increased to nearly half of Americans at 49 percent. That same report found that 25 percent of Americans use chatbots every day. In many realms of society we are now facing chatbot loops: in schools, students are writing essays using AI, which teachers then grade with AI. In the job search, employees use chatbots to spit out optimized resumes and cover letters which are then analyzed by AI systems. Increasingly, humans are cut out of the conversation entirely, our voices replaced with bots.
Should we be worried?
On a personal level, this chatbot loop can feel uncanny. Those script-like posts we see on LinkedIn or a soulless AI-generated poster at your local cafe can induce a feeling of existential dread, but the consequences go beyond personal discomfort. Bots can spread disinformation that causes real harm. AI chatbots are increasingly a source of election disinformation, and little is being done legislatively to regulate this new frontier, though government agencies have issued warnings on deepfakes and other AI-powered risks to free elections.
As AI use grows, so has the backlash: 40 percent of Americans say they think AI will have a negative impact on society in the next 20 years, according to a Pew Research study. AI detection is becoming increasingly popular, with company Pangram receiving $9 million in backing in July 2026 for its AI detection system. Following the passage of the EU AI Act, OpenAI has started watermarking AI-generated content. With measures like these, people opposed to AI will hopefully be able to more easily spot and avoid the artificial slop in favor of the human-centric connection they initially came to the internet to find.

The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) on Tuesday provided an update on the case of Indian Merchant Navy Captain Ajay Pant, who was taken into custody by British authorities on charges related to the transportation of sanctioned Russian oil. The ministry said it remains in regular contact with his lawyers and family. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, speaking at a regular media briefing, said India's High Commission in London and the ministry in New Delhi have maintained communication with British authorities, the shipmaster’s lawyers and his family to safeguard his well-being and ensure access to legal support, ANI reported. Held in judicial custody in the UK since June, Pant's case has brought renewed attention to the circumstances surrounding his arrest and his career in the Merchant Navy. In official statements, UK authorities have identified Pant as a 38-year-old Indian national and the captain of MV Smyrtos, a tanker described by the British government as part of Russia's shadow fleet. While the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and other UK authorities have not released further biographical details about Pant, information shared by the Uttarakhand Chief Minister's Office on June 25 said he is a resident of the state and is lodged at HMP Winchester. According to an Al Jazeera report, Pant has been a sailor for 18 years and would spend around six to seven months at sea each year. The Indian Merchant Navy captain is married and has two children, aged eight and one. He was also the primary breadwinner for his family. Pant's detention stems from a UK investigation into the alleged transportation of Russian oil in violation of sanctions. The case dates back to June, when British authorities intercepted the tanker he was commanding in the English Channel. Pant was detained on June 14, 2026, after British authorities seized MV Smyrtos, a tanker identified as part of Russia's shadow fleet. He was charged over an alleged breach of Russian sanctions following the vessel's interception in the English Channel. According to reports, the Crown Prosecution Service accused Pant of transporting or facilitating the delivery of Russian oil and petroleum products by sea to another country, allegedly in violation of restrictions under the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. Since his arrest, the Indian High Commission in London and the MEA have remained in contact with Pant, his legal counsel and his family, while also engaging with British authorities. On Tuesday, Jaiswal detailed the consular assistance being extended to Pant and his family. He said, "We have been in touch with the lawyers of Captain Pant as well as his family. The High Commission has paid several visits to Captain Pant to check on his well-being. We have also facilitated the visit of his family members, his wife in particular. The last such visit by his wife took place on 9th of November. We have been in touch with the UK High Commission here as well as the UK Foreign Office in this particular matter. We are trying to do our best for his safety and well-being..." The MEA spokesperson added that officials were continuing to monitor Pant's welfare and coordinate with British authorities to ensure he had access to legal assistance ahead of his trial. Earlier, in August, Jaiswal had said that although the matter was legal in nature, the Indian High Commission in London was providing consular assistance to Pant. He added that the MEA had also taken up the matter with British authorities. He said at the time, "I would say that this is a legal matter, but we are closely following this particular issue. We continue to be in touch with the lawyers of Captain Ajay Pant, as well as his family. Our High Commission paid a consular visit to him on 24th June to enquire about his well-being.
