In November, a rumor spread that activists anonymously placed a golden statue of U.S. President Donald Trump rubbing his foot on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., referring to him avoiding the draft during the Vietnam War because he allegedly had a bone spur.
The claim and photographs of the supposed statue circulated on social media, including on Facebook and Reddit. An X post (archived) shared two images and said "The satirical monument, installed just ahead of Veterans Day, mocks Trump's Vietnam War draft deferment for bone spurs":
One of the photographs showed an epigraph at the base of the statue that read:
We honor the service and sacrifice of our commander in chief, Donald J. Trump. He's a soldier in spirit, who marched to the front lines of dodging the draft, armed with a perfect diagnosis of bone spurs.
We salute a leader who knows you can't spell sacrifice without "I," and a warrior who reminds us that sometimes when you're called to stand up, it's best to just sit down and rest your feet.
"I can be very military." — President Donald J. Trump
"The foot soldier," another inscription at the bottom said.
Meanwhile, Snopes readers searched our website, seeking confirmation that the statue was real.
It was. The statue appeared in a series of photographs on the reputable image bank Getty Images. Further, the organization responsible for putting it up confirmed it had in an email to Snopes. For this reason, we rated the claim true.
It also appeared on video news reports, including one by WUSA, a CBS affiliate in Washington:
The report said the statue was the work of an organization known as The Secret Handshake, an anonymous collective that also made the "Best Friends Forever" statue of Trump and late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein holding hands.
"We did put up the Bone Spur statue," The Secret Handshake told Snopes in an email.
The statue evokes the draft deferments Trump benefited from in the 1960s, during the Vietnam War. His disqualification in 1968 cited a medical reason, without providing details. In 2016, his campaign said it was because of bone spurs.
Three years later, Trump's former lawyer Michael Cohen testified that the president had not shown medical records proving the reason for his disqualification, according to a transcript of his testimony to the House Committee on Oversight and Reform:
Mr. Trump tasked me to handle the negative press surrounding his medical deferment from the Vietnam draft.
Mr. Trump claimed it was because of a bone spur. But when I asked for medical records, he gave me none and said that there was no surgery. He told me not to answer the specific questions by reporters, but rather, offer simply the fact that he received a medical deferment. He finished the conversation with the following comment. ''You think I'm stupid? I'm not going to Vietnam.'' And I find it ironic, Mr. President, that you are in Vietnam right now. And yet, I continued to work for him.
The statue is a humorous take on the suggestion that Trump allegedly dodged the draft without providing a real medical reason for not serving his country in Vietnam. It appeared on the National Mall on Nov. 9, two days before Veterans Day.
For further reading, Snopes has reported on other statues that derided Trump, including one that showed him naked in the European Parliament.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
- Published
A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial".
The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines.
Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy.
The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns.
Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.
The BBC has asked the US department of health and human services for comment.
Here is what you need to know.
What was the trial?
The study was planned at the Bandim Health Project, a research centre that has operated in Guinea-Bissau since 1978.
It was designed to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving a hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth and the other half not being given the shot.
Bandim said the trial aimed to investigate whether the hepatitis B vaccine given at birth has broader health effects beyond preventing infection.
Previous studies in The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau have raised questions about a possible link to increased mortality.
Researchers argued that because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccinations at birth, despite WHO recommendations, they have a unique opportunity to study its effects before such vaccines are introduced in 2028.
But critics questioned the ethics of withholding the vaccine from some babies, particularly in one of the world's poorest countries, where the infection is widespread.
The Trump administration funded the proposed study, with the CDC awarding the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) $1.6m (£1.2m) in December 2025.
What did the WHO say?
Walter Kazadi Mulombo, the WHO representative in Guinea-Bissau, told the BBC they became concerned after receiving questions about the study and finding no publicly available protocol.
He said the main ethical concern was that the trial would withhold an intervention already proven to protect newborns against hepatitis B.
"The vaccine has been used for more than 30 years in more than 115 countries," he said. "A study that will withhold that intervention from other newborns is unethical."
He warned that babies could be exposed to the virus during childbirth if their mothers were infected, as well as later in life.
Nearly a fifth of the population of Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, a viral infection that affects the liver.
Those infected during infancy are particularly likely to develop chronic infections, which kill up to 25% of people, mostly through liver failure or liver cancer, according to data published in 2020.
The WHO is working with the government to bring forward the birth-dose vaccine.
"The country had been expected to add it to its routine immunisation schedule in 2028, but officials are considering introducing it in the first quarter of next year," Mulombo said.
Guinea-Bissau currently vaccinates children against hepatitis B at six weeks, which means it is less effective.
Why did Guinea-Bissau reject the trial?
Guinea-Bissau's government prohibited hepatitis B vaccine trials involving children in January. At the time, it requested a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study.
Health Minister Quinhin Nantote said in October that the suspension remained in force and had not been overturned by the Council of Ministers after reports emerged claiming that the trial would be taking place after all.
"We were surprised to learn from media reports that the study might proceed," Nantote said. "We are outraged because even I, as the minister responsible for this sector, was not informed."
The dispute intensified after the SDU said a revised study protocol had received ethical approval "from the relevant authorities in Guinea-Bissau", which Nantote denied.
Dr Gavin Yamey, a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in the US, criticised the proposal.
"The proposed trial reeks of neocolonialism," he told the BBC, questioning why the research was not being conducted in Denmark.
His criticism centred on the decision to withhold a recommended vaccine from some newborns in a country where hepatitis B is widespread.
SDU dean Jakob Grauslund said the trial had never started, no babies had been enrolled and no vaccinations administered as part of the research.
Was the trial approved by anyone?
The SDU said it had received a separate, positive assessment from the university's own research ethics committee.
Grauslund said the university had sought an additional independent assessment, although Danish law did not require one.
He added that the relevant Danish statutory research ethics bodies were unable to undertake the review.
Following the approval from the SDU's ethics committee, Grauslund decided that the project could proceed.
He, however, stressed that this did not replace the separate authorisation required from Guinea-Bissau's authorities.
What has happened to the vaccines?
On 19 October, Guinea-Bissau's Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project's facilities in the capital, Bissau, and seized a batch of hepatitis B vaccines.
Police said the batch was intended for vaccinating children but did not disclose how many doses had been seized or the specific grounds for the investigation.
They stressed that the seizure did not, in itself, mean the vaccines were defective or unsafe.
The police have not explicitly said whether their investigation relates to the proposed trial, the importation of the vaccines or other circumstances surrounding the batch.
Grauslund said he could not comment on the seizure of the vaccines.
Who is funding the research?
The proposed trial was funded by the US government at a time of significant changes to vaccine policy under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Kennedy.
Under Kennedy's leadership, a US vaccine panel attempted to end a longstanding recommendation that all newborns receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth, but a federal judge later blocked this, along with other changes to vaccine policy made by the Trump administration.
Critics have questioned whether the research could help support that policy shift, although the study's stated aim was to investigate potential effects of the vaccine beyond preventing infection.
Kennedy has praised the Danish researchers as "the deities of vaccine research", and cited earlier findings from their work in support of concerns about vaccine safety. A subsequent study by some of the same researchers, however, found no evidence of the previously reported effect.
There is no evidence that the proposed trial was designed to justify a change in US policy.

Quick Answer
Concat is a free, open-source CapCut alternative with offline AI captions, voice cloning, background removal, 100+ effects, and 4K exports. It runs locally, needs no account, and adds no watermarks. Available across major platforms, it’s promising but still in beta, with some rough edges.
When you think of video editing, CapCut is a popular name that would pop up. It has made short-form editing painless. However, it has now started to put more of its tools behind a paywall, and a few of them need an internet connection to work.
If you are looking for a way out, you have probably already seen OpenReel, the browser-based open-source editor, or gone through our list of the best free video editing software. This time we have something different. Concat takes a different route. It is a free, open-source editor that runs on your own computer and is loaded with features like captions, voiceovers, and background removal built in.
Table of Contents
What is Concat?
Concat is a video editor that is currently in beta. The idea behind its development is easy to understand: It wants to give people stuff that CapCut offers but for free, like auto-captions, text-to-speech, background removal, keyframes, effects, titles, and 4K export. Everything Concat has on offer comes without strings attached. You don’t need to sign up, no watermark stamped on your exports, and no premium tier waiting around the corner.
The other big difference is where the work happens. Concat does everything locally, on your machine. It is built on a native Rust engine with a GPU compositor, and the AI models it uses (for captions, voices, and cutouts) are downloaded once from the settings and then run offline. This means the raw footage that you upload never gets uploaded anywhere.
CapCut is still a great editor, and nobody is pretending otherwise. When we compared it with Instagram Edits, we pointed out that CapCut has the richer feature set, but also that some of its tools need a connection and that its template and music ecosystem is tied closely to TikTok, which owns it. And if you are in India, you already know CapCut is banned here. So, you have to download the modded version or depend on some ad-filled alternatives.
That is the gap Concat is trying to fill. Not a “lite” version of a big editor, but a free one that keeps the stuff you reach for every day and keeps it on your own PC.
Concat features that matter
The feature list is long. But here are the parts that stand out.
Auto-captions that work offline
Captions are quite important nowadays, as content is reaching every part of the globe. But it is a chore every Reels and Shorts editor knows too well. Concat handles them using Whisper, a speech-recognition model that runs locally. You pick a model size (you can choose larger models, which are more accurate but require a stronger machine), and styled captions appear straight on your timeline. No upload, no waiting on a server, and it keeps working without internet.
Text-to-speech and voice cloning
Concat gives you free voices for narration, which is handy for tutorials or faceless channels. You can also clone a voice from just a few seconds of recording. That’s nice to edit a flubbed line without re-recording a whole take.
Background removal
You might have removed people or objects from your images. For videos, most of the editors ask you to pay. But Concat lets you edit out people or objects from a clip for free. If the automatic cutout misses a spot, you can paint the mask manually.
Keyframes with a curve editor
With keyframes, you can animate almost anything over time: position, scale, rotation, opacity, volume, and the settings of effects. There is a built-in curve editor too. You can use this to make a zoom feel smooth instead of mechanical, something that a paid video editor offers.
100 effects, filters and transitions
Concat comes with about 100 effects, filters, and transitions. They are rendered by your GPU and show up live in the preview. This way you can see what you are doing instead of waiting for an export to find out.
Fast cutting and a proper timeline
You get everything like split, trim, ripple delete, merge, freeze frame, and speed changes. If you like clips snapping together without gaps, you can switch on a magnetic timeline. Additionally, you can stack as many tracks as you want for overlays and picture-in-picture, keep several timelines inside a single project, and use blend modes like screen, add, and multiply. Crop and flip tools are there as well.
Titles with real styling
You can change fonts, add strokes and shadows, and drop in a background plate behind the words. If you don’t have any ideas, you can start from the already available presets.
One-switch audio cleanup
If your video has bad audio because of a faulty microphone or nearby noise, it can spoil a good video more than bad lighting does. Concat has a simple toggle for noise reduction, voice enhancement, and loudness leveling. You can also change voice effects to chipmunk, robot, and telephone.
Export and performance
Now, the best part is that with Concat, there is no limitation on export. It supports H.264, HEVC, and AV1, up to 4K at 60 frames per second with 10-bit colour.
Which platforms does Concat support?
Concat is versatile and supports multiple operating systems:
- Windows
- macOS
- Linux
- Android
- iPhone and iPad
Moreover, the editor is available in 26 languages. Downloading and setting up Concat is simple. Here’s what you need to do:
- Open the official download page, which picks the right build for your device. You can also grab any version from the GitHub Releases page.
- Install it like any other app on your device.
- On Windows, your system may warn you because the builds are not code-signed yet. Click More info, then Run anyway.
- On macOS, if the system refuses to open the app, the project suggests running xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Concat.app in Terminal.
- Open Settings and download the AI models you want (captions, voices, cutout). After that, they work offline.
Concat vs CapCut
| Feature | Concat | CapCut | 
|---|---|---|
| Price | Free, no subscription | Freemium | 
| Who is behind it | Open-source project (AGPL-3.0) | ByteDance | 
| Internet needed | Only to download AI models once | Some tools need a connection | 
| Templates and music | Limited | Large library tied to TikTok | 
A few things to keep in mind
Concat is promising and has all the features you would need from a video editor that is trying to be an alternative to CapCut. But don’t forget that it is young, and there are a few caveats that you should know about.
- It is a beta. The repo had over 200 open issues at the time of writing this article. So, you may come across some rough edges. We would advise you not to trust it with a client deadline until you have tested it on your own projects.
- Unsigned Windows builds and the macOS quarantine step can feel sketchy to newcomers. But it is safe, even though they are expected for now.
- You do not get a stock library to lean on. You will need your own assets.
- iPhone users have extra work because you have to sideload it, and sideloading is not for everyone.
Once you have the clarity, you should give Concat a try and let its output help you decide if you should keep using it or not. Let us know in the comments below which editor you are currently using.

Congo's Ebola outbreak tops 11,000 cases as disease keeps spreading
The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment
Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease.
According to the latest health ministry data, 11,042 people have been infected with the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387 — nearly half of those infected in what has been Congo's deadliest outbreak.
The outbreak was declared in mid-May, and since then, Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to several factors, including armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.
The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces.
The resurgence of violence in the two major hotspots in Ituri and North Kivu provinces has sparked worry among health authorities who are calling for a halt to the fighting to allow health workers unhindered access to the sick.
Health facilities and medical professionals have also been targeted by many in communities skeptical of the virus, and there have been several attacks on health workers.
Experts have called for more efforts to slow and contain the disease in Congo, while it has spread to multiple African countries including Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.
Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared, compared with the West Africa outbreak.

Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war
- Published
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.
The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.
Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.
We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.
More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.
Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.
More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.
The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.
For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.
When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.
"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.
Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."
Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."
Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.
"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".
Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.
Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.
Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.
"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.
She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."
Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.
Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.
"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time.
There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.
Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.
Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.
After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.
For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.
- 'I can't afford to save both twins': Sudan's war left one mother with an impossible choice 
  - Published16 October 2025
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.
"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."
His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.
As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.
He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.
For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.
The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.
Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine".
"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.
Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.
Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

"It's never been for me about pointing fingers and saying, 'he did this, he said that'. That's why even when I first wrote my edit there were names, there were lots of things, and I pulled it back.
"Sometimes I'm very specific on things and sometimes they're a bit vague on things, and I do it on purpose because I'm trying to tell a story.
"My main objective here is always to try and take accountability as a team, to say, yes, this was happening. And even though one person did it or the captain knew about it and Davey Warner always took the heat for it, that it wasn't just them, that we were all involved in it as a team."
Former team-mate Warner has said the claims in Khawaja's book are "100% accurate" and that "lies will eventually get out".
Asked about Warner's comments, Khawaja said: "I'm not going to speak on behalf of Davey. I've tried my best to tell my story in an open and safe environment.
"Twenty-two pages is what sandpaper is and I've tried my best in that to explain my version of events.
"I'm not here to inflame the situation any more. I was here to tell my truth, what I saw, what I felt and to stick with those three guys that were made out to be the only people who have taken it, and I wanted that to be shown."
Pressed as to whether Cummins, who has been Australia's Test captain since 2021, knew of the ball-tampering, Khawaja said: "I'm not going to answer that."
"This has never been a witch hunt for me. It's only been those three guys who've had to cop this flak for a long time," Khawaja added.
"I'm hoping other people will come up and talk about it honestly. That's what I'm hoping, but I'm not forcing anyone to do anything.
"You've got to remember Pat Cummins is a good friend of mine, Mitchell Starc, a lot of these guys, Shaun Marsh, Mitch Marsh, they're all very good friends of mine. All I've ever wanted is for us to take accountability as a team. I don't think that's a lot to say."
Meanwhile, England batter Joe Root said "I don't want to speculate" when asked about the scandal in the build-up to his side's first one-day international against Australia on Friday.
Questioned about the idea that ball-tampering was rife across the international game at the time, Root said: "I can only speak from my own experiences. That's not how I feel, no."

- Wires Crossed is a new quest introduced in the Arc Raiders Frozen Trail update.
- Players have to attach different ARC parts to antennas and machines in multiple buildings.
- 3x Electrical Parts, 1x Renegade, 2x Zipline, and 2x Smoke Grenade are the rewards for completing the Wires Crossed quest.
As everyone knows, Celeste leads the frozen expedition to the Pendola Pass region. Thus, she has another quest for players regarding reading data from ARC enemies. So, if you would like to assist Celeste, learn how to quickly complete the Wires Crossed quest in Arc Raiders here.
How to Complete the Wires Crossed Quest in Arc Raiders
Unlike the Sizing Things Up quest in Arc Raiders, players need to travel to three locations, The Blue Gate, Spaceport, and Buried City, to complete the Wires Crossed quest.
Since you are required to travel to multiple locations, you need to complete three different raids in one go. In addition, you need a Snitch Scanner, Surveyor Vault, and Sentinel Firing Core ready in your loadout, as you need to attach these ARC enemy parts to antennas in this quest.
If you have been playing for a long time, these items might already be in your inventory, and you just need to add them to your loadout. If not, you have to take down Snitch, ARC Surveyor, and Sentinels in Arc Raiders to collect the required items.
Alternatively, you can find some of these ARC enemy parts from an ARC Courier in Arc Raiders, but there is no guaranteed loot. So, the best way to tackle this problem is to queue a raid beforehand, defeat all three ARCs, and gather their parts.
Once you have collected a Snitch Scanner, Surveyor Vault, and Sentinel Firing Core, equip them in your loadout one by one. It’s also wise to have a zipline in your loadout, as you will be climbing to the top of multiple buildings in this quest. That said, here is how to complete
On the Blue Gate, Attach a Snitch Scanner to the Antenna at Pilgrim’s Peak
- Queue for a raid on the Blue Gate map and head to Pilgrim’s Peak on the north side.
- Go behind the building, and you can take a zipline to the top of Pilgrim’s Peak.
- After climbing to the top, turn left and go near the bulky microphones.
- Interact with the machine and attach the Snitch Scanner.
On Spaceport, Attach a Surveyor Vault to the Antenna on Top of the Launch Towers
- Next, lock your destination as Spaceport.
- Head to the Launch Tower located in the centre of the Spaceport map.
- Take a zipline and reach the room at the top of the tower.
- Then get out of the room and take the stairs on your left to climb to the peak.
- Interact with the Antenna on your right and attach the Surveyor Vault.
On Buried City, Attach a Sentinel Firing Core to the Antenna on the Roof of the Grandioso Apartments
- And the last map you need to move to is Buried City in Arc Raiders.
- Make your way to the Grandioso Apartments on the southwest side of the map.
- Equip and set up the zipline to the top of the Grandioso Apartments.
- Reach the top of the apartment and interact with the Antenna on the roof.
- Attach the Sentinel Firing Core in Arc Raiders to the antenna.
Arc Raiders Wires Crossed Quest Rewards
Here are all the rewards for completing the Wires Crossed quest in Arc Raiders:
- 3x Electrical Parts
- 1x Renegade
- 2x Zipline
- 2x Smoke Grenade
Thus, you can unlock the Renegade weapon in Arc Raiders, along with a couple of essential items like the zipline and smoke grenade, in the Wires Crossed quest.
And that’s how you can complete the Wires Crossed quest in Arc Raiders. Let us know if you have completed this quest in the comments below.

Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results
Republicans were dealt a stunning rebuke in last week's midterms. But swing voters, who could be decisive in the next election, are more interested in results than investigations or impeachment as Democrats prepare to take power in Congress.
"I am hoping that we don't experience a bunch of gridlock and a lot of whining and crying and just political infighting for the next two years," said Theresa, a voter from Pennsylvania who is participating in NPR's Swing Shift project. "I'm hoping we don't have that. I fear that we will have that."
NPR has agreed not to use the full names of the Swing Shift voters, so they can speak freely about politics without fear of personal or professional repercussions.
Loading...
Theresa voted for President Biden in 2020, President Trump in 2024 and split her ticket in this year's midterms. Like many voters, her top issue this year was affordability. In a voice memo sent to NPR days after the midterms, Theresa said she is eager for the cost of living to come down.
"I just don't remember it ever being as bad in our time," Theresa said. "And I'm just hoping we get some relief and we get some relief soon."
At 9:56 PM on election night, Wally in Georgia hit send on his voice memo. He had seen enough.
"Just checking in here with a quick note. I'm not surprised at all by the outcome tonight," Wally said. "I believe that this is a lot of Trump's doing and pushback on his style of politics and how he governs."
Wally voted for Trump in 2024 but swung back to Democrats in this year's midterms. He had initially supported Trump in hopes that a Trump presidency would shake up the political system, but that didn't happen and now he says the second Trump term has been exhausting. As he sees it, the decisive Democratic wins signal that the country is ready to move on.
"Trump has been shooting himself in the foot for many months now," Wally said. "But voting isn't the end of the game here. We have to hold Democrats to some sort of tangible change and not just promises about what they want to do."
For several of the Swing Shift voters, Tuesday's results came as a surprise.
Jason from North Carolina split his ticket, voting for Democrat Roy Cooper for Senate and the Republican incumbent for the House.
"My congressman was defeated this time by someone that no one's really ever heard of," said Jason, sounding almost puzzled by the blue wave that crashed on North Carolina.
That happened in a lot of places. Jason wants the incoming Democratic Congress to focus on the cost of living and steer clear of impeachment.
"My fear is that the Democrats now are going to spend the next 2 years not focusing on any of the things that they say Trump didn't do," said Jason.
Michelle in Michigan, voted for President Biden in 2020 but chose Republicans in 2024 and again in this year's midterms.
"This is the first time I think ever since I've been voting that not one of the people that I voted for won their election," Michelle said.
Michelle says she understands why so many people voted for Democrats, even if she didn't. Americans are tired, she said, of high gas prices, the cost of living and not being able to afford their groceries. They voted for change.
John from Pennsylvania said it felt like his state went from purple to blue overnight.
"I'm just very surprised," John said. "Not surprised that Democrats had a good night, but they had a very good night. Absolutely amazed that they won in Texas and places that just seemed like they were really red."
He voted for President Biden in 2020 and President Trump in 2024. In the most recent midterms, he stuck with Republicans despite concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.
Gerald in Georgia ran through the list of states where Democrats won senate races in disbelief.
"Come on man, Texas turned blue," Gerald said. "South Carolina turned blue, Ohio, Kansas. Like, this was a referendum of epic proportions."
Gerald is a Biden to Trump voter from Georgia, who has gone all in on MAGA. He's already looking ahead to a future without Trump leading Republicans.
"The Donald Trump era for all intents and purposes is coming to an end in 2028 for certain, if not before that," Gerald said.
Before that, though, Democrats will take power in Washington, at least in part.
Swing Shift voters said again and again when asked about their hopes and fears following these midterms that they hope that the incoming Democratic Congress will focus on the issues that impact their daily lives but fear more of the same broken politics.
"I will choose to hope because that's really all we can do is hope," said Michelle. "Hope that the politicians that were voted in will live up to the promises they made and that change will truly be made."
Even though John didn't vote for Democrats this year, he still wants them to tackle the cost of living.
"Over these next 2 years I hope they are concerned with and concentrate on the affordability issue," John said. "I hope they work with President Trump to try to lower prices. I just hope it's not two years of investigations and impeachment hearings."
Anything Democrats pass in a divided government would have to be signed by President Trump. The president has been inconsistent in recent days about whether he wants cooperation or combat with the new Congress.

Many large pharmaceutical companies are taking steps to improve access to their medicines in low- and middle-income countries, but progress has been mixed and more action is needed to ensure wide availability, a new analysis found.
Notably, more drugmakers are planning to reach patients before a product launch — access plans now cover 69% of late-stage pipeline candidates compared with 18% in 2018. And across the pipeline, 95% of late-stage experimental drugs developed with a nonprofit partner have an access plan in place, versus 67% without such a partner.
Another bright spot involves cancer treatments. Access plans now cover 65% of cancer drugs in product pipelines, up from 5% in 2018. But 43% of access plans for non-communicable diseases — specifically, sickle cell disease, diabetes, and mental health — focus solely on regulatory registrations and primarily in wealthy countries.

How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
- Published
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.
Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid.
US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.
At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.
The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.
Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.
With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.
In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are getting another coat of paint. The choir rehearses. Hundreds of other residents, several of them using wheelchairs, practise their positions outside the sanctuary. Excitement is in the air, because on Monday 9 November, the Cottolengo Don Orione – a Catholic-run home for disabled people – will be the first stop on Pope Leo XIV’s first full day of his trip to Argentina.
But the pope’s visit to Claypole, about 26km from Buenos Aires, does not come at an especially happy time for the home, which counts about 400 residents with disabilities. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has made wide-ranging cuts to disability funding.
“[The government] cut off the supply of medications, special foods and diapers. They haven’t delivered any since last November. The matter is in court,” said the facility’s coordinator, Fernando Montero. The pope and Milei, he said, “have completely opposing ideologies”, arguing that the pope teaches that a person’s worth is not measured by whether they are productive, whereas Milei is a “hyper-capitalist” who believes only “those who compete the most should be rewarded”.
Pope Leo’s three days here – he began a three-country trip through South America in Uruguay on Friday, and will finish with six days in Peru – will be the first papal visit to Argentina since John Paul II in 1987. His predecessor, Pope Francis, who was Argentine, never returned during his papacy.
The trip could prove uncomfortable for Milei. A far-right libertarian economist who campaigned with a chainsaw as the symbol of his promised spending cuts, Milei called Francis an “imbecile” and “the representative of the Evil One on Earth” in 2020, and accused him of promoting communism, saying social justice was theft. Milei claims to have apologised when he met Francis in the Vatican in February 2024.
Since taking office the previous December, he has slashed public spending, which the government says was needed to curb inflation. The cost, however, was high. The thinktank Mate estimates that retirees on the minimum pension – 63% of the total – have lost about 30% of their purchasing power. Last Wednesday at the weekly retirees’ march outside Congress, a man held up a cardboard sign reading, “Save us Pope Leo XIV – Milei is killing us.”
Last month, Buenos Aires archbishop Jorge García Cuerva said Leo XIV would find “a divided Argentina and a large number of very poor brothers and sisters.”
But the differences between the pope and the president go beyond typical social issues. In May, Leo XIV called for “disarming” artificial intelligence, while Milei has said he would not regulate AI technology and has instead presented bills to build datacentres across the country and to grant legal status to “no-human corporations”. Federico Sturzenegger, a minister in charge of state cuts, says he has used AI to draft legislation.
Milagros Miceli, a sociologist and computer scientist who leads the Critical AI Lab in Berlin, said the “contradiction” between the two is “pretty evident”. She welcomed Leo’s visit, celebrating how the “powerful figure” of the pope intends to put “human beings at the centre by stripping these technologies of the values that are presented to us as taking precedence over humanity.”
Juan Grabois, a left-wing Peronist deputy and social leader who served in the Vatican’s Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development, said: “The idea of absolute deregulation is at the heart of the president’s agenda, and the replacement of the human element with these forms of algorithmic power has clearly also become a policy priority for the government.”
Disability funding has been a flashpoint between church and state. As Milei has clashed with Congress over a funding law that remains in limbo, Argentina’s conference of bishops wrote to the health minister, Mario Lugones, on 1 April, denouncing “the serious situation facing numerous institutions dedicated to the care and support of people with disabilities in our country”. The ministry has met the bishops twice since, in April and again on 5 October, but without resolving the impasse.
The government is trying to downplay potential tensions. “There’s no way the pope is going to come here to comment on local politics,” Sandra Pettovello, the minister overseeing social policy, said recently. Amnesty International, meanwhile, has written to the pope about Argentina, warning of its “concern about government decisions that affect the exercise of fundamental rights”.
All of this will be top of mind when Milei receives the pope at the airport on Sunday. From the disability home, the pope will go on to Buenos Aires and meet business and union leaders; then on Tuesday he will celebrate Mass at the grounds of FAdeA, the state-owned military aircraft factory in Córdoba, whose workers have protested against Milei’s cuts. Juan Cruz Esquivel, director of Buenos Aires University’s Barometer of Religions and Beliefs, says the itinerary speaks for itself.
“I don’t want to speculate [about what the pope will say], but clearly any mention of defending domestic production, labour, disability or social justice in the pope’s rhetoric naturally clashes with the ideology that Milei’s government has been promoting,” says Esquivel.
Mariano Oberlin, a Catholic priest in an impoverished neighbourhood of Córdoba, expects the clash to play out diplomatically. “Pope Leo has been saying it without confronting, but he keeps upholding the church’s social doctrine as the key axis of his ministry,” Oberlin said. “If Milei wants to use him, he’ll probably have to do a lot of juggling to make him say the opposite of what he’s been saying – and of what he’ll surely say when he comes: that the Gospel invites us to feel like brothers, to respect each person’s deep, inherent dignity, and to fight so that this dignity becomes real in access to rights.”
Since Francis’s tenure, social movements in Latin America have come closer to the Catholic church, and Argentina is no exception. Grabois, who was part of that process, sees the relationship as a two-way exchange. “[Francis] wasn’t the ‘good priest’ who came to help the poor,” he says, arguing that the exchanges helped Francis “develop his social thinking”. “Without the cartoneros (cardboard pickers) and the villeros (people from impoverished neighbourhoods), Francis would not have been Francis.”
To Grabois, the same is true for Leo. “Francis took notice of Leo because he saw him supporting the Peruvian indigenous movement.”
That doesn’t mean all Argentine social movements support the pope. On Saturday, a day before the visit, the LGBTQIA+ community will hold the 35th Pride March in Buenos Aires. María Rachid from the march’s organising committee said: “The church’s dogma regarding our families has not changed at any time, neither under the previous pope nor under this one”, though she notes that Francis’s words on gay rights “brought some relief to many families and their communities”.
But a new development is the rise of evangelical churches, while Catholic identification falls. Buenos Aires University found 57.7% of Argentines identify as Catholic and 17.4% as evangelical, compared with 76.5% and 9% nearly 20 years ago. Last week, Milei inaugurated an evangelical temple in Neuquén and gave a nakedly political speech promising to seek re-election next year. Although Catholicism remains Argentina’s majority religion, it has lost its cultural hegemony and its influence on legislative agenda, Esquivel said.
Nevertheless, a majority of Argentines expect a “message from the pope focused on the social and humanitarian agenda”. Grabois notes the transformative impact that first Francis and now Leo have had “with left-leaning activists” in Argentina. “I’m not speaking about atheists, but outright anticlerical people. People who, 10 years ago, held views that were very, very hostile toward the church,” he said. “I even see them as more fervent [about the visit] than typical churchgoers who attend Sunday Mass.” For Grabois, “in the face of dehumanisation, ordinary people are taking refuge in the only global voice that’s speaking out about this today – which is Francis and Leo’s.”

Three contract workers died after allegedly inhaling toxic gases during maintenance work at Tata Electronics’ iPhone manufacturing unit in Tamil Nadu’s Hosur. According to Reuters, the incident took place as workers were carrying out cleaning and maintenance work inside a nano-filtration feed tank, which was operated by US-based water treatment company Ecolabs’ subsidiary Nalco Water. Confirming the development, Nalco Water said that the workers had been employed by one of its sub-contractors. “We are deeply saddened by the tragic incident that resulted in the deaths of three workers engaged by a sub-contractor of Nalco Water… This incident occurred in a utility facility, operated by Nalco Water. We are working with the local authorities in the investigation of this incident,” said the company in a statement. Sources told the news agency that the deaths, which took place late on Monday, will now be probed by Apple, Tata Electronics and local authorities. Another source reportedly added that an Apple team will visit the plant to assist in the investigation. A separate report by Financial Express noted that Tata Electronics will also face an investigation by a joint team of officials from the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board (TNPCB) and the local Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health (DISH). As per The New India Express, one of the workers fainted after looking inside the tank and inhaling gas. The other two workers then entered the tank to check on him and also collapsed subsequently due to asphyxiation. All three workers were declared dead on arrival at the hospital, the report added. Citing official sources, the report added that there were no proper safety measures in place while handling the effluent treatment plant (ETP). While preliminary investigation suggests toxic smoke inhalation, the police have reportedly said the final cause of death would be established after the post-portem. This is not the first time that Tata’s iPhone manufacturing unit in Hosur has landed in the middle of a major controversy. In 2024, The latest incident comes nearly two years after the factory was engulfed by a massive fire, which caused injuries to eleven people and halted production. Not just this, in June this year, the TNPCB had reportedly warned the Tata Hosur unit that the plant would be shut down over alleged wastewater contamination of wells in adjacent farmland. Afterwards, Tata Electronics reportedly had said that an independent analysis showed compliance with regulatory norms. The conglomerate later also claimed that the pollution control board had dropped further action after the company confirmed that it had addressed all queries. On top of this, in June itself, a ransomware group posted more than 2 Lakh files, including sensitive supplier information, stolen from the same Hosur iPhone assembly plant on the dark web.

Labubu hype seemed unstoppable, now the fluffy monster mania is dying
- Published
For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.
Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.
Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.
The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.
Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".
He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.
But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."
Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.
It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.
Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.
The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.
The rise and fall
Pop Mart didn't invent blind boxes but its dolls certainly helped to popularise them around the world.
The sales tactic made collecting feel "nostalgic", evoking the feeling of opening gifts as a child, says marketing professional Katelynn Carlson, who discovered Labubus through social media and now owns 36 of them.
One of her first Labubus was a rare doll, making the experience "even more exciting", she adds.
Labubu, which launched in 2019, has been Pop Mart's most successful line of toys. The monsters became fashion statements and were sported by celebrities including Kim Kardashian and Blackpink's Lisa.
They regularly attracted long queues and became so popular that Pop Mart had to temporarily pull the toys from its UK shops after reports of customers fighting over them. One fan paid more than $150,000 for a human-sized Labubu.
A key part of the allure was how difficult some Labubu dolls were to find, with fans repeatedly buying blind boxes to get the version they wanted, says National University of Singapore marketing lecturer Samer El Hajjar.
Pop Mart now has 500 shops in more than 30 countries and 2,000 vending machines worldwide. The firm, which listed in Hong Kong in 2020, is worth nearly $24bn and remains one of the world's most valuable toymakers, despite its shares having fallen by more than 50% from last year's peak.
Investors worry its global success was just a viral moment rather than sustainable growth driven by long-term customer loyalty, El Hajjar says.
For Ensito, it is clear the dolls' exclusivity helped fuel the craze.
"Now it doesn't feel that way. I walk into a Pop Mart and there's a whole series of Labubus sitting there," he says.
Ashley Dudarenok of China research firm ChoZan says that sense of exclusivity faded as Pop Mart ramped up production to meet demand.
Pop Mart declined to comment on share price moves and did not respond to questions about falling sales.
Rivals take over
As the Labubu mania cools, some of its rivals have become more popular.
Blind box collectables like Sonny Angels - tiny, unclothed cherub-like dolls - and miniature glow-in-the-dark Smiski figurines have been flying off shelves. And you can now find My Little Pony and KPop Demon Hunters in blind boxes too.
Miniso, founded in the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou, sells a range of blind-boxed Disney and Marvel characters in more than 8,000 shops globally.
"Consumers aren't particularly concerned about where the brand comes from," Miniso executive Vincent Huang said earlier this year. "They're more focused on the shopping experience - the designs, value for money, and enjoyment."
Experts say one of Pop Mart's biggest challenges is creating enduring characters.
That's an area where Hello Kitty brand Sanrio, which posted record earnings in the year to March, has a clear advantage, analyst Boustani suggests.
Pop Mart has invested heavily in ways to grow its brand, including setting up a theme park in Beijing and announcing a Labubu film - following in the footsteps of franchising giants like Disney or Lego, some experts believe.
But unlike Disney, which sells a story before it sells a toy, Pop Mart is working in reverse, says Dudarenok. "The real test for next year is whether Pop Mart can make people love a character without a celebrity holding it."
'Now I only buy what I like'
After spending huge sums on the monsters, collector Ensito says he is now questioning how much time and money people invest in collections each time a new trend comes along. "There's always going to be a trend every year. There's always gonna be something that's gonna be really popular."
Melbourne-based content creator Lawrence Yu says that after two years of chasing Labubus, he's likely to be "more selective" before adding to his roughly 50 dolls.
His Labubu shopping and unboxing clips once drew up to a million views but the frenzy has faded and Yu rarely makes videos about them now. "I definitely think the trend has slowed down... People go crazy and then it fizzles."
Clara Barbero from Canada believes Labubus are a "dead trend" but is still keeping an eye out for interesting releases.
"I’m curating my collection more and only buying what I see myself liking for the next few years, and not just buying the newest series that’s out."
But the fluffy monsters still have truly devoted fans.
Hedy Khaled from Liverpool says although the hype around the dolls is cooling, she is just as attached to her collection of 70 Pop Mart figurines.
There's a distinction between those who chase trends and "real fans", she argues, so falling sales do not necessarily mean Labubus have lost their appeal.
For Carlson says it is the happiness the dolls bring, not the viral trend, that keeps her collecting. She still gets excited about new Pop Mart releases, like its recent cat-themed Labubu series, which has become one of her favourites.
"I think there's something special about embracing our inner child and enjoying things simply because they make us happy."

17-year-old accused in Bengaluru family murders may face adult trial
The law allows children aged 16–18 accused of heinous offences to be tried as adults following an assessment
The 17-year-old accused of assisting her father in the murder of seven members of their family in Bengaluru could face trial as an adult if a juvenile justice board determines she meets the criteria under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015. The law allows children aged 16–18 accused of heinous offences, including murder, to be tried as adults following a preliminary assessment of their capacity to understand and commit the alleged crime.
The girl, a second-year pre-university student at a private college, allegedly assisted S Indushekar, 52, in killing his wife, Sunitha, and six of her relatives at their home over about 15 days in October. She was arrested along with her father on November 5.
A police officer said investigators are probing the extent of her involvement, including claims by her father that she helped bring relatives to the house, conceal the killings, and transport and dispose of the bodies. “The main point being considered is whether Indushekar manipulated his daughter into helping him dispose of the bodies.”
The first information report (FIR) registered in the case on November 5 names Indushekar and his daughter as accused. Indushekar is listed as an adult accused. His daughter is classified as a juvenile in conflict with the law.
A juvenile justice board must assess the child’s mental and physical capacity to commit the alleged offence, her ability to understand its consequences, and the circumstances in which it was committed under the Juvenile Justice Act Section 15. The assessment can involve psychologists and other experts.
The officer said if the board decides that the case warrants an adult trial, it can transfer the matter to the children’s court under Section 18(3). “The children’s court must independently decide whether the child should face an adult trial or be dealt with under the juvenile justice system.”
The officer said the seriousness of the allegations alone does not determine the outcome. The girl’s understanding of the alleged crimes and the extent to which she was influenced or coerced by her father will be important considerations.
Investigators suspect that Indushekar turned his daughter against her mother’s family, portraying the relatives as enemies and allegedly telling her that eliminating them would improve their financial position because the property would eventually belong to her.
The girl allegedly contacted her maternal grandmother, Roopavathi, after her mother Sunitha’s murder and asked her to visit the house. She allegedly invited her maternal aunts for dinner, telling them that Sunitha was away on a trip. She reportedly messaged her aunt Divya’s sister, Chandana, claiming that the family was travelling.
Police are investigating her suspected role in packing the bodies, transporting them in the car, and cleaning the crime scene.
Karnataka home minister Priyank Kharge said Indushekar allegedly brainwashed his daughter and made her assist in the crime.
Police said Indushekar allegedly transported the bodies in his car and disposed of them at different locations with his daughter’s assistance. Forensic Science Laboratory and Scene of Crime Officer teams inspected the recovery sites, while postmortem examinations were conducted.
Investigators are now focusing on forensic evidence to establish the sequence and timing of the killings and are analysing CCTV footage. The bodies were recovered from locations in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.

Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.
The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.
A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.
Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

A few hours of exposure to firecracker smoke can be enough to trigger coughing, wheezing or breathlessness, particularly in people living with asthma or other respiratory conditions. The effects, however, are not limited to those with an existing diagnosis. High concentrations of particulate matter and gases can irritate the airways in anyone.
The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a numerical measure that converts the levels of different air pollutants into a single figure to indicate how polluted the air is and the likely health effects. India’s Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) calculates it using eight pollutants, including PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide.

Greta Thunberg issues urgent warning at UN climate talks: 'Everything we love is at stake'
This year’s conference is taking place in the Turkish city of Antalya
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
