Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
- Published
Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.
In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".
The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.
Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.
The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.
On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".
Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.
"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.
The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".
The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".
Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.
Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.
The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

New York will independently test AI models
The state’s research center will check AI companies’ work instead of taking their word.
As the federal government essentially leaves us all at the mercy of the AI industry, New York is taking matters into its own hands. On Tuesday, Governor Kathy Hochul launched the nation's first state-run AI testing program. Instead of trusting AI companies to police themselves, New York's system will task independent researchers with checking their work. "The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word," Hochul stated in a press release.
The work will be handled by the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University. More than 80 New York scientists will contribute. They'll use computing power from Empire AI, the state's $500 million public-private AI partnership.
Hochul's office said the center will test advanced AI systems, study their risks and provide evidence to inform public officials' decisions. It will also look at how AI can be used responsibly in areas like medicine and scientific discovery.
One potential hole in the program is that it can only study what AI companies disclose publicly. New York's RAISE Act, signed by Hochul last year, requires large AI developers to register with the state by January 1, 2027. Starting then, companies will have to publish safety frameworks and transparency reports and report critical safety incidents within 72 hours. The RAISE Act won't plug the hole on unreleased models, but it will at least force companies to disclose more.

Kenya discharges last Ebola patient, beginning countdown to Ebola-free declaration
Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient, starting a 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Kenya on Wednesday discharged its last Ebola patient, officially beginning the 42-day countdown toward being declared Ebola-free, even as the number of cases recorded in the wider region topped 11,000 since the outbreak began in May.
The country recorded nine Ebola cases in October after the first patient traveled from Congo through Uganda, transmitting the virus to four family members and four healthcare workers.
The first patient and his mother died of Ebola, while the other seven patients have fully recovered. The government had identified 135 contacts who had interacted with the first patient.
Kenya now begins the 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free, provided no new infections are recorded during that period.
But while Kenya's cases have now been discharged, elsewhere in the region the number of infections continues to climb. In Congo, the epicenter of the outbreak, 11,042 people have been infected and 5,387 have died, the government said Wednesday.
The outbreak also spread to Uganda and Nigeria through individuals who traveled from Congo.
Kenya's Health Minister Aden Duale on Wednesday said the 42-day waiting period is twice the longest Ebola incubation period and would end on Dec. 23, but insisted that the country would continue with its prevention measures.
The Ministry of Health had earlier expressed confidence that the outbreak was under control, noting that all confirmed cases were linked to the first patient’s contact list. This indicated that there had been no community transmission.
Kenya has faced travel restrictions following the Ebola outbreak, with Saudi Arabia announcing an indefinite suspension of visas on Oct. 30. The decision affected hundreds of Kenyan workers traveling to the Gulf for employment, particularly as domestic and hotel workers.
The Ministry of Health had urged Saudi Arabia to reconsider the travel restrictions, explaining that Kenya’s first Ebola case was imported and that all subsequent cases were traced to the initial patient’s contact list. The ministry said all contacts had been identified and traced in line with established outbreak-control guidelines.
The current Ebola outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus and has been described as one of the worst outbreaks on record.
Kenya tightened its border controls designating a specific gate at the country's main airport for passengers traveling from 10 countries that have reported Ebola cases or border those that have active cases. Passengers are being screened using thermal technology and all new arrivals fill a health declaration form that provides their travel and health information.

Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
- Published
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.
In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

Austria tightens laws against spying to protect the international organizations it hosts
Austria has launched plans to tighten its espionage laws, which currently only ban spying against Austria itself
BERLIN -- Austria's government on Wednesday launched plans to tighten the country's laws against spying, which at present explicitly ban espionage directed against Austria itself but not if it targets other countries or international organizations.
Austria is a European Union member that has a policy of military neutrality dating back to the 1950s. Its capital, Vienna, is host to several U.N. agencies including the International Atomic Energy Agency. It is also the home of other international groups such as the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe and the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, or OPEC.
“Espionage is a real threat to our security, to security in our country, but above all to our reputation as Austria, as the capital of dialogue, as an official location of the U.N. and over 40 international organizations,” Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said as Cabinet ministers presented the draft legislation. “We have a responsibility ... and we are fulfilling this responsibility.”
Meinl-Reisinger acknowledged that Vienna has often been described as a “capital of espionage,” a reputation dating back to the Cold War, but said she wants to dispense with any “romantic idea” of spying.
She said that “we are responding to the current hybrid threat situation.” That's a term for non-conventional hostile acts such as sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and an array of other methods.
Austria’s criminal code currently states that anyone who “sets up or operates a secret intelligence service to the detriment of the Republic of Austria or supports such an intelligence service in whatever way” faces a prison sentence of up to five years. It also bans setting up, operating or supporting a “military intelligence service” for a foreign power.
The new legislation, which requires parliamentary approval, will increase the maximum sentence for espionage to the detriment of Austria to 10 years, Meinl-Reisinger said. It will explicitly criminalize spying against international organizations or the EU, with a maximum sentence of five years.
Officials said that the legislation also will explicitly ban recruiting agents and being recruited as an agent, among other things. That's a measure targeted in particular at the recruitment of so-called “throwaway agents,” people recruited for low-level espionage actions without necessarily knowing what they are getting into.
The justice minister in Austria's last government announced a similar plan in 2024 but that administration didn't agree on legislation before that year's election.
Meinl-Reisinger said that “we are no longer looking away.” She said that entry visas for diplomats have been denied in 63 cases since she took office in March 2025, and noted that eight Russian diplomats have been expelled from Austria in that time.

Five arrested for allegedly desecrating Santal place of worship in Odisha's Keonjhar
The arrest came 12 days after the alleged incident was reported and almost three weeks after it occurred.
Odisha Police have arrested five persons for allegedly desecrating a sacred place of worship of the Santal community in Basantpur village of Keonjhar district,
The accused, identified as Chandan Sethy, Dibyajyoti Puhan, Akshay Kumar Sahoo, Suresh Mallick and Srichandan Puhan, were arrested by Ghasipura police on Tuesday.
The arrest came 12 days after the alleged incident was reported and almost three weeks after it occurred.
What allegedly happened
According to the FIR lodged by tribal villagers on October 29, the incident occurred on October 23 when members of the Santal community were worshipping at a sacred grove, locally known as Jaher Than. The complaint alleged that around 15 to 20 people, allegedly armed with knives, iron rods and sticks, barged into the place of worship and abused the worshippers.
When some women tried to resist the intruders, they were allegedly manhandled and subjected to inappropriate behaviour, the FIR stated. The attackers also allegedly dragged two youths along with their motorcycles for around 30 to 40 metres while leaving the spot, leaving them injured.
The complainants further alleged that the villagers were threatened with the discontinuation of their subsidised rice quota and government allowances if they reported the incident to the police.
Rabi Hembrum, one of the villagers, alleged that police had refused to register a separate FIR over the desecration of the Jaher Than and clubbed the matter with the case relating to the assault on villagers.
Anandpur sub-divisional police officer Kamal Lochan Panda said an investigation into the incident was underway.
Political turn
The incident triggered a political controversy, with a BJD delegation led by former minister and the party's Tribal Cell president Sudam Marndi alleging that people associated with the Bajrang Dal were behind the attack and demanding an independent investigation.
"When the chief minister himself belongs to the Santal community, the attack on tribals clearly demonstrates how unsafe the communities have become in the state," the BJD said in a statement.
No reaction from the Bajrang Dal or the ruling BJP is available so far.

At St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, Keralam, faith and fitness go hand in hand. An open gym on the church premises is drawing parishioners of all ages to stretch, sweat and stay fit. The unusual initiative is adding a healthy new dimension to church life.
Set up in a corner of the church campus, the facility has quickly become a meeting point for fitness enthusiasts. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass. The altar boys, numbering around 60, are among its regular users. Parents also bring their young children, while senior citizens use the basic equipment to stay active.
Roots in fitness routine of vicar
The initiative has its roots in the personal fitness routine of the church’s vicar, Fr. Frederick Eluvathingal, 69. A footballer and basketball player during his student days, he has never allowed age or a demanding schedule to come in the way of exercise.
“I have been working out for the past 51 years, ever since my days at the Papal Seminary in Pune,” he says. His fitness routine continued during his higher studies in Rome and Jerusalem and his church assignments in Australia.
When he arrived at Kuriachira more than a year ago, he began looking for a suitable space to continue his regular exercises, including push-ups and pull-ups. Parallel bars were installed first, followed by a basketball hoop. The idea gradually grew into a community gym.
“I wanted to create a space where people could develop the habit of working out. We generally do not have a strong workout culture. If people can fit in some basic exercise when they come to church, they may gradually make fitness part of their lives,” he says.
The need is particularly pressing at a time when lifestyle diseases and obesity are on the rise. The initiative also seeks to draw more youngsters into church activities and channel their energy into constructive pursuits.
The parish welcomed the proposal, and a space around a well on the church premises was chosen for the facility. The limited space available in Kuriachira meant that the gym had to be modest, but the response has been encouraging.
“Within a week of starting the gym, quite a few people began coming here. If the demand grows, we will have to think about expanding the facility,” says P.R. Wilson, one of the church trustees.
For regular user John Vazhappilly, a real estate broker who lives nearby, the gym has come as a timely help. “I have been coming here every evening for the past week. After an accident and surgery, the muscles in my leg became weak. I want to strengthen them. This is a comfortable place to exercise, with fresh air and an open campus,” he says.
‘A form of spiritual service’
The church sees the initiative as more than a fitness facility. “We want to groom a healthy generation. Many people suffer from lifestyle diseases, while youngsters often turn to private fitness centres. We felt that providing basic facilities here would benefit the community. Spirituality is also about nurturing a healthy mind and body. We consider this a form of spiritual service,” says assistant vicar Fr. Jees Akkara.
For Fr. Eluvathingal, there is another purpose. “Youngsters rarely come to church or participate in its activities these days. This is also an opportunity to bring more of them into the church community,” he says.

Microsoft's Automatic Super Resolution is now officially out for the ROG Xbox Ally X
It’s the company’s response to NVIDIA’s DLSS and other similar upscaling tech.
Back in April, Microsoft revealed that it had started testing Automatic Super Resolution (Auto SR) on the ROG Xbox Ally X. Now, the upscaling technology designed to compete with similar video game tools like NVIDIA's DLSS, is officially rolling out to the Ally X, ROG Xbox Ally X20 and select Windows Copilot+ PCs powered by AMD Ryzen. The official version of Auto SR works even when the console is undocked, unlike the preview version that doesn't support handheld play.
Auto SR allows the docked handheld to offer "1440p-like detail alongside smooth framerates on larger screens." It means it can upscale your game up to 1440p in resolution to make it look sharper if you're playing on the TV. While that was its original purpose, Microsoft said it made the upscaling tech available even in handheld mode due to popular demand. Auto SR can "smooth things out" if a demanding game "feels a little choppy on the go," the company wrote in its announcement.
The new version of Auto SR works with games running at 1080p on default, which would be most games played on the ASUS consoles. During its preview, you'd had to lower the game's resolution before the tech could kick in. Now that's no longer necessary. Microsoft warned, however, that when using 1080p on handheld, "performance may not be as optimal as other configurations." You're bound to still see visual quality improvements, though, especially for older games.
In addition, the new Auto SR can reach framerates up to 120 fps, wheres the preview version could only hit between 60 to 75 fps. Microsoft explained that it would make fast-past and competitive games like shooters feel and look smoother on screen. Finally, Auto SDR now supports HDR visuals. Both the higher framerate capability, which Microsoft calls "Performance Mode," and HDR support will be rolling out with future Windows updates.

Most people seem to be deploying melatonin and magnesium supplements, over the counter, but the question that remains is: are they effective, and if so, at what combinations or levels?
The consensus among most sleep specialists, is that both melatonin and magnesium (glycinate) can have an ameliorative impact – in the short term. Both these supplements, however, work differently – while melatonin is a key body clock signal, magnesium helps relax the body. When and how you take both supplements makes a great deal of difference to your hours of sleep and sleep quality as well.

Brilliant Noskova dismantles Gauff to reach WTA Finals last four
- Published
Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova dismantled Coco Gauff to become the first player to reach the last four of the WTA Finals.
Czech Noskova played with controlled aggression and served brilliantly to beat the American 6-3 6-3.
World number eight Noskova was composed throughout and broke Gauff's serve four times in the first set alone.
She sent powerful winners to all corners to outmuscle her opponent, who is one of the best movers on the WTA Tour, and committed only one unforced error in a dominant second set.
The 21-year-old fittingly sealed victory with an ace to secure a place in the semi-finals on her tournament debut.
"Thank you guys for the cheers I'm getting now - but it was a little weaker in the match, guys, I'm not going to lie," Noskova joked to the California crowd afterwards.
"I feel like I stayed in the match through every moment, from beginning to end."
It is a sixth top-10 victory of the season for Noskova, who won her maiden Grand Slam at Wimbledon in July.
Gauff, who won a thriller against compatriot Jessica Pegula on Sunday, had a poor day on serve.
She hit the same amount of aces and double faults - eight apiece - and won only six of 24 points behind her second serve.
Fourth-ranked Gauff can still qualify for the last four, as can Pegula.
Earlier in group one, Pegula claimed her first win since September to eliminate alternate Marta Kostyuk.
American Pegula won 6-2 7-5 in a scrappy match that saw seven breaks of serve.
Ukraine's Kostyuk, who has been dealing with a wrist injury since August, only found out she would be playing on Saturday after world number one Elena Rybakina withdrew.
She lost her opener to Noskova on Sunday and struggled for rhythm and consistency in a low-quality match against Pegula.
Pegula made only five unforced errors to Kostyuk's 17 as she took the first set, and the home favourite quickly went up a break in the second.
However, four breaks of serve then ensued, with Pegula eventually sealing the decisive break at 5-5 before serving out victory.
Elsewhere, Britain's Toby Samuel fell 6-1 6-4 to world number 25 Lorenzo Musetti in the Basel Open second round.

Amid rising concerns over the spread of Ebola to neighbouring countries, the Department of Health, Medical and Family Welfare, A.P., has stepped up surveillance at three airports — Bhogapuram (Visakhapatnam), Vijayawada, and Tirupati — as a precautionary measure.
According to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, an official U.S. government website, the outbreak is spreading “substantially faster” than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record.
In this connection, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare held a video conference on November 5, Thursday, with State governments regarding the precautionary measures to be taken. The Union government officials also reviewed the implementation of the Ebola guidelines.
A.P. Health Secretary G. Veerapandian, who took part in the conference, explained the arrangements being made in the State as part of the preparedness.
Arrangements at 5 govt. hospitals
According to a release from the department on Thursday, isolation beds at five government hospitals, medical personnel, emergency equipment have been readied. Mr. Veerapandian informed the Union government that medical teams had been deputed at three airports to screen passengers arriving from Ebola-affected countries for any symptoms. Similar arrangements are also in place at Visakhapatnam, Kakinada and Nellore ports.
A total of 46 beds, 3,288 personal protective equipment (PPE) kits, 104 sample collection kits and five ambulances had been kept ready to deal with any eventuality, he said.

If any person exhibits any symptoms, they should be taken to the hospital where isolation beds have been set up, the officials told the States.

Sports Personality of the Year returns - with five awards decided by public
- Published
The 2026 BBC Sports Personality of the Year show will be held on Sunday, 13 December - with five winners decided by public votes.
Clare Balding, Gabby Logan and Alex Scott will again host the programme, which will be hosted in Salford and broadcast live on BBC One, BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app from 17:45 GMT.
Five of the nine awards to be presented on the night will be decided by public vote.
The show will celebrate another great year of sport, including Team GB's most successful Winter Olympics, England's best finish at a men's Fifa World Cup since 1966, and record-breaking displays at the European Athletics Championships.
There will be two new award categories at the ceremony this year - Men's Footballer of the Year and BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year.
The latter has been a BBC World Service award since 2015 but will now be presented as part of the BBC Sports Personality of the Year awards for the first time. Voting - for global audiences - opens on Tuesday, 10 November.
In addition to crowning the winners of both football awards, fans will also select the winners of the World Sport Star of the Year, Team of the Year and Sports Personality of the Year award itself.
An independent panel made up of industry experts, sports broadcasters, sports journalists and former sportspeople will determine the shortlists for the Sports Personality of the Year, Team of the Year and World Sports Star awards, with the winners chosen by public votes. The independent panel will also determine the winners of Young Sports Personality of the Year and Coach of the Year.
Separate panels of football experts will provide the shortlist of contenders for Men's Footballer of the Year and Women's Footballer of the Year.
Alex Kay-Jelski - director of BBC Sport - said: "What I love about BBC Sports Personality of the Year is that it brings together all those moments that stopped us in our tracks. The goals, the medals, the upsets, the records, the stories that had us talking at work, in the pub and around the dinner table.
"And what a year we've had. This year's shortlists will be packed with athletes and teams who have achieved extraordinary things, but what's especially exciting is that audiences will have a bigger say than ever before in who takes home the trophies."
The nine award categories are:
- BBC Sports Personality of the Year
- Helen Rollason Award
- Young Sports Personality of the Year
- Coach of the Year
- Team of the Year
- Lifetime Achievement award
- Men's Footballer of the Year
- Women's Footballer of the Year
- World Sport Star of the Year
Full voting details, dates and T&Cs will be announced in due course.

Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”
Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.
“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.
Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.
Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.
“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.
During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.
“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”
Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.
Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.
For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?
“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”
Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.
“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.
On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.
“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.
However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.
“No woman in the city is fully free,” Sinha says.
Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”
In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.
“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.
Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.
“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”
Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.
Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.
But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

India, Norway explore joint technology to turn industrial waste into construction material
The discussions follow the elevation of India-Norway relations to a Green Strategic Partnership during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Norway in May.
India and Norway are exploring joint research and technology initiatives to convert industrial and construction waste into valuable resources, with a focus on sustainable building materials, hazardous waste treatment and a circular economy.
The initiative was discussed at the India-Norway Dialogue on “Waste to Resource Solutions in the Cement and Construction Sector”, organised jointly by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), Norway’s research organisation SINTEF and the Research Council of Norway at the India Habitat Centre on Tuesday.
The dialogue brought together scientists, regulatory authorities and representatives of the cement and construction industries to identify opportunities for bilateral research and technology development.
The discussions follow the elevation of India-Norway relations to a Green Strategic Partnership during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Norway in May, with circular economy, clean technology and scientific research identified as key areas of cooperation.
India stresses circular economy, C&D waste potential
Addressing the inaugural session, CSIR-CBRI director R Pradeep Kumar emphasised the need to move from a linear to a circular economic model by converting construction and industrial waste into usable resources.
Kumar highlighted the potential of construction and demolition (C&D) waste, steel slag, fly ash, and red mud, while underlining challenges related to processing technologies, standardisation, economic viability, and market acceptance.
A key technical session examined the use of cement kilns for the environmentally safe treatment of hazardous waste, including persistent organic pollutants (POPs) and materials contaminated with DDT and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).
SINTEF chief scientist Kåre Helge Karstensen and CSIR-NEERI scientist Ramesh Kumar discussed how cement kilns, operating under controlled high-temperature conditions, could destroy hazardous organic contaminants while replacing conventional fossil fuels with waste-derived alternatives. The experts stressed the importance of emission monitoring, regulatory compliance and controlled industrial trials.
Research presented by CSIR-CRRI and CSIR-AMPRI highlighted the potential of fly ash, copper slag, red mud, plastic waste and steel grit in road construction, geopolymer concrete and specialised construction products.
Another session, led by SINTEF’s Christian John Engelsen, examined international practices in C&D waste recycling, including mobile recycling units and techniques to improve the quality of recycled aggregates.
The dialogue identified two to three joint India-Norway research proposals, pilot projects for hazardous waste treatment, technical guidelines for DDT- and PCB-contaminated waste and industry-academia partnerships as priority areas.
The initiative aims to accelerate the adoption of resource-efficient technologies in India’s cement and construction sectors.

AI unicorn Sarvam has appointed former Google Cloud India managing director Sashikumar Sreedharan as its president and chief business officer (CBO), as it looks to strengthen its enterprise and government business and scale the commercial deployment of its AI technology. In his new role, Sreedharan will lead Sarvam's business across enterprises and government institutions while expanding its engagement with digital-native companies, developers and partners. He will also oversee marketing, finance, forward-deployed engineering, service delivery and commercial operations, the company said in a blog post. Sreedharan will also join the company's board of directors. Before joining Sarvam, Sreedharan served as MD of Google Cloud India for over a year. Across a career spanning about 35 years, he has served across companies like Microsoft India, IBM, Wipro, Happiest Mind Technologies, among others. His appointment comes as Sarvam looks to move beyond developing indigenous AI models and build a larger enterprise business around its technology. The startup said it provides its full-stack AI offerings to over 100 enterprises and government institutions. “The next phase of Sarvam is about advancing our research, developing products loved by people around the world, and building a company that can operate at a much greater scale,” the startup said. Sarvam AI's Push To Build The India Stack Founded in 2023 by Pratyush Kumar and Vivek Raghavan, Sarvam develops foundational AI models, computing infrastructure, and enterprise applications. Its offerings target businesses and government agencies seeking tools tailored to Indian languages, data-security requirements, and local use cases. The new CBO appointment comes shortly after Sarvam expanded its AI portfolio with the launch of Prism. The "System One" decision model built on top of Sarvam AI's Sarvam 105B foundation model. Rather than generating open-ended text token-by-token like a conventional LLM, it evaluates a given context, a question, and a predefined list of options in a single processing pass to return calibrated probabilities for each choice. The startup has also released several other models in recent months, including Sarvam Vision 2.1, a vision-language model for processing documents and recognising text in Indian languages, and Saaras V4, its speech-to-text model. How to get this Siri camera upgrade for your iPad before its public release
You’ll be able to access Visual Intelligence from a new tab in the tablet's Camera app.
Apple users willing to install beta versions of its OS updates can get their hands on upcoming features sooner than most, as long as they're comfortable contending with the possibility of buggy software or apps breaking. And one such feature is the Siri Mode that's already available in the camera app on supported iPhones. It's also coming to compatible iPads as part of iPadOS 27.3 and will let you ask Siri AI questions about things you point your tablet's camera at.
We got our first look at this mode when Apple properly unveiled Siri AI at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June this year. It basically brings the company's Visual Intelligence tool for asking questions from photos to the camera app. But there's one distinguishing feature that's unique to iPads which isn't available on iPhones.
On iPads, Visual Intelligence includes Apple Pencil support. So, much like with Google's Circle to Search feature, you can snap a photo of something with your iPad, use your Apple Pencil to draw a circle around an item and learn more information about the object with the help of Siri AI.
It's worth noting that Visual Intelligence is already available on compatible tablets — iPad Pro and iPad Air with the M1 chip and newer, and iPad mini with the A17 Pro or A20 Pro chipset. As things stand, you can access it in the Camera app by long-pressing the Camera Control button or pressing the Action button if you've set it up to activate the feature (and your iPad has an Action button, of course).
In iPadOS 27.3, you'll have another way to access Visual Intelligence in the Camera app. All you'll have to do is swipe through the options in the viewfinder (i.e. photo, video and portrait modes) until you get to the Siri tab.
The company is expected to release the public version of iPadOS 27.3 in December. However, you can try it on your tablet right now, because Apple released the first beta in early November.
How to install the iPadOS 27.3 beta
To install the iPadOS 27.3 beta, open the Settings app on your iPad, then tap General > Software Update. If you haven't already done so, you'll need to enable beta updates. Tap the Beta Updates option, then iPadOS 27 Public Beta. After you go back to the Software Update tab, you should be able to install the iPadOS 27.3 beta.
Before you install the beta, it's best to create a full backup of your iPad using iCloud, a Mac or a Windows PC. Beta builds aren't the finished product, meaning they're more susceptible to bugs and errors. Backing up your data should be standard practice anyway, but it's especially advisable to do that before installing a beta version of an operating system, just to make sure your files and other information stay safe.
If you don't feel comfortable enough to install a iPadOS beta, that's perfectly fine! The public version of the OS update is likely coming soon. You can check out the Siri tab on your iPad's Camera app at that point.

Malaysia's disgraced former PM leaves jail for house arrest after embezzling millions
- Published
Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest.
There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy.
Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund.
The 1MDB scandal brought down his government and made headlines around the world when it came to light a decade ago, embroiling prominent figures from Malaysia to Goldman Sachs and Hollywood.
Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors.
Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large.
Najib's mansion in one of the capital's most exclusive neighbourhoods was declared a federal prison ahead of his homecoming on Tuesday.
Critics said his release from jail undermined efforts to fight corruption and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law made no provision for house arrest.
Najib, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2018, denied wrongdoing but was convicted at two separate trials.
In the first trial he was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal.
In September, the King of Malaysia granted him a conditional pardon to see out the remaining two years of his sentence at home.
The transfer to his mansion was to take place on Friday but put on hold after the attorney general sought clarification of the royal decree. On Tuesday the high court ruled the house arrest was effective immediately.
Najib's party paid a $12m fine as part of the terms of the royal pardon allowing him to serve the rest of his term at home.
He was sentenced after being convicted of abuse of power, money laundering and breach of trust over 42 million ringgit ($10m; £7.7m) transferred from SRC International - a former unit of 1MDB - into his private accounts.
Najib is appealing against a 15-year prison sentence, handed down at a second trial in December 2025, in a case involving much larger sums of money. In that case he was convicted of misappropriating nearly 2.3 billion Malaysian ringgit ($569m; £422m) from the nation's sovereign wealth fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
He is due to start serving that sentence after his house arrest ends, which is expected in August 2028.

Judoka determined to prove refugees belong at Dakar 2026
- Published
Arno Yafunga Botay was six when his family fled the Democratic Republic of Congo after threats to his father's life culminated in an attack on their home which claimed the life of his seven-month-old sibling.
Following a spell living in the Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya, the family settled in Nairobi. There, Arno used to watch his father Arnold practising judo and eventually asked him to teach him the sport.
Now, having coming through trials in East Africa, he will compete for the Refugee Olympic Team in the under-55kg category at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games.
"I didn't expect to be selected," the 15-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"I was so excited. I was crying tears of joy."
This is the first time that a team of refugees will appear at a Youth Games.
"It [means] a lot to me to represent other refugees, represent my community," Yafunga Botay added.
The family have been in Kenya since they were forced to leave DR Congo in 2017.
"There were people who wanted to kill me," Arnold said.
"At the time, I was detained somewhere when people came to our house and attacked my family. The situation led to the death of my child."
- All you need to know about the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics 
  - Published5 days ago
- Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 
  - Published23 July
After finding safety, Yafunga Botay and his elder brother Christian would watch their father training before he headed out to work as a labourer.
Yafunga Botay began receiving instructions in judo rules and techniques at the age of seven.
However, life in their adopted East African nation provided its own challenges.
"I [did] not have the judogi clothes or transport fees for local competitions," he explained.
"It's been difficult going to school. There's no money for school fees.
"My father has no work. He needs to go to work and give us money to go and pay the school fees.
"And here we don't have support. As a refugee, to stay in Kenya, you need to have documents.
"[Thankfully] the IOC (International Olympic Committee) came with this programme of helping refugees achieve their dreams."
An Olympic first for refugees
The Refugee Olympic Team was first introduced at the Rio 2016 Olympics and Cameroon-born boxer Cindy Ngamba won the team's first ever medal at Paris 2024 when she claimed bronze in the women's 75kg category.
In a double first, the team will now make its Youth Olympics debut at Dakar 2026, which is the first Olympic event hosted on African soil.
"As a refugee, we have a right to compete," Yafunga Botay said.
"A refugee is a human being like other people."
Father Arnold says the team serves as a message of hope to people around the world who have been displaced.
"Being a refugee does not mean your life is over," he said.
"Refugees can also do things that surprise people.
"My message to fellow refugees is don't give up. Keep pushing until the end."
The six-strong team competing in Senegal is being mentored by two-time Olympic marathon champion Eliud Kipchoge.
"He teaches us [to] respect the coach, focus on what you are doing," Yafunga Botay said.
"I promised him I'll bring the gold medal [back] so he can see [what] I achieved."
Discipline and respect
Judo has become a central part of life for the family.
Arnold still coaches Yafunga Botay and Christian, now 17, occasionally serves as his younger brother's sparring partner.
The teenager describes his father as "strict" even at home, with a firm focus on the importance of discipline.
"Maintaining his weight is not easy. He [Arno] has to keep training consistently," Arnold said.
"Judo teaches him respect and helps him interact with others, whether at school or at home.
"Those lessons follow him everywhere. In judo, every time you fall you gain the strength to keep going."
The owner of the dojo in the Kenyan capital where Yafunga Botay has trained since 2020 says his selection for Dakar 2026 has "changed perceptions" of judo in the community.
"It is helping parents understand that judo is not just a fighting sport - it has real value," Lawrence Karisa Nyundo told the BBC.
"I have received calls from parents who want to enrol their children.
"It is a big achievement for this club that one of our athletes is going to compete at the Olympics. We are praying that he performs well."
After Dakar, Yafunga Botay hopes other refugees can benefit from his experience in the future.
"In Kakuma, there are good judokas.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins on Friday, with the opening ceremony a day later and judo events running from 1-3 November.

Bethell out of Australia trip and doubt for SA
- Published
Jacob Bethell has been ruled out of England's white-ball tour of Australia and is a huge doubt for the Test tour of South Africa following the recurrence of a knee injury.
Bethell has not played for England since July after suffering discomfort in his right knee while making 91 in a one-day international against India at Lord's.
He had surgery in September and looked set to return down under when he travelled to Australia for the series that begins with the first of three one-day internationals in Perth on Friday.
But the 23-year-old did not play in the warm-up match against Western Australia at the weekend and suffered what England have described as a "setback" in training earlier this week.
Bethell underwent a scan and is now set to return home to see a specialist.
England have called up Sussex all-rounder James Coles as cover, while uncapped seamer Eddie Jack has also been added to the one-day squad as a replacement for Josh Tongue, who had previously been ruled out with a toe injury.
Following the three ODIs, England play five T20s in Australia, before the Test series in South Africa begins on 17 December.
Bethell's continued absence is a huge concern for England, given the time he has already missed and his importance across all three formats.
It is also a huge blow for Bethell, whose 154 in the final Test against Australia in January was one of the few highlights of England's dismal Ashes tour. Instead of being able to build on that innings, he has been stalled by the knee injury.
The Warwickshire man was named in the squad for the three Tests in South Africa on Monday.
At the time, selector Marcus North admitted England did not know who would make way from the team that beat Pakistan 3-0 during the home summer in order to accommodate Bethell's return.
Opener Emilio Gay and Jordan Cox, batting at number three, both came into the England Test side for that series and one of them looked set to be left out of the final XI in South Africa.
Now, both Gay and Cox could be set for further opportunities to stake their long-term Test credentials.
In the summer, Ollie Pope was recalled to the Test squad as the spare batter in Bethell's absence.
Pope is due to be with England Lions in South Africa in a tour that overlaps with the Test series, so the Surrey man looks a strong contender to be promoted if Bethell is ruled out.
James Rew, who has one Test cap, and uncapped Durham opener Ben McKinney have both been in strong form on England Lions' white-ball tour of West Indies and would be other options to replace Bethell in South Africa.
Speaking before the first one-day in Australia, Test captain Joe Root told BBC Sport: "It's disappointing for Jacob. I don't know much more. I know how hard he works and everything he's done to get himself right.
"Hopefully it's not too serious and he's not out for too long."

Google’s Pixel phones get an update every month, but most are just security patches and bug fixes. The bigger changes are bundled into quarterly Pixel Drops, and one is rolling out today. The update brings a few new things, and many of the Gemini features previously exclusive to the latest Pixel phones will also expand to Google’s Pixel 10 lineup.
The Pixel 11 was Google’s first foray into “Gemini Intelligence” branding, something we’ll see a lot more of going forward. The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN.
 
The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.
Now, two more men fear becoming the latest victims of Beijing’s repressive crackdown against the largely Muslim ethnic group, condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity.
The girlfriend of one of the men said her boyfriend, whose name is being withheld for security reasons, told the Guardian he wanted to go “anywhere else but China”.
Human rights groups said two Uyghur men were at risk of deportation after recently being transferred to an immigration detention centre and they feared Thai authorities may once again give in to pressure from Beijing.
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” she said.
The men had been serving a seven-year prison sentence for offences related to an attempted escape from immigration detention in January 2020. They were part of a group of more than 200 Uyghur men, women and children who were apprehended by Thai police in 2014 near the border with Malaysia after they fled from China.
Since 2014, women and children in the group have been released to Turkey, while the men have been deported to China, in separate batches, attracting criticism from the United Nations and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.
Uyghurs, a Turkic minority mainly from the Xinjiang region in China, have been subjected to decades of oppressive and discriminatory treatment from the Chinese authorities. This has included the incarceration of hundreds of thousands of people in detention camps aimed at stamping out their cultural identity.
Beijing has defended its policies in Xinjiang as being aimed at poverty alleviation and counter-terrorism.
In July, Marzeyya Kasem’s (who asked to be referred to by her Islamic alias) boyfriend wrote to her in a letter that he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back to China. “Sometimes I thought why I’m a human being. What I do wrong against China … no want to go back to China,” he wrote. She shared the letter with a Thai rights group.
The two men facing imminent deportation reportedly pleaded their case to Thailand’s office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday.
Relatives of Uyghurs have said the Chinese government was “paranoid about Uyghurs going to a safe country in large numbers and living together”, and preferred to have them deported.
It is not clear whether China has issued a formal extradition request for the two men. But Chaipruak Doungprapat, Thailand’s national security council chief, told reporters that the men, along with three other Uyghurs who are still in prison, had arrest warrants outstanding in China.
Some have questioned whether criminal warrants could be credible considering that at least one of them, Kasem’s boyfriend, was a minor when he left China. “If they are really wanted for a crime in China, why didn’t China immediately issue a [Interpol] red notice [when they were detained in 2014]?” asked Kasem.
Kasem believes that because Thailand was criticised for last year’s mass deportation, this time the authorities were trying to establish a more credible legal basis for the move.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign affairs ministry said: “The cooperation between China and Thailand in combating cross-border illegal and criminal activities such as smuggling is consistent with the laws of the two countries, international law and international practice.”
A spokesperson for Thailand’s foreign affairs ministry declined to comment.

Under its new global head Kunal Shah, WhatsApp is looking to expand beyond messaging. In a social media post, Shah said that the Meta-owned platform would focus on making services such as bill payments, financial transactions and international connectivity as seamless as sending a message. Shah, who took charge of WhatsApp earlier this year, said the messaging platform would focus on three broad areas — making communication more expressive, simplifying everyday tasks and using AI to improve user experiences. WhatsApp users could potentially complete tasks such as paying bills, borrowing money and staying connected while travelling without having to navigate multiple platforms or services. “We’re working with financial services and telecom partners so that finishing something feels as easy as starting it,” he said. Shah’s statement signals WhatsApp’s intent to deepen its push into financial services and commerce, building on its existing payments and business offerings. In India, the platform has been expanding its payments capabilities through WhatsApp Pay, although its adoption has remained limited compared with established UPI players. It also outlined plans to integrate AI more deeply into the messaging experience, with the technology expected to help users find relevant information, complete tasks and keep track of bookings and appointments. “The best technology saves you time, so you can get back to the connections that matter,” he said. However, Shah did not specify which AI capabilities the company plans to introduce or whether these would involve more advanced agentic features. It currently offers AI-powered features through Meta AI, including assistance with queries and content generation. WhatsApp's Three Priorities On the communication front, WhatsApp wants to make features such as voice notes, groups, stickers and video simpler and more expressive. Shah said users send more than 10 Bn voice messages and 4 Bn stickers on the platform every day, highlighting how communication habits continue to evolve. It also wants to reduce the number of steps involved in completing everyday activities that originate in conversations. This could involve deeper integrations with financial services and telecom partners, although Shah did not disclose specific partnerships or timelines. The third priority is the use of AI to make the platform more efficient by helping users retrieve information and manage everyday tasks. However, Shah emphasised that these changes would not come at the cost of user privacy. He reiterated that personal messages and calls on WhatsApp would remain end-to-end encrypted. “Whatever we build, WhatsApp must remain simple, reliable and private. These principles we’ve had for years aren’t changing,” he said. Shah's remarks come nearly five months after he moved from CRED to Meta to take over as the global head of WhatsApp. In June 2026, Shah announced that he would step down from day-to-day operations at CRED to join Meta. CRED cofounder Miten Sampat took over as interim CEO, while Shah retained his personal shareholding in the fintech startup. His appointment also marked a leadership transition at WhatsApp, with former head Will Cathcart moving to a new role within Meta. Shah's move came alongside Meta's investment in CRED as part of the fintech startup's ₹8,550 Cr Series H funding round, which valued the company at ₹43,239 Cr post-money. At WhatsApp, Shah now faces the challenge of expanding the platform's utility beyond communication while maintaining its simplicity and privacy standards. India, WhatsApp's largest market globally, has an estimated 535 Mn to 550 Mn monthly active users, with some industry databases putting the figure as high as 853.8 Mn. Globally, the platform has more than 3 Bn users. However, driving adoption of its payments, financial services and other offerings will remain a key challenge.

Since Valve announced its Steam Deck Verified program in 2021, players have found that a game’s “Verified” status doesn’t always match how well it actually runs on the handheld. Now, new Steam Deck frame rate data being shared by Valve itself can help players dig deeper into the performance they can expect from many Steam Deck games.
Valve has been collecting anonymized frame rate data from Steam players who opt in since February. Yesterday evening, the company announced it has started sharing that data on many Steam Store pages as averages and histograms for both the Steam Deck and Steam Deck OLED.
Valve acknowledges that players enabling VSync or frame rate limits can bias the collected data somewhat and that the measurements don’t account for custom in-game settings that Steam Deck users may tinker with to get a game running. Regardless, Valve says it has nonetheless “found that the framerate data consolidates around relatively narrow ranges.”
Beyond the badge
This kind of data can be extremely useful for distinguishing between the wide range of performance levels that can exist among “Verified” Steam Deck games. Both Cyberpunk 2077 and Skyrim: Special Edition earn the same Steam Deck Verified badge, for instance, but the former sees average Deck frame rates in the 30–40 FPS range, while the latter usually achieves 50–60 FPS on the hardware.
Valve’s frame rate data is even more useful for games that the company insists are “Unsupported” on Steam Deck because their “graphics setting cannot be configured to run well” on the hardware or because Valve is “still working on adding support for this game.” Despite warnings like these, games like Starfield, Silent Hill 2, and Assassin’s Creed Syndicate, to name just a few, all show extremely playable frame rates reported by actual Steam Deck users. Assassin’s Creed Syndicate in particular approaches a 60 FPS average on the Steam Deck OLED hardware despite its “Unsupported” status.

Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows.
The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.
You had one job
Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.
“We were shocked,” Claroc said in a Tuesday post. “The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it. Had the sales team bought a tool for this, it would have sat behind company sign-in, open only to the team. Built with AI, it went live open to anyone with the link.
Claroc notified SpaceXSI of the privacy spill on Sunday. When no one responded, a Claroc official took to X to tag both Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer about the threat. At the time this post went live almost all data remained available with one notable exception: the contents from the 24 SpaceXSI apps. All of them were exposing the information on Monday evening. SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending an email with questions for this article. At the time this post went live, links for all 24 apps returned an “app not found” error.
That's fine for Google Docs, because all the pages are running Google's JS code and Google can ensure it doesn't move data between unrelated documents. Similar for the simple documents shared on Claude/ChatGPT/etc. But it's no good for hosting multiple independent applications that are potentially running arbitrary JS, since even if one application is non-public and properly authenticated with session cookies, any other application could freely read sensitive data from it.
I think you'd need a unique (but non-secret) element in the domain name to keep each application on a separate origin, as a security boundary, and also put a secret element in the URL's path which won't be leaked over DNS.

Whenever divorce comes up in conversation, everybody seems to raise their eyebrows. People want to know what happened, who did what, and whose fault it was. We treat a marriage ending like a mystery to solve. Interestingly enough, this does not happen just for celebrities; ordinary people get the side-eye, too.
On Sunday, actor Amanda Seyfried shared something that I wrote last year on her Instagram Stories. I was thrilled she shared my work, of course. But it was the words she chose to share that caught people's attention, and one word in particular: boring.
I'd written those words while reflecting on my own divorce and my family's history. My parents are divorced. Both sets of my grandparents were divorced. I grew up in a family where divorce was absolutely normal, yet society still treated it like a scandal or a failure. I think it's high time we reframe divorce as just another life transition.
As I wrote in the post she shared, "The most radical thing we can do is make divorce boring. Make it normal. Make it accessible."
Seyfried then shared a photograph of herself embracing Thomas Sadoski, the father of her children, from whom she announced her separation in September. She tagged him, too.
By Monday morning, my words were appearing across celebrity news outlets. Seyfried was making headlines for normalizing divorce, something I've championed for five years through Fresh Starts Registry, which I co-founded with my sister.
Yet amid the excitement, I kept thinking about the two people I most want to understand why this matters: my sons.
Divorce allowed a different kind of childhood
When my divorce was finalized in 2020, my boys were 4 and 7. I worried that the end of my marriage would become the defining tragedy of their childhood. Despite growing up around divorce, I'd still absorbed the cultural message that a family became "broken" when a marriage ended.
My sons are now 10 and 13. We live upstairs in my childhood home, with my mother and stepfather downstairs. Their days are filled with homework, snacks, school pickups, activities, and endless negotiations about whose turn it is to watch a movie with Mom. Their grandparents are part of that rhythm. Their lives are steady and complete.
I want my sons to recognize this as a whole family, not as a consolation prize for the one we supposedly lost.
I tried to send a realistic message about divorce
That doesn't mean pretending divorce was easy. Children can miss things, wish things were different, or have complicated feelings about the decisions adults make. My boys don't have to celebrate my divorce to love their family exactly as it is.
I want them to understand that adults can change their minds and their lives. Sometimes putting yourself first is a radical decision. They know me as their mother, but also as someone who writes, runs a business, and makes art at night while they hang out nearby. Marriage isn't the only measure of a successful adulthood, and staying married certainly isn't the only way to be a good parent.
Energy changes form, and so does life
The question I hear most often from parents in my divorce work is whether ending a marriage means harming their children or blowing up their family. I completely understand that fear. A family changing shape can be scary, even when the change is necessary.
I explain it to my boys using a scientific principle: energy doesn't disappear, it changes form. I think of divorce like an atom splitting. The structure changes, sometimes dramatically, but the people in that family don't vanish. The love and support my children receive haven't disappeared since our household changed.
More on divorce
Two people can live under different roofs and still be a family. Two people can share a roof and still live in an emotionally unhealthy home. Children need care and stability through difficult transitions. But why declare a family damaged based on marital status, or how many roofs it lives under?
Making divorce boring doesn't erase its pain. It means the end of a marriage doesn't have to become a scandal, a moral verdict, or a burden our children carry for life.
People grow and change throughout their lives. Sometimes we grow together, and sometimes we grow in different directions. I want my sons to understand that choosing a different future doesn't mean the past was a mistake, and that changing a relationship doesn't have to mean erasing everything that came before it.
Most of all, I want them to grow up knowing that their family isn't defined by whether their parents are married or live under the same roof. It's defined by the people who love them, care for them, and continue to show up for them.
My marriage may have ended, but the family we created didn't disappear. It evolved, and I hope my children grow up knowing that they're allowed to evolve, too.

Your iPhone Duo can do more than multitask! These 10 quirky apps turn the foldable into a retro computer, cassette player, Nintendo DS, accordion, instant camera, virtual fridge, and even a grilled cheese toaster. Some are free, others paid, but all make clever, fun use of its folding design.
The iPhone Duo is perhaps the most radically different iPhone since the original iPhone. While its arrival was rumored for over a year, Apple finally launched it this September. The phone can fold in half to become nearly passport-sized and can be unfolded to shape-shift into a bigger, tablet-ish smartphone. Ever since its launch, we have been constantly hearing about its multitasking prowess, its computer-like processing abilities, how well it handles productivity apps, yada yada yada…
But all this is pretty basic, something we expect with all new iPhones, or rather flagship smartphones at this point. With the kind of price and specs these high-end smartphones come with, it hardly is a surprise that they can handle power-hungry tasks with ease. The foldable form-factor and the added display real estate make it a different experience, surely. But surely there is way more to the device than the same old tasks and apps? So, we are on a mission to make your iPhone Duo fun, using all that processing and multitasking magic that it possesses.
The result is these ten apps.
They are not at all useful. But they make the Duo a-not-just-another-serious (read: boring) device out there. They add an element to it that we all so need to survive – they make it fun. Got an iPhone Duo? Download! (Note: relax, all of these are optimized for the iPhone Duo)
Table of Contents
Top 10 Wacky and Fun iPhone Duo Apps
| Sl No | App | Price | What it does | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tiny Computer | $3.99 | Turns the Duo into a retro PC with vintage keyboards, games, and interfaces. | 
| 2 | Deck Man | $4.99 | Recreates a cassette Walkman with realistic tape controls and sounds. | 
| 3 | MD Vinyl | Free | Turns the screen into a vinyl turntable with spinning records and music controls. | 
| 4 | Fold Accordion | $2.99 | Uses the folding hinge as accordion bellows to create music. | 
| 5 | Delta | Free | Recreates the Nintendo DS gaming experience with dual-screen controls. | 
| 6 | Toastie | $2.99 | Turns the Duo into a virtual grilled cheese maker that works when folded shut. | 
| 7 | TypeDraw | $4.99 | Recreates a paper notebook with handwriting, page turns, and paper effects. | 
| 8 | Snapshots | $1.99 | Turns the Duo into a Polaroid-style instant camera with developing photos. | 
| 9 | Phridge | Free | Creates a virtual fridge you can decorate, stock, and mess around with. | 
| 10 | ChompDuo | Free | Adds six animated monsters whose jaws open and close as you fold the phone. | 
Tiny Computer (USD 3.99): Unfolding Retro computer feels
Imagine getting a vintage PC feel on something as new and pristine as the iPhone Duo? That is exactly what the app Tiny Computer can deliver. Using the half-fold setting of the iPhone Duo, the app turns your phone into a proper vintage computer. The upper half of the screen becomes the display while the lower half becomes the keyboard. You get to choose from ten different computers in total, including the Apple Macintosh, IBM PC, iMac G3, IBM ThinkPad, Windows XP, Amiga 500, and more.
It is not just all show; you can actually use some retro paint apps, run old command-line interfaces, play games like Solitaire, and even type on clicky keyboards. Each machine also hides secret commands and files paired with occasional crashes to make the whole experience even more believable.
Deck Man (USD 4.99): Go cassette crazy!
Another app that brings retro feels to the Duo is the Deck Man. It is one of the most visually appealing apps for the Duo because it essentially turns your iPhone Duo into a 1980s cassette Walkman player. The app uses the unfolded version of the phone as the collection of cassettes in your music library that you can browse. You then “insert” the cassette of your choice into the deck, and once you fold it, the secondary screen mimics the look of a cassette Walkman player.
The app has realistic mechanical clicks, background tape static, and if you fast-forward or rewind it too aggressively, the virtual tape inside can get all tangled and then would have to be untangled manually, just like a retro cassette player. “Tape” this one to your Duo!
MD Vinyl (Free): Spin those discs!
If cassettes are “too” modern for you, then you can go even further back in the music era with the iPhone Duo by installing MD Vinyl. This essentially turns the Duo into a virtual turntable with spinning records and album art. The record design determines the aesthetics of the app. The app allows you to pick and drop the needle to play or pause the tracks. It can pair with music apps like Apple Music and Spotify. It is not a new app and has existed for years, but it attains a whole new dimension on the Duo, adding a vintage touch to the modern audio experience.
Fold Accordion (USD 2.99): Fold and unfold to create music
If there is one app that makes the most use of the iPhone Duo’s form factor, it is the Fold Accordion. It literally turns the hinge of the iPhone Duo into working accordion bellows. When you launch the app, it places the keys on the display, which you can press with your right hand while opening and closing the Duo with the left hand to create music of your own. The app comes with a learning mode which highlights keys you have to press to create something pleasant, instead of getting straight to the chaos of keys. A great way to test that folding mechanism too.
Delta (Nintendo DS) (free): Double screen gaming magic, DS style!
Popular Retro Game emulator Delta has launched an updated version of its app, specifically for the iPhone Duo. The app brings specially designed skins for the iPhone Duo, and the most interesting one of the lot is the Nintendo DS portable gaming console, which interestingly was the world’s first mainstream foldable device. The app uses the inner display of the iPhone Duo to bring a DS-style layout and controls across the displays. The game even enters sleep state when the device is folded, similar to the Nintendo DS. Trust the Duo to bring back the magic of double-screen gaming.
Toastie (USD 2.99): Smartest thing since sliced bread!
Unleash the inner chef in you with the absolutely useless but equally fun app called Toastie. This app turns the iPhone Duo into a – wait for it – virtual grilled cheese toaster. You get 15 seconds to assemble your sandwich, and once you are done, you have to hit the ‘grill’ button and physically close the iPhone Duo shut. You then have to wait, listen to the sizzle, or get a slight peek to ensure your toastie is grilling well. If you open the phone too soon, the cheese won’t be melted; if you wait too long, it might end up getting burned. Once you are done with it, you serve it, and you get a star based on your accuracy, recipe, timing, and so on. Useful? Not. But definitely the smartest thing since sliced bread. Actually, the smartest thing done to sliced bread!
TypeDraw (USD 4.99): Paper-like Moleskine
The iPhone Duo looks like a handy pocket notebook or a passport, and TypeDraw literally converts it into a handy little Moleskine-like notebook. It even comes with a digital thread, just like you find on a notebook, which you have to move or swipe aside to open the notebook (or just open the Duo). You can write anywhere on a page using an Apple Pencil or your finger and can even fiddle and curl up paper corners, as well as choose fonts (you can convert your handwriting into one, if you wish), types of paper, and even plain, ruled, dotted, or grid patterns on paper. And the page turns on the internal display are absolutely paper-like. It is like carrying a real notebook.
Snapshots ($1.99): Unfold to Polaroid
Snapshots is an app that helps your Duo morph into an instant camera. It is one of the very first community-developed apps optimized specifically for the iPhone Duo. When bent in half (90 degrees), the top half of the primary display becomes the viewfinder while the bottom half holds the controls. Once you hit the shutter, the photo captured on the upper half of the viewfinder is virtually printed on the lower half with the same mechanical sound and effect as on an instant camera. Just like with a real instant camera, the photo does not appear right away but takes a few seconds to develop, giving us those Polaroid feels.
Phridge (free): Chill…literally!
This is perhaps the most quirky and our personal favorite app in the list. It turns the iPhone Duo into a – wait for it – refrigerator. When folded, you can decorate the ‘door’ of this fridge with magnets, to-do lists, photographs. And when you open it, you can see groceries and food and drink inside and arrange them. This is when the real fun happens, because you can topple something over, drop a fizzy drink, or break a glass jar or bottle. You can also place your hand in a slingshot to shoot stones at the shelves, or get a sword to slice things in half, if you feel like some chaos. You can only close the fridge when you fold the phone shut, making the hinge integral to its operation. How cool is that? Just chillin…
Chompduo (Free): Jaw-dropping (and closing) stuff!
We all need an app that adds six hungry monsters to your iPhone Duo. Well, we do, anyway. That is exactly what ChompDuo does. When installed, it unleashes six hungry monsters on your Duo that open their huge mouths when the device is unfolded, making the inner display a giant mouth. You can tap on the open mouth to make it bite or drag it to squeeze it shut. When you fold the phone, the jaws close shut with a chomp sound, and a pair of googly eyes appear on the outer display, which can jump when you tap on them. What more does one need on a foldable?
