Nations worldwide have spent the last few years obsessing over bigger models and the compute power needed to train them. However, as models move into everyday products, it is becoming difficult to run AI models faster, cheaper and reliably at scale. This is where inference platforms are emerging as saviours. Now, before we dive into the topic, let’s first understand what inference actually means. Simply put, inference is the process through which a trained AI model uses what it has learned to respond to new inputs, such as questions, images or instructions. For context, when you ask an AI model to summarise a health report or a business document, it uses its existing capabilities to process your request and generate a response. But achieving this is not as simple as it reads. Now, the challenge is that every interaction with AI requires computing resources, whose costs can quickly add up as millions of users interact with AI-powered products every day. This is where inference platforms have found their niche. These platforms deploy, manage and optimise AI models without having to build and maintain the entire infrastructure themselves. In India, companies such as Simplismart, Pipeshift and E2E Networks are building different layers of the inference stack, betting that businesses will increasingly pay for faster, cheaper and more reliable AI. But with global cloud giants and AI providers competing for a share of this growing market, where do Indian startups stand? And what will it take for them to build sustainable businesses? Let's explore in today's edition of The AI Shift… Why Inference Became A Business Problem The need for inference platforms becomes clearer when we look at how businesses are using AI in their everyday operations. After integrating an AI model into their product, businesses want to make sure that it is delivering reliable results at the right speed and cost. Take Apna, a jobs and professional networking platform and a customer of Indian inference startup Simplismart. The company uses AI for tasks such as improving candidate profiles and onboarding employers. The challenge for Apna's CTO, Abhishek Ranjan, is to make its AI faster, more efficient, and economically viable. Apna uses inference platforms to run smaller open-source and proprietary models for relatively simple tasks. As the number of AI interactions grows, even small differences in cost and response time can add up across millions of requests. "But this does not mean businesses need to depend on external inference platforms for every task," said Ranjan, who is also the CTO of Blue Machines AI, a subsidiary of Apna that has built its own inference platform for conversational AI applications. Unlike some recruitment-related tasks, conversational AI needs much faster responses and must be able to handle many users at the same time. Even a small delay can affect the experience of someone interacting with a voice AI assistant. This is why Blue Machines has built its own inference platform, allowing it greater control over speed and performance. Depending on the task, it can use advanced AI models, open-source models or models it has fine-tuned itself. Apna uses an external inference platform when it wants flexibility across models without having to manage the entire serving infrastructure. Blue Machines, meanwhile, offers more specialised requirements around response times and concurrent workloads. Simplismart's examples show how the problem changes by workload. The startup claims it has reduced inference costs by 53% while retaining 99.99% accuracy through model quantisation and latency optimisation for voice AI platform Sanas. When it comes to customer support platform Exotel, Simplismart claims to have reduced inference costs to ₹0.90–₹1.30 per minute from ₹2.10 for a closed-model API, while cutting latency from 1.1 seconds to under 300 milliseconds. The common thread is that inference is not about finding the cheapest or most powerful model but finding the combination of model, hardware and serving configuration that fits the business. Inference Comes In Different Flavours The term “inference platform” can sound like one product, but businesses can consume inference in very different ways. The choice depends on how much control they need, how much traffic they handle and how much of the infrastructure they want to manage themselves. “Inference platform is too generic a term,” said Vishnu Subramanian, founder at JarvisLabs, an AI infrastructure company, acquired by E2E Networks. He pointed to four broad ways businesses can consume inference: Shared model APIs: Ready-to-use models accessed through an API, with the infrastructure managed by the provider. Managed inference: Dedicated model deployments where the provider handles much of the technical setup. Self-managed inference: Businesses bring their own models and decide how those models are deployed and scaled. Dedicated infrastructure: Reserved capacity for workloads that need predictable performance, latency or reliability. The simplest option is a shared model API, according to Subramanian. JarvisLabs' Token Factory, for instance, lets businesses access hosted open models through an API and pay for the tokens they consume. The GPU capacity is managed by the platform, allowing a company to start using a model without building its own serving infrastructure. For businesses with larger or more specific workloads, managed inference offers more control without requiring them to manage every technical layer. Therefore, a startup experimenting with an open model may be comfortable with a shared API, while a high-volume voice application may need dedicated capacity. Similarly, a regulated enterprise may want greater control over its models, data and deployment environment. Why Are Startups Betting On Inference? It is a no-brainer that inference has created infrastructure opportunity, with startups building different layers of the inference stack rather than simply competing to offer more GPU capacity. In India, Simplismart is one of the companies trying to capture this opportunity. The startup raised $14 Mn in Series B funding in October, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. Its software helps application companies run AI within their cost, performance and deployment requirements, while also allowing cloud providers to turn GPU capacity into managed AI services. Listed company E2E Networks is approaching inference through both managed and self-managed offerings, while startups like Pipeshift are focusing on production inference for open-source models, particularly workloads where latency matters. Pipeshift recently partnered with Neysa to bring its managed serving layer together with Neysa's sovereign AI cloud for Indian businesses, targeting use cases such as voice agents, coding agents and enterprise copilots. The same fragmentation is visible globally. YC-backed startups are building businesses around increasingly specific inference problems. Hopper, an AI inference platform for voice agents, for instance, focuses on optimising inference for real-time agents and post-training open models on production traces, while RouterPlus is building an inference marketplace that selects models and providers based on a company’s actual traffic, cost and capacity requirements. As of now, the inference opportunity is unlikely to settle into a single category. For Indian startups, it could mean opportunities across low-latency voice AI, open-model serving, sovereign inference, agent workloads and specialised enterprise deployments. Therefore, the white space for the next big opportunity is right there — make that intelligence faster, cheaper and easier to scale. Control Room keeps a constant watch on all of these experiments. The moment staff spot unusual or potentially dangerous behaviour, they can hit a single stop button and shut the entire job down in roughly 35 seconds. This is not a public product for everyday users. It is an internal tool designed to give OpenAI tighter real-time control over its own most advanced research. In an era when AI systems are becoming more independent and capable of long stretches of unsupervised work, even the labs building them need reliable ways to stay in charge. Vecton AI aims to address these challenges with AI consulting and strategy, process automation, custom-trained models and autonomous agent development. The startup uses a forward-deployed engineering model, with its teams working alongside financial institutions through implementation rather than limiting its role to consulting. It builds production-ready AI agents and machine learning workflows designed to meet BFSI regulatory requirements, with applications across sales acceleration, customer engagement, document processing and intelligent copilots. Vecton AI is targeting India’s growing ‘AI in BFSI’ market, which is projected to reach $9.4 Bn by 2034. The startup’s focus is on helping financial institutions operationalise AI across high-volume processes while navigating the compliance and infrastructure constraints of the sector. The Governance Review Committee will report its initial recommendations after being tasked with undertaking a thorough review of the ICC’s governance.

Cardiologists have called for a review of a recent order issued by the Director General of Health Services (DGHS), strictly prohibiting the sterilisation and re-use of single-use devices and disposable surgical items used in critical specialties like cardiology and cardiothoracic and vascular surgery, citing issues of patient safety
At the annual conference of the Cardiological Society of India (CSI), Kerala chapter, here on Sunday, the CSI Kerala Chapter president Asokan P.K. said the association would seek a review of the order by DGHS as the exorbitant cost of medical devices and accessories would make crucial procedures such as angioplasty unaffordable and inaccessible to many.
Prathap Kumar N., organising chairman of the conference, said the rising cost of complex angioplasty, particularly procedures requiring multiple specialised devices, had become a major concern. Reimbursement package rates under government-funded health insurance schemes were often inadequate to cover the actual cost of advanced cardiac interventions.
With an increasing proportion of the population requiring advanced cardiac interventions, making complex procedures affordable to ordinary patients was a major challenge. Permitting the regulated re-use of select interventional devices, wherever scientifically proven safe, could help reduce treatment costs and extend the benefits of modern cardiac care to a wider section of the population, Dr. Prathap Kumar pointed out
He said cardiologists had sought a review to determine whether selected catheters, guidewires and other equipment could be safely re-processed under scientifically validated protocols and re-used for patients.
“Patient safety must remain paramount. Any proposal for re-use must be supported by scientific evidence, validated sterilisation, functional testing and strict regulatory oversight,” Dr. Prathap Kumar said.
He called for wider consultation among medical specialists, infection-control experts and regulatory authorities to develop an evidence-based policy regarding the sterilisation and re-use of medical devices, balancing affordability with patient safety.
The order by the DGHS said the practice of re-using single-use devices and disposable surgical items was a serious concern from the perspective of patient safety, infection prevention and control, regulatory compliance and healthcare expenditure. It said such re-use may also expose patients to significant risks, including cross-infection, device malfunction, loss of performance and other procedure-related complications
However, it is a fact that sterilisation and re-use of medical devices, ensuring the integrity of the devices and patient safety, is a common practice in both private and public sector hospitals across the country.
The Cardiological Society of India had in 2017 brought out a consensus document, “Guidance on reuse of cardio-vascular catheters and devices in India”, which clearly endorsed re-use, but set out certain requirements which had to be met for re-use to be safe and effective.
The devices, which can be reused, should be clearly defined, a meticulous process for disinfection and sterilisation followed and its functionality ascertained before use. Also, “an appropriate consent should be obtained where necessary” and the cost saving entailed should be directly passed on to the patient, the document said.
The CSI(K) conference also featured discussions on the evolving roles of drug-coated balloons and drug-eluting stents in coronary angioplasty, leadless pacemakers, laser-assisted coronary interventions, invasive coronary function testing, newer cholesterol-lowering therapies, complex valve procedures and advances in heart failure management.

Revised Maximum Retail Prices (MRPs) of 1,364 anti-cancer formulations have come into effect from Monday (November 9, 2026), a move projected to save consumers an estimated ₹3,540.38 crore annually, according to an official release.
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), functioning under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, capped trade margins on the MRP of 137 anti-cancer drugs based on recommendations submitted on October 17, 2026, by an Expert Committee constituted by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.

According to the Ministry, 85 pharmaceutical companies have reported revised MRPs for 1,364 anti-cancer formulations across 121 drugs as of November 8, 2026.
Price reductions of over 50% have been reported for 679 brands, with the highest price cut recorded at 96.45%, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers: Department of Pharmaceuticals said in the release.
The Ministry stated that no chemist or hospital pharmacy is permitted to charge more than the revised MRP.
Consumers can verify medicine rates via the revised MRP printed on packs, the 'Pharma Sahi Daam' mobile application, or the official NPPA website (nppa.gov.in), it said.
Consumers can lodge complaints against instances of overcharging or other pricing-related issues through the Pharma Jan Samadhan portal or contact the NPPA helpline at 1800-111-255, the release added.

A post is being widely circulated on social media (here, here) claiming that Members of Parliament (MPs) in India are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. It also claims that MPs are entitled to toll tax exemptions and free train travel. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Indian MPs are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. They are also entitled to toll tax exemption and free train travel.
Fact: MPs are entitled to free train and air travel, as well as toll fees exemption. However, they are not exempt from paying GST on purchases of cars and air conditioners. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
First, according to the details of benefits available to MPs on the official Parliament website (here and here), each MP is entitled to 34 free single air journeys per year anywhere within India. They can use these tickets to travel with their spouse, relatives, or friends.
Additionally, MPs are entitled to free first-class AC or executive-class train travel anywhere in the country. Their spouse or another accompanying person can also avail of this facility. An accompanying assistant is entitled to a free AC two-tier (2-Tier) train pass.
According to the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) regulations (here and here), vehicles used by MPs are exempt from paying toll fees on national highways. MPs are also entitled to toll-exempt FASTags for two vehicles during their tenure.
However, there is no evidence to suggest that MPs are exempt from paying GST on cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase. Neither the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954, which outlines the benefits and entitlements of MPs, nor any official government notification mentions such a GST exemption.
To sum up, while MPs are entitled to certain travel benefits, they do not receive any GST exemption on the cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase.

Why your Roku might be plugged into the wrong HDMI port
Your Roku might lose a few features if you plug it into any old HDMI port on your TV.
Depending on your smart TV, an add-on media streaming device isn't necessarily essential, but they can still provide a lot of value. Perhaps your TV's processor can't keep up with the latest apps and features, or you might prefer a specific ecosystem. That's what Apple is banking on to sell the 2026 Apple TV 4K, which is now an extremely pricey box at $299.
Roku streamers are far cheaper, but can still come with other concerns. You might be worried about your Roku monitoring what you watch, for example, or the implications of Fox's pending takeover. On a more mundane level, there's an issue applicable to any connected device: getting the best possible performance from your TV.
To do that, it's vital to you select the right HDMI port and cable. It's hard to go too far wrong with Roku devices, but a mistake could still mean getting inferior video or sound.
Picking the right HDMI port for your Roku
The reason it's hard to go wrong is that for the most part, Roku devices don't exploit any features unique to HDMI 2.1 or later, and all modern TVs support at least HDMI 2.0. Standards like 4K, HDR10+, Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision can all work over 2.0, if not necessarily in their optimal form. Optimal would include 120Hz-plus refresh rates — but even Roku's top-of-the-line Ultra is capped at 60Hz, regardless of which port you plug it into.
That's acceptable, since 24fps is the most common playback speed for TV and movies while 30fps is used for news. 60fps content (equaling 60Hz) is common on YouTube, Twitch and many live TV streaming services; any modern Roku will support this. 120Hz would simply enable clearer motion, which is mostly relevant for gaming.
The Roku Ultra does support an HDMI 2.1 feature called Quick Media Switching (QMS). This allows refresh rates to shift up or down seamlessly, like if you're flipping from the 30fps evening news to the 24fps cinematic standard. Without QMS, you're going to run into temporary blackouts when a frame rate shift occurs.
In some cases, only certain HDMI ports on your TV will support HDR standards like Dolby Vision. Or if that barrier doesn't exist, you might have to go into your TV's input settings to flip a port over to the appropriate "enhanced" option. Ports are often set to reduced capabilities by default for the sake of compatibility. But since it's unlikely that you'd run into conflicts, you might as well enable modern functionality across the board. Check your manufacturer's website to figure out which ports support HDR and which menus you might need to navigate.
On sound, cables and similar
Another important point here is that you shouldn't plug a Roku into your TV's ARC or eARC port. While that technology is essential for some audio features like Dolby Atmos, labeled ports are intended for compatible output devices like soundbars, receivers and other speaker systems. If a TV supports ARC or eARC, it's automatically pulling audio from every HDMI 2.x input, regardless of how it's marked.
Along with the right ports, it's also important to choose a matching cable. If your Roku does support HDMI 2.1 features, a 2.0 cable will prevent them from working. If there's any doubt about what you have, HDMI 2.1 and even 2.2 (also known as Ultra96, which is not in wide use yet) cables are easy to find at low prices.
Computers and game consoles should always get priority for available HDMI 2.1 or 2.2 ports, since they can fully take advantage of high refresh rates and VRR (variable refresh rate). Streamers like Rokus are further back in the line, at least until manufacturers start taking advantage of everything newer TVs are capable of.

India’s anaemia burden is not in doubt. The fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) found that more than half of women and about two-thirds of young children are anaemic. In this context, double-fortified salt (DFS) — fortified with iodine and iron — is often proposed as a potentially transformative solution. However, the case for DFS rests on convenience: everyone consumes salt, so why not add iron to it? But convenience is not efficacy, and a policy that asks the country to continue consuming salt to deliver iron deserves closer scrutiny.
Iron fortification of salt is a vehicle that cuts against public health. Indians consume, by most estimates, roughly twice the five grams of salt a day recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). About one in three adults has hypertension, and India’s own non-communicable disease (NCD) action plan commits to a 30% relative reduction in salt intake.

Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling
In northern Ethiopia, conflict pushes a strained healthcare system to the brink
"It was a mess, it was chaos, and that continued for almost seven, eight days. Without (cell) network, without electricity," recalls a surgeon in Ethiopia.
On September 24, a two-year ceasefire between rebels and the Ethiopian government began to collapse. As injured people streamed in from the countryside, this surgeon and his colleagues treated as many as they could at a hospital in Mekele, the capital city of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Fearing repercussions for treating rebel fighters, the surgeon asked NPR not to publish his name.
"The whole emergency (room) was flooded with war trauma patients," he recalls. "The floors were all filled up, there was no place to step."
For the past several weeks, the violence has continued at a steady pace, raising concerns that Ethiopia could again face a civil war. The Ethiopian military has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of backing Tigrayan militants, who have aligned themselves with seven rebel groups in Ethiopia with the goal of ousting Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
After drone strikes in late October killed at least 15 people, including children, the director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, posted on X that the violence in northern Ethiopia "is pushing an already fragile health system closer to collapse."
During the initial outbreak of violence in September, the surgeon in Tigray says he spent days operating on victims of gunfire, drone attacks, and mortar shells. Some were clearly civilians, but others were fighters in uniform. Complicating matters, he recalls, there was no way to know how many patients were coming because cell service and the internet were cut.
"We don't know where they're from — you just go ahead and do whatever you can, you know?" he told NPR.
There had been signs that the war between Ethiopia's federal government and rebel groups could reopen. In May, Tigrayan rebels ousted regional leaders and installed their own. In response, Ethiopia's federal government cut funds to Tigray — including to hospitals run by the regional administration. Doctors, he says, haven't been paid in months.
"It's an open wound, which was never closed, you know. Left for healing and never healed," he says. "I guess now it's infected."
For Tedros of WHO, the situation is deeply personal. He is Tigrayan and previously served as Ethiopia's minister of health. In his social media post, he wrote that hospitals are facing shortages of workers, medicine and ambulances, and that WHO and the U.N. are working to deliver medical supplies to the affected regions.
"As fighting continues, more people are likely to lose access to essential healthcare … civilians must be protected," Tedros wrote. "The most courageous choose peace."
A worldwide worry
Public health experts say targeted attacks on healthcare —– generally considered a war crime —– have become a growing concern in conflict zones around the world.
So far in 2026, attacks on health care facilities and workers in 19 countries led to more than 960 deaths, according to data collected by WHO. While the largest mass casualty event occurred in a Pakistani airstrike on a drug rehabilitation center in Afghanistan, hundreds of people have died in attacks on healthcare settings in Sudan, Lebanon, and Ukraine.
Complicating matters are funding cuts to global health initiatives, including the dismantling of USAID shortly after Donald Trump took office in 2025.
"The continual attack against healthcare is eroding the norm of healthcare being a protected part of conflict," says Lindsey Green, a researcher focused on Ethiopia for the U.S. nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights.
The Tigray war lasted two years, killing an estimated 600,000 people. The majority of Tigray's health facilities were only partially functional, as the Ethiopian government imposed an aid blockade on the region — home to more than 7 million people.
Attacks continued, despite a peace agreement
The government struck a peace agreement with Tigrayan rebels in 2022, ending most hostilities, but attacks on healthcare continued. In August of this year, Physicians for Human Rights worked with the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa to publish a report detailing these attacks.
Of more than 600 health workers surveyed across three regions of northern Ethiopia, 63% reported attacks on ambulances, some as they tried to reach injured patients, and 57% reported witnessing an armed takeover of their clinic or hospital between 2020 and 2024. One health worker in Mekele recalled Ethiopian forces occupying a hospital and placing the uniforms of Tigrayan rebels on the floor and forcing staff to step on them. "Nonsense stuff," he said.
"Armed groups were occupying facilities to take resources or to destroy resources, to destroy machines and equipment, really with the goal of making healthcare harder to access," Green says.
In the report, researchers confirmed targeted attacks on health care workers perpetrated by both rebels and government forces – often as retribution for a community's perceived alliances or against doctors who treated an enemy. But there has been no way for victims to seek justice from either party.
"It's very clear that this ongoing pattern of attacks on healthcare links back to impunity for these violations," Green says.
NPR reached out to Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry and Office of the Prime Minister, but did not receive a response.
Doctors in northern Ethiopia say the one-two punch of a war that specifically targeted healthcare, followed by foreign aid cuts, have left the region without a chance to recover.
A health worker in Tigray counted more than 100 women who died in childbirth over the past year. He attributed their deaths to the dire state of the health system. He spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity, due to fear of being targeted for speaking out.
"They died during delivery because of a lack of medicine, lack of health care providers, a lack of fuel. So the ambulances are not functional," he said.
An independent review of birth data during the Tigray war from 2020 - 2022 showed that the maternal mortality rate per 100,000 live births increased fivefold, compared to prewar data. Researchers in 2022 found that 83% of clinics and hospitals were no longer able to serve pregnant women. Additionally, systemic rape and sexual violence were regularly used as a weapon of war.
"They told us, the people should be punished, because we are supporters of the TPLF (Tigrayan rebels)," the health worker says.
Ayoda Werede, a California-based physician with the nonprofit, Health Professionals for Tigray, says that since the latest outbreak of violence, the Ethiopian military has not targeted health centers. But other unidentified groups have stolen supplies, "including medication, equipment, even mattresses off of patient's beds," Werede says. "This was just the opportunistic vacuum space that was created because of this conflict."
Her fear is that Ethiopia's healthcare system is already stretched beyond its capacity — and as the conflict reignites, injured people will have nowhere to go. The surgeon in Mekele has similar concerns. Many of Tigray's doctors, he says, have already left the country.
"We've lost our sense of being secure," he says. "It's a repeat of what's happened in the past."

It’s tempting to seek out the do-everything wireless gaming headset with noise cancellation, phenomenal sound quality, multiplatform connectivity, swappable batteries — you name it. But if you just want the basics done well, Sony’s new $99.99 PlayStation Pulse headset is worth considering. It has very good sound and just enough extras, even if you use more gadgets than just your PlayStation 5.
Sony’s latest Pulse wireless headset packs planar magnetic drivers at a good price
A comfortable, minimalist option that supports concurrent low-latency audio and Bluetooth.
Inside the Pulse’s nondescript ear cup shells are custom planar magnetic drivers, which deliver clean, detailed sound whether you’re gaming, listening to music, or both. They aren’t bass-heavy or too shrill; their default equalizer is pleasing and punchy, though you can also tweak it in the PS5’s interface, like other Pulse headsets. They’re not Sony’s first audio gaming product to feature this type of high-end driver (the first was in 2023), but they are the most affordable at $99.
The Pulse comes with either a white or black headband, with a soft-touch underside and a decent amount of give near the top of your head where it rests its weight. Thankfully, the headset is lightweight and offers size adjustments that go beyond what my large head requires for comfort. These are some of the only headphones I’ve used with ear cups that can rotate 180 degrees in either direction.
Functionally, the Pulse stands out as a semi-affordable wireless headset that can stream audio from PlayStation Link (Sony’s low-latency, lossless wireless connection) and Bluetooth simultaneously. It includes a USB-C Link dongle that lets you pair it quickly with whatever you plug it into, whether it’s a PS5, PC, or Nintendo Switch 2.
The headset’s ear cup controls include a dedicated Bluetooth button that, beyond pairing with another gadget, lets you pause or resume Bluetooth content (it can also answer or hang up calls). You can also control Bluetooth audio volume using the integrated volume rocker, but only when a device isn’t connected via PlayStation Link. In simultaneous audio mode, the rocker adjusts audio solely for the device connected via the Link dongle.
If you have Sony’s PlayStation Portal, the Pulse can connect directly to the handheld without the Link dongle, just as Sony’s Pulse Elite and Explore can. It’s so convenient, and I hope Sony pushes for more devices that integrate the Link wireless technology in the future.
The Pulse isn’t the only headset that Sony has in the works. Its Pulse Edge wireless headset doesn’t have an exact launch date or price, but the company touts that it packs in twice as many magnets in its drivers (eight versus four), active noise cancellation, and a detachable boom mic that will likely provide better-sounding voice audio than the built-in mic in the standard Pulse. It will also include game / chat audio controls, a 3.5mm jack, and a carrying case.
While the $99 Pulse is comparatively light on features, Sony’s focus on providing standout audio quality and comfort makes it worth seeking out if you have a PS5 and are on a strict budget for your next wireless headset.

The claim referred to a segment from an extended interview with El-Sayed on "60 Minutes," available to view on YouTube. In it, El-Sayed was asked about parental control over education and the interviewer cited one example being the debate over transgender kids playing sports. In response, El-Sayed made the argument that rather than try to shield kids from things they may not understand, it is a parent’s job to guide them through it. There was no mention of locker rooms or male genitalia, nor was there evidence El-Sayed ever made such a statement.
Rumors that Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed allegedly said it was OK for girls or young women to see male genitals in their locker rooms because they could see them just as easily on the internet are circulating.
People on X shared a purported clip of an interview with El-Sayed, with one person claiming, "Abdul El Sayed just embroiled himself in national scandal by saying we should let girls see men in their locker room because they can SEE IT ANYWAY on the internet."
The claim, including different versions of supposed direct quotes from El-Sayed on the matter, circulated online in anticipation of the 2026 midterm elections, in which El-Sayed opposed Republican Mike Rogers.
Can someone please check his hard drive? 😳 "Your daughters are going to see male g***tals anyway…so who cares if they see it in their locker room…" -Abdul El Sayed
— Liz Churchill (@liz_churchill10) November 2, 2026
The clip shared with the claim was authentic, but the alleged quotes on the subject attributed to El-Sayed were fabricated. We reached out to El-Sayed to ask if the alleged quotes accurately reflected his views and will update this article if we hear back.
Neither the clip itself nor the full-length version of the same interview showed El-Sayed made the statement, and there was no evidence he ever made such a statement publicly.
Rather, those sharing the claim were hyperbolizing one of El-Sayed's responses during an interview on "60 Minutes."
On Nov. 1, "60 Minutes" aired a segment about the contentious Michigan Senate race between El-Sayed and Rogers that featured interviews with both candidates. The segment is available to watch on the "60 Minutes" YouTube channel, and a transcript of the segment that aired is available to read on CBS News.
"60 Minutes" also posted extended interviews with the candidates to the show's YouTube page.
Social media users twisted El-Sayed's response to the question at the 44:30 mark of his extended interview into the version of the claim that circulated on social media.
The response came during a conversation about the protection of rights, including rights to religious and sexual preferences, that some individuals might not understand.
Interviewer Ross Douthat asked El-Sayed:
What about the rights of parents to control over their children's education? Because a lot of places where there's tension between Islam and Muslim voters and what I'm calling cultural liberalism are around issues like what is taught in school, what happens with transgender kids on sports teams, and so on, right? These are places where rights are in conflict. What do you think happens there?
El-Sayed did not immediately address the transgender kids in sports specifically. Instead, he explained a broader approach to his thinking behind the issue:
You have a phone in your pocket. You can get access to anything and everything in the whole world. All the world's information in your pocket. The notion, somehow, that you are going to prevent your child from being exposed to something that you may find disagreeable, and that that is going to be because of school, is so profoundly outdated.
Because of course, you have all the information and they have all the information. So here's the thing about it. I think it's really important for us to recognize that the free flow of information is actually a beautiful thing. It's really important. And the most important thing you can do is not try to protect a person from seeing a thing, it's about trying to make sure that as you coach your kids through the world, that you are engaging with them and saying, "Here's what I believe. Here's what you may see in the world."
You get to make your choices about who you're going to be in the world, but that's going to require us to make do with the fact that the internet is a real thing and this debate about "what's taught in a classroom," I think, has been made intro a cultural flashpoint because a lot of the folks who want to make this a topic of conversation don't want to be talking about the real issues that we face in our lives.
It was this part of his response that critics on social media latched onto, turning it from a hypothetical conversation about fundamental rights to a made-up example about male genitals in girls' locker rooms, presumably in an attempt to extend his line of reasoning to that specific scenario despite him not doing so himself.
Regarding transgender kids in sports specifically, El-Sayed said:
A lot of the culture war issues that get fought right now are about trying to distract us from the fact that we can't afford our gas, can't afford our groceries, can't see a doctor, are worried about whether or not our kids are going to have a good life. And instead, we're out here talking about who gets to play what sport. Which should be a question for the people who govern sports. I'm not running to govern sports.
My interest is in making sure people have the ability to live a good life, that they can get the healthcare that they need. That they can breathe clean air, drink clean water. That they've got good schools are well-funded in the first place.
A comprehensive search of Bing, Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo about El-Sayed saying a statement such as the one in the claim yielded no credible results.
Given the tumultuous nature of the Michigan Senate race and the national attention it drew, had El-Sayed actually said the statement or one like it, major media outlets would have reported on it.
El-Sayed won election in Michigan on Nov. 3 and said during his victory speech of his opponent, "You chose hate and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again."

On 4 November 2026, the results of the 2026 US midterm elections were announced, with the Democratic Party winning a majority in the House of Representatives & the Senate. Against this background, a video is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows US President Donald Trump destroying his office following the Republican Party’s defeat in the 2026 US midterm elections. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing US President Trump vandalizing his office after the Republican Party’s defeat in the midterm elections of 2026.
Fact: We found no credible reports confirming such an incident. This is an AI-generated video by a creator named Iman Rus. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
We found no credible reports confirming such an incident. A reverse image search using keyframes led us to the original video, which was uploaded on 4 November 2026 by the Iranian Embassy in Lebanon on X. The video clearly carries the label “AI Generated” in the upper-right corner. It also credits the creator, Iman Rus, at the end.
A keyword search based on the information gathered above led us to the same video uploaded on the YouTube channel ‘Iman Rus’ on 4 November 2026. The video title clearly identifies it as AI-generated. Additionally, YouTube’s AI disclosure in the video also confirms that the content was created using AI.
We also analysed the viral video using AI detection tools, Hive AI and SynthID, both of which indicated the video was AI-generated.
To sum up, the viral video claiming that Trump vandalised his office following the Republican Party’s defeat is AI-generated.

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
- Published
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.
Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."
After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.
But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
Huang's position vulnerable unlike other tech bosses
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.
Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.
Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.

  - Published6 hours ago
Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Conflicts abound on influential federal panel
Federal officials have granted waivers to every member of an influential, yet little-known panel that evaluates preventive medical services, allowing them to serve despite some having clear financial stakes in decisions they might make.
The waivers, signed by a top federal official and obtained by STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo, show a willingness by Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s health department to overlook financial conflicts of interest, despite the secretary frequently decrying corporate influence in health care. Read more from Chelsea on what the filings reveal.
The U.S. may lose measles elimination status this week
Today begins a four-day meeting of a committee of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional World Health Organization body that will announce whether or not the U.S. has maintained measles elimination. All signs point to no: Cases have soared in the last few years, and at least eight deaths have been reported this year. In January, then-CDC official Ralph Abraham told the late Helen Branswell that losing measles elimination status would be “the cost of doing business.” Still, we will have to wait and see how the experts rule.
If you want to review how the decision is made, the chair of the U.S. committee that analyzes the data and sends a report to the PAHO committee wrote a First Opinion essay in August about what they look for in that process.
A new tactic in the war over out-of-network bills
What do Amazon, Walmart, Eli Lilly, United Airlines, General Motors, PepsiCo, State Farm, and Toyota have in common? All of these companies are being sued by PHI Health, a national air ambulance chain, which claims the employers are responsible for bills that health insurers haven’t fully paid, or have delayed paying. And it’s not just targeting big companies — the owner of a family-run plumbing and heating company in Kentucky (above) was in disbelief when he learned he was being sued for costs related to an employee’s emergency airlift after a heart attack.
In the latest installment of his series Out of Pocket, Out of Reach, STAT’s Bob Herman explains this evolving tactic in the raging war over out-of-network bills. “It kind of undercuts the narrative that this is provider versus insurance company,” said Katie Keith, an attorney who tracks No Surprises Act lawsuits. Read more from Bob, who examined hundreds of pages of court documents to unravel this story.
The issues doctors are prioritizing post-midterms
The American Medical Association’s legislative and policy-making body met in Orlando, Fla., for its annual interim meeting earlier this week. There, voting members instituted a number of policy positions that will at least partially dictate how lobbying dollars are spent. Amanda explained one in yesterday’s newsletter, on the threat moral injury poses to doctors. Here’s a quick rundown of some of the other policies adopted:
- Artificial intelligence isn’t a doctor. One new policy argues for establishing a framework for physician oversight of artificial intelligence in medicine, including liability protections for instances where doctors choose not to use an AI tool or follow an AI recommendation. And interestingly, the policy uses the phrase “artificial intelligence” and not “augmented intelligence” as the group has previously insisted on, STAT’s Brittany Trang pointed out to me.
- Going after peptides: Under another policy, the AMA plans to urge HHS, the FDA, and other regulatory bodies to revoke any policies that ease restrictions on compounding and distributing synthetic peptides that don’t have FDA approval.
- Piggybacking off this summer’s sunscreen success: In June, the FDA approved the first new sunscreen ingredient in more than 25 years. The House of Delegates voted for the AMA to advocate for more federal reforms to the process of assessing and approving ingredients.
- Prioritizing deprescribing: The AMA offers a new definition of deprescribing as the “planned, supervised process of reducing or discontinuing medications” when use no longer provides a clinical benefit, causes harm that outweighs the benefit, or is misaligned with a patient’s goals for care. The new policy argues that it should be a routine part of patient-centered care.
The high stakes of a picky eater when money is tight
As high food costs and cuts to food assistance squeeze family budgets — just yesterday, the Trump administration proposed changes that would cut 6.3 million more families from SNAP — there are growing concerns about how low income families will get meals on the table. It’s hard no matter what, but for families with picky eaters, there’s a high-stakes calculus going on.
“For well-off parents, watching a child push away a helping of vegetables is annoying but manageable,” write two experts from the Global Food Institute at the George Washington University in a new First Opinion essay. But for parents with little money to spare, “it represents money that could have been spent on something their child would have actually eaten.” Read more about how, for some families, fruits and veggies can actually be a bad investment.

The Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that the July 2025 Upper House election was conducted in an “unconstitutional state” due to vote-value disparities of up to 3.13.
The top court’s Grand Bench, presided over by Chief Justice Yukihiko Imasaki, issued the ruling on a total of 16 lawsuits filed by two groups of lawyers seeking to invalidate the election across the country. It dismissed requests to invalidate the election.
Imasaki said that the maximum disparity in the election was at a level that raises constitutional concerns. The ruling was backed by 10 of the 15 justices, while the other five found the 2025 election to be constitutional.
This is the first time the top court has found an Upper House election with a maximum vote-value gap of less than 4.00 to be held in an unconstitutional state. The court last recognized such a state for an Upper House election in 2013, when the maximum disparity was 4.77.
The 2025 election was held under the same framework as the previous poll in 2022. However, the maximum disparity rose to 3.13 from 3.03.
Prior to the top court’s decision, high court rulings were split on the lawsuits, with 11 finding the election to be in an unconstitutional state and five finding it constitutional.

Popular weight loss drugs including Ozempic and Wegovy will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, U.S. health regulators announced Monday, November 9, 2026.
The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labelling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.
The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn't understood, the FDA said.
FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Eli Lilly's Ozempic.
An FDA analysis of more than 125 clinical trials found that the problem occurred in roughly 6 of every 100,000 patients who took a GLP-1 for at least one year. The comparable rate for people taking a placebo or other types of glucose-lowering medications was less than 4 per 100,000, the FDA said.
The agency also found reports of the problem in its electronic reporting system for drug injuries and side effects.
Symptoms of the problem include blurred vision, blind spots, distorted colors and other visual disturbances, according to the FDA. Patients experiencing such problems should contact a health care professional immediately, the agency said.

This teen boy set out to get people talking about periods. He's now a Diana honoree
Can a teenage boy change the way people think about menstruation?
At just 14, Aadvik Jain, studying in India's capital city, Delhi, set out to do exactly that. It all began when he had to watch a close friend struggle with debilitating menstrual pain that wasn't being taken seriously.
This year, he's among the 198 young people from 44 countries who were honored with the Diana Award, an international recognition for young changemakers working to improve lives in their communities. The awardees were announced on November 4 at a virtual ceremony streamed internationally.
Established in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales, the international award recognizes young people ages 16 to 25 for their social action and humanitarian efforts. This year, India accounted for nearly a quarter of the recipients, with 49 honorees.
Among them are Shiv Mandlik, who invented a bendable pole to help construction workers avoid working at dangerous heights and who developed an app to detect falls; Krish Aggarwal, who created an inexpensive filter that can be fitted onto ordinary fans to reduce indoor air pollution; and Kushal Sachdeva, who at age 11 began feeding a starving street dog. His organization, Protect Paws, has reportedly helped more than 1,500 stray dogs by arranging for medical treatment, vaccinations and reflective collars.
And then there's Jain. Now 18, he leads Team Period, an initiative he started in 2024 with three close friends. Together, they are challenging menstrual stigma through workshops, street performances, awareness campaigns and efforts to improve access to menstrual pads and products. He's also set to start studying medicine and public health at the University of Bologna in Italy in February.
NPR spoke to Jain through a video call about the experiences that inspired him, the challenge of persuading boys and men to join the conversation on periods and what he has learned about changing deeply entrenched attitudes.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
You were just 14 when you became concerned about menstrual health. What happened to make you realize that something needed to change?
It started with something that happened to a very close friend of mine in 2023, when we were in the tenth grade. We had been friends since the fifth grade. She used to call me her brother and would tie a rakhi every year [a sacred thread that girls tie around the wrist of a brother or brother-like figure, as a symbol of their bond, during the Indian festival of Raksha Bandhan].
During our midterm examinations, I noticed that she was struggling. She was in so much pain. I could not put a finger on it. What's happening? Does she have a fever? What's going on? So I checked in on her, and she said "I'm on my period, and I'm having really bad cramps." And then she just started crying. We took her to the medical room, where she was given a painkiller, and her parents were called to take her home. In India, menstruation is something that is very concealed. It's a very hush-hush topic. Not a lot of people talk about it openly in their families.
She had been experiencing severe cramps for six to eight months, and before that, her periods had been very irregular. But the next day, she was back in school, with the same pain. Her parents thought she was trying to get out of her examinations.
She is such a bright person, but for one or two weeks every month, she would become like a wilted rose. She couldn't concentrate in class or do well in her tests.
I went home and asked my mother what we could do. My mother spoke to our teacher, who contacted my friend's parents and encouraged them to take her to a doctor.
She was subsequently diagnosed with PCOS [now referred to as PMOS, or polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome], and doctors were also investigating the possibility of endometriosis. She received treatment, made changes to her lifestyle and gradually improved. She's so much better now, because of her own efforts, and because she got the help she needed at the right time.
That experience really stayed with me.
Why did her experience affect you so deeply?
I remember once breaking my little toe against the edge of my bed. My father left his office, which was two hours away, came home and took me to the emergency room. I had an X-ray, and my foot was bandaged.
I thought, what if we responded to menstrual pain with the same concern?
What if a girl could simply tell her father, "Dad, I'm having really bad cramps, and I can't go to school today," and he would say, "Okay, let me get you a heating pad"?
But because menstruation is such a hush-hush topic, especially around the men in a family, that kind of conversation often doesn't happen.
And sometimes, even the women in a family aren't able to support other women in the way they deserve.
I realized that this was something that needed attention.
How did that concern and empathy develop into Team Period?
I studied at Amity International School, and our school runs a program called Youth Power through its student newspaper, The Global Times. [the only registered school newspaper in India].
Schools form teams of four students, choose a social cause and spend several months working to create change in their communities. Then the schools compete with each other [to see who has the best ideas]. Our team consisted of me, Shivansh Arora, Aaratrika Jha Anand and Navya Manglik — so we're two boys and two girls.
Initially, Team Period began like any other school competition. We spent about six months working on the issue. But when the competition ended, I didn't want the work to end.
There is a certain feeling you get when you're talking to people, knowing that what you are saying matters, and maybe one day it could even change someone's life. But it wasn't just about that feeling. It was about the change we were creating at the grassroots level.
I have always been interested in public health, and I hope to work with an organization like the WHO or the United Nations one day. But as a 16- or 17-year-old, you can't just show up at the WHO and say you want to change things.
You have to start somewhere.
As a teenage boy, did you encounter resistance when you began talking about menstruation? Did girls ever accuse you of mansplaining?
Of course, people were surprised that a 15-year-old boy wanted to tackle menstrual shame.
But our friends were very supportive because we never approached the issue as experts. We approached it as learners. I never thought that I could explain what happens to a woman's body better than a woman herself.
At times, I was the face of the campaign. I was the spokesperson delivering speeches and talking to young women about menstruation. But it never came from a place of thinking that I knew more than they did. It came from a place of wanting to help solve a problem.
Everything we did was approached with empathy, sensitivity and respect. One girl might be completely comfortable talking about her periods in front of a classroom, while another might be deeply embarrassed.
Our goal is to end that shame, but we don't want to do it by shaming the person herself.
Were there moments when you realized that it might be harder than you thought to include boys in this conversation?
Yes. There was a workshop we organized at a school where the boys were asked to leave the room, so the girls could discuss these issues freely.
Initially, I was very upset because the whole point of our project was that boys should learn about menstruation, too.
But once the boys left, I saw girls who had been completely silent suddenly asking questions, laughing and speaking openly.
That was a learning experience for me.
Sometimes, girls need their own space to talk about these things. You can't force everyone to be comfortable immediately. We later held a separate session for the boys and eventually brought everyone together for a discussion. So at the end of the day, boys and girls were able to talk about it openly. I learned that creating an open environment is a process.
Can you describe an experience that convinced you your work was making a difference? Anything that really surprised you?
We once held an activity with middle-school students where we taught them to make simple heating pads using socks filled with lentils or chickpeas.
There was a boy, about 12 years old, who was very disruptive. He kept interrupting us and asking why he needed to learn about periods. His attitude was essentially that this had nothing to do with him. The teacher wanted to send him to another classroom, but we said no. We wanted him to stay and participate. About a year later, after I had finished school, I returned to visit my teachers and met that boy again.
He told me that his younger sister, who was barely 9 years old, had got her first period when they were alone at home. She was terrified. She had gone to the bathroom, seen the blood and started crying and screaming for help. But because of our workshop, he knew what was happening. He called his mother and asked where she kept the sanitary pads. He reassured his sister, helped her get cleaned up, made her a heating pad and even ordered chocolates for her.
By the time his mother returned, his sister was feeling much better.
He came up to me and thanked me. He said that when we first held the workshop, he couldn't understand why he needed to know any of this.
But when his sister needed help, he knew what to do. The fulfillment I felt in that moment was incomparable. To know that you've touched even one life is such a big honor.
You have used some unusual ways to get people talking about menstruation, including dance performances and flash mobs. How did those work?
We wanted to tackle menstrual shame from different directions, including through culture and performance.
One of our productions was a dance drama set during Durga Puja [a major Hindu festival honoring Goddess Durga's victory over a demon].
In the story, a young girl is performing the aarti [a Hindu ritual where a lamp is lit and prayers are offered] when her grandmother notices a menstrual stain on her clothes. The grandmother immediately excludes her from the prayers.
But Durga [the goddess] sees what has happened. She appears, comforts the girl and brings her back. I came up with the story, but the whole school helped put it together — the dance teachers, art teachers, costume designers, students and everyone involved in the production.
We performed it before an audience of more than 500 people in April 2025, and we've since performed or screened it at other events.
We also organized a flash mob at a mall and held activities at our school's winter carnival, where students, parents and grandparents participated in games about menstrual health.
One game involved picking colored chits containing questions about menstruation. People had only a short time to respond, which encouraged spontaneous answers instead of rehearsed ones. Sometimes a young boy would play, pick up a question and ask, all confused, "What is PCOS?"
We would stop the game and spend 10 minutes explaining it.
Our goal was to spark conversations.
You conducted surveys. Did this give you an insight into the way people think about menstruation?
We have been conducting surveys among students, parents and the wider community. At this point, we have collected around 4,000 responses.
One response that really struck us came from an eighth-grade girl.
She was angry that nobody cared if someone got a vegetable stain or ketchup on their clothes, but if a girl had a red menstrual stain on the back of her uniform, it became a huge issue.
Until then, our approach had been to teach boys to be sensitive — if a girl had a stain, you could quietly tell her or offer her your jacket.
But her response made us question that approach. Why should a menstrual stain be so embarrassing in the first place?
So we decided to normalize it.
We began wearing red stains on our uniforms. Some were stitched from red cloth, while others were stickers. At first, everyone laughed at us. Even the school objected because we were ruining the look of our uniforms with these big red patches.
But over the course of a week, more and more students joined in.
By the end, there was a sea of students wearing red stains. Some wore them on their backs, others on their shirts or identification cards.
When we conducted another survey months later, many students said they no longer felt that it was such a shame to spot or have a red stain.
We can't change attitudes across all of India immediately, but we were able to change something in our school.
In addition to changing attitudes and addressing stigma, what other aspects of menstrual care are you looking into?
There are several aspects to our work.
One is cultural — breaking down taboos and stigma. Another is logistical. How do you ensure that girls and women have access to menstrual products without feeling ashamed to ask for them? We installed a sanitary pad dispenser at our school.
Now we're talking to companies about how we could make dispensers available to other schools at a nominal cost. We are also exploring the possibility of developing our own design.
Disposal is another major issue. Used sanitary pads are often wrapped in newspaper and thrown into the garbage. But think about the people who sort that waste. How are they supposed to know what is inside the newspaper?
We're exploring a disposal system in which used pads can be sealed in specially designed bags, with clear warnings and illustrations in different languages. We want to think not just about the people using menstrual products but also those who handle the waste.
Your work has largely been concentrated in Delhi. Any plans to expand?
Until now, we've worked in government schools, orphanages, underserved neighborhoods and our own school in Delhi. We've also organized health camps.
But we were students, and our budgets were limited. We couldn't simply fly to Chennai or another city to replicate everything.
Now we want to decentralize Team Period and create local chapters.
Our team members are already spreading out to different cities and countries for their studies.
We'd like to bring in volunteers who speak different regional languages so that we can communicate more effectively with communities.
What does winning the Diana Award mean to you? Does it provide funding to help expand Team Period?
The Diana Award doesn't come with prize money.
But I think what it gives us is something equally valuable: recognition that our work matters.
When you're young and approaching potential sponsors or partners, people naturally have questions. They want to know whether you're legitimate and whether your work is making a difference. An international recognition like the Diana Award helps establish that credibility.
It gives us a platform to take our work to a larger audience.
For me, personally, it's deeply meaningful because we've faced moments when people questioned why boys were talking about menstruation. We've received strange looks from older people and even people of our own generation.
But this recognition tells us to keep showing up, even when things are difficult.

Europe wants to ban 'dark patterns' in apps and loot boxes for minors
Tech companies in breach could face fines up to six percent of their global revenue.
Europe just released a proposal for a new set of consumer protection rules called the Digital Fairness Act (DFA), the EU Commission wrote in a news release. The bloc is targeting practices that harm children and push people into spending more, including things like unclear pricing, addictive design features, ads aimed at minors and "dark patterns" like hard-to-cancel subscriptions. The penalty for non-compliance could be up to six percent of a company's annual revenue, according to the draft copy.
"Our consumer protection rules will help ensure that businesses compete on the merits of their products and services, not on their ability to exploit consumers or their ability to evade the rules," said EU justice chief Michael McGrath in a statement. "We are not making it harder to do business, we are making it harder to do business unfairly."
The act seeks to protect consumers in a number of ways, like banning dark patterns, forcing clear and transparent online pricing for cultural and sports events and allowing consumers to turn off "addictive design features that encourage excessive or compulsive spending. It would also restrict unfair practices that encourage overspending by minors, like pay-to-win in games (loot boxes) and persistent prompts.
The DFA also addresses influencer marketing, requiring transparency from content creators about commercial content. It would also take on unfair personalized ads and prices that target minors, while putting an end to "subscription traps" that are difficult to cancel.
The EC also proposed to shift enforcement power from member states to a more centralized system. It would give the Commission direct powers to investigate large-scale cases with a major impact on consumers, speed up and improve coordination with member states and strengthen enforcement against non-EU companies.
This could be seen as an attempt to remove the patchwork of enforcement that currently happens around Europe in countries like France. It could also be an attempt to tilt regulatory power away from Ireland, a nation that hosts major tech giants including Apple, Google, Meta and Microsoft. A recent report from UN experts raised concerns about the independence of Ireland's privacy regulator, citing the risk of "undue influence" from tech firms hosted there.

Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called “big math” is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means, and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World, by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend.
Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London’s Millennium Bridge.
An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019).
This time around, Strogatz has found a well-matched co-author in Townsend, a younger colleague recently hired at Cornell who studies numerical analysis and deep learning. As senior faculty, Strogatz was assigned to mentor Townsend, and the two men began regularly lunching together in Risley Hall. Strogatz was intrigued by the popular book potential of Townsend’s course on the top 20 algorithms of the 20th century and suggested co-authorship. That concept slowly morphed into a book about big matrix calculations, and then into what became Big Math.
“There are so many books about pure math, as if computers didn’t exist,” Strogatz told Ars. “Alex and I are both very applied mathematicians. We thought there should be a book on computers and math, especially the class of really big problems with billions of variables or parameters that you just can’t approach in your head. A lot of the math we’ve had for centuries perfectly scales up to this computer moment. What the abacus did for arithmetic, the fangcheng (“rectangular array”) board did for systems of linear equations. It was a matrix you could manipulate with your hand and bamboo sticks. So this externalizing of math outside of our heads into our tools is a 2,000-year-old idea.”
“The mathematician in each of us will always want to know more,” Strogatz and Townsend wrote. “The human being must insist that knowledge serves something larger than itself. That might be the work of our century: letting our power grow without losing our soul. Big Math keeps getting bigger. So must we.”
Ars caught up with Strogatz to learn more.
Ars Technica: Let’s start by defining “big math,” because it’s such a broad umbrella term.
Steven Strogatz: Operationally, big math is “big” relative to human cognitive capacity. So it can be surprisingly small and yet big. We also wanted to expand it to things that people would think of as computational engineering—in the building of the Burj Khalifa, that’d be civil engineering or design architecture. It’s there in medical imaging. It’s in getting us to the Moon. The lunar module was controlled by a tiny computer that only had to think about 20 or 30 variables at a time to steer the LEM down to the Moon’s surface. But it’s not something a person could do in their head.
Big Math is not simply big in the ordinary sense of big numbers. There’s an undercurrent in the book about the importance of linearity and sparsity. When problems are linear, they can be scaled up to immense size, and they stay tractable. If they’re non-linear, you don’t have any hope of dealing with them with pure math. You can do them with computers. But for the people who want rigorous theorems, we’re in terra incognita when we deal with anything that’s non-linear and big.
Small math can be very hard. Historically, we had small math problems with one or two variables, arithmetic, algebra that you learn in high school. Even to this day, a lot of pure math is relatively small. It doesn’t concern itself with enormous numbers of variables simultaneously because it’s totally intractable. Cryptography can be small, but it’s so complicated with its non-linearities and other algebraic difficulties. So big is one way to be difficult, but there are a lot of other ways.
Nowadays, trillions of parameters are typical in the biggest of the large language models. But infinity is not big from this point. Infinity, which you would think of would be the biggest of big math, is not because calculus fits perfectly nicely in a human head. Infinity turns out to be very tractable in a way that a billion is not.
