The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
- Published
As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.
This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.
Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.
Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes.
"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.
The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara.
But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers.
Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea.
Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity.
"Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says.
At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species.
Guiding tours runs in Sucdi's family. Her father worked in the profession for over three decades, taking journalists, photographers and visitors from different countries around Somalia.
He introduced her to the business nearly three years ago.
"I started this job as a hobby, but it has become something that I like and am passionate about," she says.
She now works alongside her father and a team of guides, building on his experience while using social media to reach a wider audience.
She shares videos of her tours on TikTok, offering people outside Somalia a glimpse of places they may never have imagined visiting.
She is also considering producing content in English to reach audiences who do not speak Somali.
Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu.
The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow.
However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security.
Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down.
But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation.
Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital.
Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life.
About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department.
Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city.
But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive.
"What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says.
Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue.
She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen.
"I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says.
Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.
Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade.
For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking.
American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice.
His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media.
"I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says.
What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere.
"It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says.
During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes.
"The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says.
Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage.
"If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines."
But visiting the country challenged those perceptions.
"Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says.
Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia's natural beauty.
Although she has spent only a few hours in Mogadishu, she has already visited the sand dunes and taken in the Indian Ocean coastline.
"The desert was so beautiful to see. I have also enjoyed the beach, and the ocean. It is inspiring," she says.
Having travelled to Somalia from neighbouring Ethiopia, she says she has been struck by the people's friendliness.
"I don't see anything dangerous. I feel safe and the people are warm," she says.
An experienced traveller, Mihaela says she prefers to visit new countries without having preconceived ideas.
"I travel the world to see new places, to see countries, to see the differences. I don't take a picture in my mind to compare the reality with. I'm just expecting the new to come to me," she says.
She hopes to share her experience and encourage others to visit Somalia.
"I'm going to post my pictures and say good things about what I'm experiencing. I'm going to promote it," she says.
For Sucdi, that potential is personal.
She is continuing a family profession while building a business in an industry with few women and using digital platforms to reach audiences far beyond Mogadishu.
"Somalia still has a long way to go before tourism becomes a major industry," she says.
"Through my tours, I am giving visitors an opportunity to experience its landscapes, our culture and people beyond the familiar negative headlines."
For her, every visitor is another opportunity to tell a fuller story of Mogadishu.

Amazon is betting that many Ring customers will also want an AI-powered security drone and robot patrolling their homes or offices. But the company’s upcoming Ring Robotic products are also certain to intensify privacy concerns previously raised around a prior Amazon attempt to popularize a flying security camera.
The Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10. Amazon describes the devices as relying on an AI Pilot system that uses each device’s cameras along with “specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing” to plan patrol routes while autonomously navigating around obstacles such as furniture.
Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor plan of the customer’s home or business. This setup process occurs after the customer carries the Ring drone through their indoor spaces or allows the Ring Rover to do some autonomous exploration.
The AI Pilot can supposedly use that guided- or self-tour information to identify specific rooms and suggest patrol points near side doors, windows, or even sensitive locations such as a cash register in the case of a business.
However, flying and roving cameras with AI-enabled features could introduce new privacy risks for homes and businesses, on top of existing concerns involving fixed Ring cameras installed in room corners or as doorbell cameras.
Return of the Ring drone
Amazon’s Ring Drone appears to be a direct successor to the company’s Ring Always Home Cam that was only temporarily available for purchase by invitation as a “Day 1 Edition” product in September 2021—even having the same starting price of $250.
But the Ring Drone still requires authorization from the Federal Communications Commission before going on sale. Assuming that comes through, Amazon aims to make the drone available on January 27, 2027, with customers able to register for email updates through the product page.
The drone can supposedly follow a set route and schedule for customers who subscribe to the Amazon Ring Protect plan. It can automatically fly along those set routes when responding to a notification from a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm.

Street boxing matches gain popularity in Bogota
Santiago Abril has been organizing pop-up boxing matches in parks around Bogota, Colombia, without official permits
BOGOTA, Colombia -- In a park on the outskirts of Colombia’s capital, Santiago Abril set up a mat made with interlocking rubber panels and assembled an octagonal structure resembling a mixed martial arts cage.
The portable ring, made of rubber and plastic, serves as the stage for the improvised boxing matches that Abril has organized for months at parks in Bogota, mostly without official permits.
Dozens of young men and women gather on weekends for Abril’s pop-up fights, where strangers face off without the lengthy preparations required for regular boxing matches. Some want to test their boxing skills. Others are looking for a new thrill.
Women pay around $5 to compete, while men pay $15. Organizers provide boxing gloves but no headgear. Cash prizes of around $100 are given to those who can win two or three fights in a row in hastily organized tournaments.
For Ingrid Prieto, a 29-year-old who recently participated in a fight, boxing is a form of therapy.
“When I was young, I used to get in a lot of fights, so I began to practice taekwondo,” she said, adding that contact sports have helped her to channel her emotions.
Eliber Parra García, 27, repairs mobile phones for a living. He said he joined the pop-up fights to experience what it feels like to be a professional boxer, and also for the adrenaline that comes with fighting and the chance to make some money. “I have an orange belt in judo,” Parra García said. “But I know very little about boxing.”
Bogota’s municipal government told the Associated Press that the fights require permits and a plan for dealing with emergencies that must be submitted to authorities.
Police have asked Abril to dismantle his octagon in several parks around the city, after failing to present a permit.
Abril said participants are asked to sign a consent form stating they are in good health before fighting. He also said obtaining a permit to organize boxing matches is difficult because the sport is “monopolized” by promoters.
Abril’s fights are limited to two rounds lasting 90 seconds each. Participants are sorted into weight categories and given gloves that are heavier than those used by professionals.
“The gloves are so heavy that the boxers get tired faster, and that means they will not throw such hard punches,” said Abril, who has a degree in physical education. He said that sometimes there are bloody noses or burst lips in his fights, but that “no one has had their cheekbones broken.”
Despite the lack of permits, and being chased from parks by police, Abril says interest in his street fights is growing. He promotes them on social media under the nickname King Abril and runs a YouTube account with 131,000 subscribers.
“We started doing this on streets, on the pavement,” Abril said. “Now we have a cage, gloves and a mat.”

AR Rahman's Gurugram concert postponed over ‘unforeseen circumstances’, rescheduled for next year
The concert was originally scheduled for next week on November 21, and was to take place at 7 pm at Backyard Sports Club in Gurugram.
Two-time Oscar-winning composer AR Rahman’s concert in Gurugram on November 21, which was part of his ongoing Wonderment Tour, has been postponed and rescheduled to next year.
The concert was originally scheduled for next week on November 21, and was to take place at 7 pm at Backyard Sports Club in Gurugram. The event has now been postponed over “unforeseen circumstances.”
Speaking exclusively to HT, Eva Live, the primary national producer for the concert, said, “Due to unforeseen circumstances and last minute critical developments that cannot be avoided, AR Rahman will be postponing the date of Delhi concert to next year.”
No official announcement regarding the revised date of the concert has been made so far.
Refund process initiated
Ticket-booking platforms have also begun notifying customers about the cancellation, with refund processes initiated and emails being sent to those who had booked tickets.
The ticket prices for the concert ranged from ₹2,499 for general standing access to ₹1.5 lakh for premium VIP decks.
The postponement has left fans disappointed, especially those who had been looking forward to witnessing the musical maestro perform live in the city. Nidhi Sharma, a resident of Gurugram who had purchased premium tickets for the concert, expressed disappointment over the postponement.
“We were really looking forward to this concert and had bought expensive tickets because we wanted to experience his music live. One of my friends was even travelling from Lucknow to attend the show. However, we received an email informing us about the postponement, along with the refund details. This was completely unexpected, and we are really disappointed,” she said.

Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak
BUNIA, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease.
According to the latest health ministry data, 11,042 people have been infected with the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387 — nearly half of those infected in what has been Congo's deadliest outbreak.
The outbreak was declared in mid-May, and since then, Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to several factors, including armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.
The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces.
The resurgence of violence in the two major hotspots in Ituri and North Kivu provinces has sparked worry among health authorities who are calling for a halt to the fighting to allow health workers unhindered access to the sick.
Health facilities and medical professionals have also been targeted by many in communities skeptical of the virus, and there have been several attacks on health workers.
Experts have called for more efforts to slow and contain the disease in Congo, while it has spread to multiple African countries including Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.
Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared, compared with the West Africa outbreak.

Update | November 11, 17:18 IST Months after Inc42 exclusively reported on Greenjoules’s fundraise, the cleantech startup announced the closure of its Series B round at ₹150 Cr ($16 Mn). The round was co-led by Amazon’s Smbhav Venture Fund and Climate Pledge Fund, with participation from Rainmatter and Singularity’s Strategic Autonomy Fund. The startup said that the fresh funds will support its new plant at Pune’s Khed City with the capacity to produce 2 Lakh litres of biocrude a day from agricultural waste. The facility will be developed in phases from 2027, which is expected to be the largest of its kind in India. Additionally, Greenjoules also secured a ₹100 Cr debt from Technology Development Board (TDB), under the Government of India’s Department of Science and Technology. “Greenjoules was built without a map; every step forward meant first inventing the path. We took two things that looked irreconcilable — low-energy-density agricultural waste and specification-grade fuel — and spent more than six years proving they were one and the same. With the concept proven and partners such as TDB and our Series B investors behind us, we are ready to make a deep impact on the global energy market, and to carry that pioneering spirit into sustainable aviation fuel,green hydrogen and sustainable materials.” said Shweta Viraraghavan, cofounder and chief technology officer, Greenjoules. Original | August 21, 18:58 IST Pune-based green energy startup Greenjoules has raised about ₹62 Cr ($6.5 Mn) in what appears to be an ongoing Series B funding round. While Amazon’s investment arm, Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings, is leading the funding round, Singularity AMC’s Singularity Strategic Autonomy Fund also participated in the round. As per MCA filings accessed by Inc42, the startup’s board allotted 40,338 Series B1 compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) at ₹11,155.5 apiece for ₹45 Cr to Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC. Separately, it also allotted 15,238 Series B1 CCPS to a sum of about ₹17 Cr to Singularity Strategic Autonomy Fund. Greenjoules declined to comment on Inc42’s queries regarding the total size of the round. Founded in 2018 by S Viraraghavan, V Radhika, VS Shridhar and R Sethunath, Greenjoules converts farm residues into renewable fuels that can be used in existing diesel engines and industrial equipment, effectively substituting crude oil with agricultural waste. The startup is developing green fuels that can cater to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), green hydrogen and biomethane areas. Prior to the ongoing round, the climatetech startup raised $4.5 Mn in a combination of equity and debt from Blue Ashva Capital in 2021, to set up commercial scale waste to energy plants and invest into new R&D initiatives. The investor interest in the eight-year old startup aligns with India’s broader push to scale renewable fuel sources in a bid to attain the country’s net zero goals. India aims to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by the year 2070. Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced this target during the COP26 climate summit in Glasgow, backed by a climate plan known as the "Panchamrita". The country's long-term low-carbon development strategy rests on seven key transitions to low-carbon development pathways. These include low-carbon development of electricity systems, enhancing forest and vegetation cover consistent with socioeconomic, development of CO2 removal and related engineering solutions, among others. Amid this push, India’s cleantech market is projected to become a $152.5 Bn market by 2030, creating a suitable market opportunity for new and emerging players as well as more established industrial players to leverage the opportunity.

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

Scientists have long known how to make cells younger—at least in the sense that adult cells can be converted into pluripotent stem cells very similar to those found in embryos. While this capability has been foundational for biological research, these methods aren’t viable for anti-aging technologies, for a few reasons.
“You don't want to have a pluripotent cell in your body, because it can become all types of cells,” says Oliver Brüstle, a professor who studies stem cells at Germany’s Bonn University.
Additionally, the few key genes involved in the stem cell conversion process can drive the formation of cancer if left active. That’s why Brüstle and his team have looked for other ways of de-aging cells without going through a pluripotent state. In their recent study published in Aging Cell, the researchers started with blood cells from people of various ages, including an infant and a 101-year-old donor.
They guided these cells into a younger state but not all the way toward becoming embryonic-like stem cells. And as this transformation progressed, the chemical signals in the DNA that help estimate a cell’s age also changed. In less than two months of reprogramming, one biomarker in particular was set back as far as 60 years.
Aging continued to reverse even when the scientists drastically reduced the cells’ ability to multiply. Therefore, the apparent rejuvenation can’t be explained solely by the fact that the cells were dividing and producing new cells over and over again. However, the mechanism that did erase these signs of aging is still unclear.
“The hope is that you actually can do this systemically in the entire animal,” Brüstle says. “But if you think about applying it in a patient, then you want to be sure this is not a lab experiment, so it's about finding the mechanism.”
The researchers also shifted the blood cells specifically into a kind of cell that produces neurons. One caveat is that blood cells and neurons age on different timelines, so the extent of the reversal could be exaggerated by the use of a different measuring stick. The authors acknowledge this limitation in their paper, though this discrepancy couldn’t account for all the age-associated biomarkers that reversed course.
Blood cells getting brainy also would not be a desirable result if you gave a patient a de-aging drug, but it would be useful for other regenerative medicine purposes. However, what Brüstle sees as one of the most exciting outcomes of the study is the information gleaned about the process of de-aging.
Usually, making stem cells is quick. That’s useful for many experiments, but it doesn’t give researchers the chance to study cells as they shed the markers of age. In this recent study, since the scientists were able to slowly turn back the cells’ biological clocks, they could track each step of de-aging. “Now we can actually try to dissect the process much more easily than having an instantaneous event,” Brüstle says.
Scientists began converting adult cells back into stem cells two decades ago, but we’ve known very little about how the subsequent de-aging occurs. This means when clinical researchers test potential medical interventions for age-related conditions, they haven’t always had a reliable measure to compare against.
“Now we have a model” Brüstle says. “You can work along this, and now you can probe a zillion things. What impacts the process? This will lead you to the mechanisms. That’s our hope.”

As Delhiites burst firecrackers well past the 10 p.m. deadline set by the Supreme Court for Deepavali night, air pollution shot up to over 50 times World Health Organisation (WHO) limits in parts of the city, official data showed.
The level of PM2.5 (a major pollutant) in Akshardham was 760.99 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) data. This is about 50.73 times the WHO permissible limit of 15 micrograms per cubic meter for a 24-hour period.
Deepavali 2026: All you need to know about Supreme Court-permitted time slots, green crackers and other directives
PM2.5 (Particulate Matter 2.5) are fine inhalable particles, which can get into lungs and bloodstream and lead to a range of respiratory and other diseases.
The level of PM2.5 in Anand Vihar was 767 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per DPCC data — This is about 51.13 times the WHO permissible limit.
The level of PM2.5 in Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium was 702 micrograms per cubic meter, as per DPCC data, which is about 46.8 times the WHO permissible limit.
The overall air quality of Delhi continued to be in the “very poor” category while many parts of the city continued to reel under “severe” air quality.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

Actor Sidharth Malhotra has revealed that he was once set to collaborate with filmmaker Aditya Dhar on a project backed by Dharma Productions. The actor shared the information during his recent appearance on Koffee With Karan, where host Karan Johar brought up the long-discussed collaboration while asking him about directors he would like to work with.
Koffee With Karan 9: Sidharth Malhotra was to headline an Aditya Dhar film at Dharma Productions – Karan Johar makes SURPRISING revelation!
During the conversation, Johar named several filmmakers, including Aditya Dhar, Mohit Suri, Sandeep Reddy Vanga and Sanjay Leela Bhansali, and asked Malhotra, “Aditya Dhar, Mohit Suri, Sandeep Reddy Vanga, Sanjay Leela Bhansali, the directors of the moment. Is there anyone you're willing to do anything to work with?” Responding to the question, Malhotra said, “Oh wow, I think all of them are extremely exciting. Maybe Aditya, because I've interacted with him in the past.”
Johar then brought up their earlier association, reminding the actor of a project that had been planned several years ago. “You were meant to do a film many moons ago.” To which Sidharth replied, “Yes, in Dharma itself.”
The brief exchange brought attention to a collaboration that never materialised. The project was reportedly in development during Aditya Dhar’s early years in the industry, before he made his directorial debut with Uri: The Surgical Strike in 2019. Although the film with Malhotra was to be backed by Dharma Productions, it did not progress to the shooting stage. Neither the actor, nor the filmmaker shared further details about the proposed project during the conversation.
Interestingly, both Malhotra and Dhar have since explored stories rooted in action, military operations and national security, albeit through different projects. Malhotra has essayed defence personnel and characters associated with national security in films such as Aiyaary (2018), Mission Majnu (2023) and Yodha (2024). His performance as Captain Vikram Batra in the 2021 biographical war drama Shershaah earned him considerable appreciation and remains a notable film in his career.
Dhar, meanwhile, established himself as a filmmaker with Uri: The Surgical Strike, which went on to become a significant milestone in his career. His subsequent work in Dhurandhar and Dhurandhar The Revenge has further strengthened his association with large-scale action narratives and technically ambitious storytelling.
While the Koffee With Karan conversation did not indicate whether the two are considering working together in the future, Malhotra’s revelation offers a glimpse into a collaboration that was planned long before either had established their current standing in the industry.

The Enforcement Directorate (ED), Chennai, has provisionally attached movable and immovable assets worth approximately ₹14.2 Cr in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment fraud operated by Pan India Cryptocurrency, HashPe. The attachment was made on October 30, 2026, under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002. The ED has also filed a prosecution complaint before the Special Court (PMLA), Puducherry. According to the ED, Hashpay allegedly operated a fraudulent cryptocurrency-based ponzi investment scheme that lured investors with promises of daily returns of 1%, returns of up to 3X the invested amount, referral commissions and rewards such as luxury cars and foreign trips. The agency said the attached assets include immovable properties in Tamil Nadu, Haryana and New Delhi, a BMW car and funds deposited in bank accounts. The investigation was initiated based on an FIR registered by the Cyber Crime Police Station, Puducherry, under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, and the Information Technology Act, 2000. How The Ponzi Scheme Worked ED's investigation found that HashPe operated through a website, hashpe.io, and a multi-level marketing network. Its promoters allegedly used cash payments, bank transfers and cryptocurrency transactions to mobilise investments from the public. The scheme reportedly used USDT (Tether), a stablecoin, and Bitcoin to facilitate transactions. However, the agency found that the purported trading activities were not backed by actual cryptocurrency trading. Instead, money collected from new investors was allegedly used to repay earlier investors and pay commissions to agents. Withdrawals were eventually stopped and the platform was frozen, leaving investors with financial losses. The ED further found that the promoters allegedly created fictitious cryptocurrency tokens, including TCX and HashPe, at an almost zero acquisition cost and assigned artificial values to them. The platform displayed profits to investors despite the absence of genuine cryptocurrency trading activity to generate the promised returns. To attract investors, the promoters used celebrity endorsements, promotional events featuring luxury cars and gold, and foreign cruises to build credibility. They also established a multi-level marketing network, with agents designated as 'Leaders' receiving commissions for bringing in new investors. The ED said approximately ₹112.91 Cr was collected through the scheme, a portion of which was returned to investors. The remaining funds were transferred to bank accounts of ‘HIFY Circle’ and other related entities before being converted into cryptocurrency. The proceeds were allegedly diverted towards personal expenses, loan repayments, hefty commissions and promotional activities, among other purposes. The agency has identified approximately ₹49.54 Cr as proceeds of crime in the case. The development comes after the ED conducted search operations at premises linked to HashPe, its promoters and associates on September 1. Following the searches, four individuals namely Imran Basha, Hitesh Kumar, Syed Usman alias Babu, and Dharmendra were arrested under Section 19 of the PMLA, 2002. All four accused are currently in judicial custody while the investigation is ongoing. The investigation revealed that Usman handled large cash investments and operated the HIFY Circle bank account, while Dhamodharan managed HashPe's software, database and cryptocurrency operations, including its wallet functions. Heightened Crypto Crackdowns Branches of ED across the country have stepped up the heat on suspected illegal cryptocurrency activities in recent months. On November 7, the ED in Bengaluru conducted searches at premises linked to crypto exchanges CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India (DEI) over alleged unauthorised cross-border transactions involving crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks. It had earlier conducted similar searches on October 29 at premises links to crypto platforms Mudrex and Saber.money, as well as decentralised finance (DeFi) protocol Instadapp and its associated platform Fluid, over alleged unauthorised cross-border fund transfers worth more than ₹4,940 Cr. Prior to this in June this year, the ED had also searched six premises linked to five platforms, namely Transak, Carret, Xpat, Onramp.money and Onmeta, over alleged unauthorised cross-border crypto transfers.

WASHINGTON — Federal officials have granted blanket waivers to every member of an influential, yet little-known federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services, allowing them to serve despite some having clear financial stakes in decisions they might make.
The waivers, signed by a top federal official and obtained by STAT, show a willingness by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s department to overlook financial conflicts of interests, though Kennedy frequently decries corporate influence in health care. In the case of two members, the documents show that they own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care.
Other conflicts being waived include stock holdings in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and employment at public research universities that provide medical care. Some members of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, especially the newer ones, have more extensive conflicts than others.

How SCSKiller is trying to fix shader stuttering in PC games
It's difficult to state just how much I hate shader stutter, even in the best PC games. I'm probably the world's biggest arachnophobe and absolutely loathe mushrooms, yet I'd rather have a trained tarantula serve me deep-fried shiitake than endure the infamously stutter-heavy Star Wars Jedi: Survivor. At least, that was until I downloaded Shader Compilation Stutter Killer (SCSKiller).
This free app promises to heavily reduce or even completely get rid of shader compilation in modern PC titles. But can this open-source software actually deliver? I've tested it out with a handful of games that are notorious for stuttering, and when it's working at its best, SCSKiller is ingenious. Are you a frame-obsessed PC gamer? You need to download this app ASAP, and here's why.
Why does shader stutter happen in PC games?
Before explaining why SCSKiller is great, let's address what shader stutter actually is. In short, it's a brief visual hiccup that looks like a frame rate drop to the untrained eye. Why is this a PC-specific issue and not a console one? Because PC development isn't based on fixed hardware, whereas studios can pre-compile shaders focused on exact PS5 or Xbox Series X specs pre-release.
While frame dips and shader stutters can occur at the same time (here's how to improve FPS for better gaming), they're actually separate issues. Frame drops normally happen because of hardware-related bottlenecks; where either the GPU or CPU can't render certain visual elements or physics tasks quickly enough.
Shader stuttering is different. These little programs tell your GPU how to draw various in-game effects, like shadows, reflections or lighting. In many modern PC titles — especially Unreal 5 Engine games — shader stuttering occurs because the rendering pipeline is having to produce effects in real-time. As the next frame waits for the shader to compile, a brief frame spike may easily occur. Once you're aware of them, in-game stutters can be so distracting that they ruin immersion.
Common variety stutters can sometimes be largely overcome if you own a VRR display. Variable Refresh Rate screens (like NVIDIA G-Sync and AMD FreeSync models) dynamically match the refresh rate of your panel to the number of frames your GPU is currently drawing, substantially smoothing out visual performance. VRR displays can also help fix screen tearing in PC and console games.
CPU-based compilation stutters can't be fixed by screen or GPU tech. In these cases, stuttering can last for a couple of seconds, dropping in-game action to 0 fps, thus completely breaking gameplay. This happens because your PC is seeing a particular effect for the very first time. That's why compilation stutter is at its worst when initially entering new areas.
Does SCSKiller fix shader stutter?
SCSKiller can vastly reduce stutter in the PC games I've tested it with, but it can't fix all stuttering. Instead, this app has been designed specifically to target and eliminate shader compilation stutter. In that regard, it's hugely successful.
I picked out a few games on my rig that are infamous for compilation stutter. In all but one instance, SCSKiller slayed this horrible PC defect. Once you install it, the tool automatically reads your game libraries, instantly flagging the titles that can benefit most under a "Recommended to compile" list.
By pre-compiling shaders into my graphics card's driver cache before I launched each title, I found compilation stutter was more or less eradicated in Silent Hill f, Silent Hill Townfall, Elden Ring and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered. Before I discovered SSCKiller, I found both Townfall and Wild Hunt to be unplayable due to shader comp stutter. For context, I'm super sensitive to frame spikes. After I let this app pre-compile the shaders for both, the ruinous hitches I experienced before disappeared. SSCKiller is a complete game-changer in the titles I've just mentioned.
My results from Silent Hill f have proven equally impressive. Before I pre-compiled the Japanese spookster's shaders, SSCKiller's advanced stats informed me my previous 10-minute session had been blighted with precisely 25 compilation stutters (highest being 246 ms), 67 shader hitches, with a 1 percent low of just 3 fps. After using the app, comp stuttering went down to zero, with my G-Sync monitor making any smaller hitches incredibly difficult to spot. As I said, total game-changer.
The pros and cons of using SCSKiller
The pros are abundant and obvious; the cons relatively few. SSCKiller is free, intuitive to use, boasts handy before and after compilation stats, and that instant library-reading feature I mentioned means you don't have to go about digging for specific game inventories. When SSCKiller's mojo is cooking, it comprehensively fixes this loathsome defect.
The app is refreshingly upfront about its current limitations. As I type this, most of the games I have installed on my custom-built rig show as unsupported via the in-software filter. There's a handy "Why?" button that explains this limitation. At time of writing, a lot of titles throw up a "Not supported yet" error, explaining "shaders are compressed or packed: needs an engine reader".
Thankfully, you can get around this fairly easily via the built-in recorder feature. Simply click the "Record while I play" slider located in the bottom right corner of the app after you select a game and SCSKiller can analyze the rendering pipeline and pre-configure shaders after 10 minutes or so of gameplay. Be warned though: Using the app can trigger bans when playing games with anti-cheat software, so make sure you set Elden Ring to launch offline when using this tool.
Pre-compilation cycles can take a while, too. Though most of the games I configured only took a few minutes to process, even my mighty AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D needed 17 minutes to compile Hogwarts Legacy's 291,688 shaders.
On that note, SSCKiller can't fix Hogwarts. Even on my NVIDIA RTX 5090 rig, Portkey Games wizarding open-world has always been a horribly optimized port. It threw up six major compilation hitches during a 10-minute run despite the app's best efforts. For games blighted with traversal stutter and CPU spikes (like Hogwarts and 2023's Dead Space remake), unless you use a VRR display, stuttering will remain visible. For a gratis piece of software though, SSCKiller does one heck of a job at smoothing out compilation stutter.

Quick commerce has tilted the balance for India's beauty and personal care (BPC) brands. So much so, that some brands are now entirely reliant on quick commerce for growth and reevaluating how much they should invest in horizontal marketplaces. At roughly $1 Bn in annualised gross merchandise value (GMV), sales of beauty products on quick commerce is growing by about 90% a year, according to Redseer. Separately, Elara Securities estimates the channel will grow to 25-30% of online BPC sales by FY30. Karan Taurani, executive vice president at Elara Capital, says that BPC as a category was a natural progression for quick commerce platforms after they had figured out the grocery supply chain. "Beauty has got a very premium gross margin, and higher EBITDA margin as compared to other categories.That is why quick commerce is also getting on this aggressively,” Taurani said. But while the balance is shifting, the contest between quick commerce and ecommerce marketplaces is far from settled. Marketplaces are still the biggest destinations for shoppers to compare, read reviews and discover new products, especially those with a premium price tag. But the likes of Nykaa, Myntra, Amazon and Flipkart are having to play the game started by Blinkit, Instamart and Zepto to catch up. For D2C brands, this is the time to recalibrate and optimise for both channels. From sizing their SKUs and dividing their marketing budgets to rethinking how shoppers find them, the brands Inc42 spoke to, are adapting to what they call a "tectonic shift" in consumer behaviour. And it all started after the sales on quick commerce channels zoomed over the last couple of years. How Brands Are Recalibrating It’s not that long ago that marketplaces ruled the market. "A year ago, they (quick commerce as a channel) didn't even exist for us. So it's growing very fast. Our largest channel used to be marketplaces, but that’s not the number one any more," skincare brand Asaya cofounder and CEO Neeraj Biyani. Others are reporting a similar boost from quick commerce as consumers splurged during the festive season. At haircare brand Moxie Beauty, whose annualised revenue had crossed ₹100 Cr last December, quick commerce is now the largest channel accounting for more than 30% of sales, cofounder Nikita Khanna told us. Renee Cosmetics, which reported ₹440 Cr in FY26 revenue, has seen quick commerce's share of sales grow from about 3% to over 13% in two years. Typsy Beauty, which raised ₹20 Cr in August to double down on quick commerce and offline retail, is also keeping up with the fast paced trend. "The biggest change has been quick commerce. A year ago it was a single-digit share of our revenue. Today, it has grown about 5x in absolute terms, faster than any other channel," Typsy cofounder and CEO Kairavi Bharat Ram said. That growth has pushed brands to rethink how much they spend on marketplaces vs quick commerce, when it comes to ads as well as in product development. Quick Commerce Gets The Ad Money As sales on quick commerce rose, brands have followed up by allocating more budget for visibility. The likes of Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart have reimagined placement of ads in a bid to grow their average order value and this means brands have more real estate to get that all-important click. "We are spending more on quick commerce since we are selling more on quick commerce. It's not that we spend more on ads and therefore that channel grows, it's that people are choosing to buy there. And so then you want to be easily found on the platform where they're going to be buying their hair care," added Moxie Beauty’s Khanna. Social media spending is still the largest part of ad spends, but At Typsy Beauty founder Bharat Ram believes the share going to quick commerce ads has risen through the year, following the shift in sales. The data also points to a change in how shoppers search. Volumes for 10 generic makeup keywords rose 236% on Blinkit between Q1 2025 and Q2 2026 and fell 76% on Amazon, though Amazon's volume still appears larger, according to a report by 1DigitalStack (1DS), which was accessed by Inc42. Quick commerce has not suddenly eliminated marketplace or social media ad costs, but it is becoming a dedicated channel by itself. Awareness is still built elsewhere. "Most new customers still find us on Instagram, through creator content and reels far more than polished brand ads. A lot of that discovery then converts somewhere else: someone sees a creator video and later searches for us on Nykaa, Blinkit or our website," says Bharat Ram. Brands Rethink Pricing, Packaging The second biggest learning for brands is to customise SKUs and pricing to suit the replenishment cycles and consumption patterns on quick commerce, which typically involves faster stockouts. These are somewhat interlinked because repricing is often forced by SKU resizing. "We realised that the typical consumer habit on quick commerce apps was not to buy full packs. Our product was usually a last minute purchase. Hence, we had curated special packs for Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart. And that really hit the spot,” Renee Cosmetics cofounder Ashutosh Valani said. Brands are also curating a combo of small and full size packs depending on the demand from each one of the quick commerce platforms even as some BPC startups say that it is too early a stage to go full throttle on producing small size SKUs across all quick commerce channels. "Eventually if you find something that works for you, you will continue to purchase that and you will want your regular size. So it's a very healthy mix,” according to Moxie Beauty’s cofounder. Founders like Asaya’s Biyani or Bharat Ram of Typsy Beauty warn that the biggest risk for a beauty brand on quick commerce is stockouts. A few days where the product is out of stock from key dark stores costs more than the lost sales. It hurts rank, visibility and results in poor return on advertising. "Replenishment cycles have gone from monthly to weekly and we had to move from warehouse-level planning to much more frequent, city and SKU-level planning for quick commerce. This requires tighter forecasting around platform sale events,” the Typsy founder said, indicating that brands have had to make changes in their own supply chain operations to meet the rush. Pricing and discount math is also undergoing a change. Quick commerce should not be necessarily regarded as a cheaper shelf, but it is true that brands encounter more value-conscious shoppers there. "We agree that value and entry price points gain on quick commerce. We see it less as people trading down and more as quick commerce being where a first try or a top-up happens," according to Typsy Beauty’s Bharat Ram. While the average order value may be smaller on quick commerce, the frequency of purchases makes up for that. Why Ecommerce Marketplaces Still Matter None of this has, however, made marketplaces optional. The majority of the founders we spoke to say that serious, intent-based shopping is still prevalent in ecommerce. Horizontal as well as vertical marketplaces enjoy a premiumisation moat which is not easy to displace. PAC Cosmetics, the self-funded makeup brand that crossed ₹100 Cr in FY26 revenue, has stayed off quick commerce thus far. "Consumers are evolving, and some of them choose convenience. But for an informed decision, many still prefer to see more in front of them: shades, swatches, reviews, and the full range. Staying off quick commerce is a conscious choice, because we'd rather present the brand with clarity than make it available quickly,” said founder and director Bonish Jain. Elara Capital’s Taurani highlighted that one of the reasons that Nykaa will be tough to beat is the exclusive tie-ups with the niche and international brands, which complements the company’s private label and owned brands business. Nykaa has also shifted to an inventory-led model, which allows the company more flexibility in negotiating procurement. "Marketplaces do have their own value. It is not like they can be completely replaced by quick commerce. If you are just looking for what to try, you will go to an Amazon or a Nykaa where you get to see the user experience and reviews, whereas this is not possible on quick commerce," Moxie Beauty's cofounder says. For the past two years, vertical and horizontal marketplaces have been gradually moving to the quick commerce lane, using the learnings of the industry to enable 10-minute deliveries. Nykaa has hired former Swiggy Instamart COO Ankit Jain to run Nykaa Now, which went to operate from three cities to 13 in a year. Myntra's M-Now, which runs in over 12 cities, now carries 596 beauty brands, while Flipkart says beauty on Flipkart Minutes grew 5X in a year. Taurani reads Nykaa Now as defence. "A Nykaa customer doesn't really want a quick delivery," he said, indicating that it is more of a need for marketplaces. Quick commerce, she said, lacks the depth of product content because it is a platform geared towards faster transactions and fulfilment. "The apps don't want you to get lost in the discovery. They want you to go from home to checkout in 60 seconds or whatever. So that kind of slower discovery, cart building is not happening there. And hence marketplace channels are still quite strong in our category,” Khanna told us. The early trends indicate that quick commerce and 10-minute delivery models have taken over the beauty aisle. But don’t write off the ‘plain jane’ ecommerce marketplace that may still have a trick or two up its sleeves. THE STARTUP SPOTLIGHT | HOW FORMIAL LABS IS TAKING THE GUESSWORK OUT OF SKINCARE Formial Labs aims to address the trial-and-error approach to skincare by offering customised formulations tailored to individual skin concerns, including acne, pigmentation and uneven skin texture. The startup combines dermatological expertise with personalised treatment plans, seeking to simplify skincare decisions and deliver more targeted solutions. As India's beauty market becomes increasingly crowded, Formial is betting on personalisation and professional guidance to differentiate itself from conventional skincare brands and build long-term consumer relationships. ECOMMERCE BUZZ Nykaa’s Q2 Profit More Than Triples: Beauty and fashion ecommerce major Nykaa reported a more than threefold jump in its Q2 profit to ₹101 Cr, while revenue grew 28% YoY. The strong performance reflects the company’s growing scale as it continues to expand its beauty and fashion businesses. Lenskart’s Q2 Profit Surges 125%: Eyewear major Lenskart reported a 125% YoY jump in Q2 profit to ₹233 Cr, while revenue climbed 36%. The numbers highlight the company’s improving profitability alongside its expanding eyewear business. GIVA Bags ₹975 Cr Funding: Jewellery startup GIVA raised ₹975 Cr in a funding round led by Multiples PE as it doubles down on offline expansion. The company plans to open 160 new stores in FY27, signalling its ambitions to scale its omnichannel jewellery business. Blue Ashva Exits iD Fresh In ₹50 Cr Deal: Early investor Blue Ashva Capital exited iD Fresh Food by selling its entire stake for ₹50 Cr in a secondary transaction. The deal, co-led by Upsurge India, Triumph Global Fund and White Whale Ventures, saw around 1% equity change hands as the ready-to-cook food brand continues its growth journey ahead of its IPO ambitions. THE DEEP DIVE THE OPERATOR QUESTION How Should Premium Beauty Brands Choose Between Marketplaces And Quick Commerce Without Compromising Their Positioning? Bonish Jain, founder and director at PAC Cosmetics which targets professional makeup artists and everyday consumers, says these are the five things that matter: Understand Purchase Behaviour: Not every beauty purchase is driven by convenience. Consumers buying foundations, concealers or setting sprays often want to compare shades, explore swatches, read reviews and understand product performance. The channel should support this decision-making process. Protect Positioning: Being available everywhere isn't always the right strategy. Quick commerce screens offer limited room to showcase an extensive portfolio or communicate the brand story. For premium brands, how products are presented matters as much as where they are sold. Look Beyond Transactions: Marketplaces are more than sales channels. They enable discovery, allowing consumers to explore different categories and products. Alongside influencers, makeup artists and tutorials, they help build brand presence, improve product visibility and strengthen consumer engagement. Evaluate Channel Economics: Every additional platform requires investment, inventory planning, marketing support and operational bandwidth. Assess the overall contribution of each channel, including opportunities to improve assortment, understand consumer preferences and strengthen platform partnerships. Prioritise Sustainable Growth: Focus on improving product discovery, online experiences and repeat engagement across existing channels. Evaluate new opportunities, including quick commerce, based on business potential, consumer needs and brand fit. Growth isn't about being present everywhere, but choosing platforms that support long-term scalability.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.
- This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

Quick Answer
Samsung’s latest Galaxy Z Fold 8 ad mocks Apple’s iPhone Duo at a difficult time. Reports of cracked displays, long delivery delays, and missing features have raised concerns about Apple’s first foldable. With its reputation for hardware excellence at stake, Apple needs more than silence to restore confidence.
Believe it or not, Samsung might finally have landed an ad glove on Apple. While the two brands have been taking digs at each other for years, Apple has kept things subtle, while Samsung has never been shy about being more direct. So when Apple finally decided to join the foldable race with the iPhone Duo, it was hardly surprising to see Samsung going all out against its rival – from Apple’s late arrival to the foldable party, the Duo name, the features, the price, you name it, and Samsung probably has tried to make fun of it. But as in the past, these attempts seemed just that… attempts to ruffle a leading brand on a perceived weakness, and to reassure their own fanbase. But very recently, we think Samsung struck a bit of a serious nerve in the Apple nervous system.
The Samsung Z Fold 8 slices up an apple (no, really!)
Samsung released a 32-second video on Instagram that shows an apple (duh) with a “new” sticker on the open screen of the Galaxy Z Fold8. The phone folds, and the apple gets sliced. This slice rolls down the floor, through all the old versions of the Z Fold in the past to show how many foldables Samsung launched before Apple made its first.
The video also boasts about the Z Fold 8 being thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo, all while comparing it to a slice of apple. This is not the most clever or cinematic Apple attack we have ever seen, but it is entertaining and thankfully is not over the top (unlike some others). What it also is, is a direct jab at something that Apple rarely has had to face – a perceived hardware problem with the iPhone.
iPhone Duo: from potential elixir to possible albatross
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, we thought it would be just the thing the foldables needed. Foldables have been a regular part of tech news and product portfolios since pre-COVID times (the first Galaxy Z Fold came in 2019), but even after years of iterations and multiple devices from multiple brands, the foldable segment was actually running out of steam.
So, when Apple launched the iPhone Duo, we thought that foldables would finally get some serious momentum. After all, once Apple launches something (even if it has been in the market for some time), it usually becomes more desirable and eminently “inspirational” for the competition: we have seen new features, specs, and design get picked up by the competition from Apple products, and become mainstream. From accepting touch to rejecting 3.5 mm audio jacks, it has all happened. So you could hardly blame many for thinking that Apple would launch a foldable phone, and voila! All foldable phones would start selling like hotcakes.
That scenario, however, does not seem to be playing out.
When Apple launched the iPhone Duo, the tech world went abuzz, which is business as usual when a new iPhone launches. But when the iPhone Duo became available for purchase, all the news that came in was not good. In many markets, due to supply and production issues, consumers had to wait for two months or more to get a device even after paying an advance. The brand’s decision to limit sales to two devices per person was also not well-received in some markets. It would have been understandable in the case of a new brand launching its first product, but from the first trillion-dollar company in the world, it just seemed unusually odd. The fact that it came with a super premium price tag did not help matters.
All those who have got their hands on Apple’s first foldable phone have not been thoroughly impressed with it either. There has been talk of users missing the speed and convenience of Face ID, the lack of app optimization, the new placement of the status bar, and more. And as if that were not enough, there was news that landed Apple in perhaps the hottest soup it has been in a very long time – reports have started coming in of the internal display cracking at the hinge, and a line of dead pixels appearing on it.
Often coming late to the party and rocking it…but perhaps not this time!
Once again, such problems from a new brand’s first product might have been treated with more patience. But imagine spending Rs. 2,99,900 and getting a device whose display has hardware issues. Imagine also being a person who has booked the device and is waiting for their unit, which is two months away. While Apple has acknowledged the issue, insisted that the issues exist in a small number of devices, and has assured users that all devices facing the issue will be replaced, a lot of damage has been done.
Apple’s reputation has, in some ways, worked against it. With Apple, the tech world has become accustomed to waiting for features, functions, and form factors that were seen on other devices. Android users have mocked Apple fans for getting the features that were on Android after years. But while Apple has delayed the addition of a feature or an entry into a segment, it has generally delivered an excellent performance. And that has been the defense of many Apple fans – Apple might not be the first to make a certain kind of device or bring a certain feature, but its implementation (whether it was capacitive touchscreens, Touch ID, App Store, and more) has been excellent and often an industry benchmark.
With Duo, that belief is being rocked. The brand has stepped into the foldable zone almost seven years after others, and launched a device with what seems to be a hardware flaw– not a software bug that can be fixed with an update, but a problem that can only be fixed with replacement.
Is silence golden for the communication wizard?
Apple’s handling of the issue so far has been a little unusual. The brand has found itself in trouble in the past as well with issues such as Antennagate and Bendgate, both of which generated a storm of criticism. But Apple officially addressed those issues publicly – Steve Jobs himself came out with an explanation in the case of the iPhone 4 when its stainless steel band interfered with the phone’s cellular performance, and the company also issued a very detailed statement on BendGate, famously pointing out that the issue had occurred with only nine users.
While there has not been radio silence from Apple with regard to Duo’s screen, no major management figure has come out to explain the issue or build back confidence – even in his first earnings call, new Apple CEO John Ternus limited himself to saying that while the issue existed, it affected a very small percentage of units. This relative silence could be (mis)interpreted by many in the public. To many, it does not seem as if the brand is working out solutions, as it has actually been launching devices left, right, and center since the Duo was launched.
To see management showcasing new products and talking of record earnings, even while complaints trickle in about a high-profile flagship does not make for great optics. We hope that changes soon, or alternatively, Apple comes out with a strong defense of its first foldable – it needs it. The longer it keeps silent, the more space it gives to its competitors to score points off its perceived weakness. And Apple cannot really afford to let cracks develop not just on the Duo, but in its own reputation for hardware excellence. As Samsung has shown, its competitors will not hang back in taking potshots at it. And unless credibly explained, these shots will start to hurt.
Given its potential and the hype around it, the Duo could still prove to be the elixir the foldable sector needs, but Apple needs to address the issues around it swiftly and effectively. This is a challenge unlike any other the brand has faced in recent times. Even the relative failure of the Vision Pro was more about a product being too futuristic (almost a prototype of sorts for an elite audience). The Duo, however, is supposed to redefine how we use foldables in particular and even smartphones in general. Many have even called it Apple’s most radical iPhone since the OG iPhone. How John Ternus tackles the issues surrounding the Duo could well define the tone of his tenure.

Srinagar, Nov 11: Jammu and Kashmir Health and Medical Education Minister Sakina Masood Itoo on Wednesday supported the demand for age relaxation in Jammu and Kashmir Bank recruitment, urging the bank authorities to raise the upper age limit to 40 years to provide a fair opportunity to aspirants who have lost valuable years waiting for recruitment.
In a post on X, the minister as per news agency Kashmir News Service (KNS) said thousands of aspirants had spent years waiting for recruitment opportunities and should not be penalised for delays beyond their control.
“Dreams shouldn’t have an expiry date! Thousands of J&K Bank aspirants have lost precious years waiting for recruitment opportunities. They must not be punished for delays beyond their control,” she said.
Appealing to the bank authorities, minister Ittoo said the upper age limit should be extended to 40 years to ensure that eligible candidates get an opportunity to compete.
“Give our youth a fair chance. Their future cannot wait,” she added.
Her statement comes amid growing demands from job aspirants and political representatives for relaxation in the age criteria prescribed under the bank's latest recruitment notification.
The bank has advertised 1,356 vacancies, including 323 Probationary Officer posts and 1,033 Banking Associate posts. The upper age limit for candidates belonging to the Open Merit category has been fixed at 30 years, with applicable relaxations for reserved categories.
Aspirants have been seeking an increase in the upper age limit, arguing that the prolonged gap between recruitment cycles has rendered several candidates ineligible despite years of preparation.
The Jammu and Kashmir Students Association has also sought the intervention of Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha, demanding that the upper age limit be extended to 40 years.
Minister Ittoo is the first minister in the Omar Abdullah-led Council of Ministers to publicly support the demand for age relaxation in the ongoing J&K Bank recruitment process.

Mumbai: Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) state president Sunil Tatkare and senior party leader Dhananjay Munde met Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis on Wednesday, amid growing speculation about a possible merger between the two NCP factions.
While Tatkare described his meeting as a courtesy visit on the occasion of Diwali, Munde said he discussed the severe drought conditions in Marathwada and sought additional assistance for farmers.

Dhananjay Munde Meets CM, Seeks Drought Relief For Marathwada Farmers
