Malaysian high court clears final hurdle for former Prime Minister Najib's transfer to house arrest
A high court in Malaysia has cleared all legal hurdles for former Prime Minister Najib Razak to serve the rest of his graft sentence under house arrest
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- A high court in Malaysia on Tuesday cleared all legal hurdles for the transfer of imprisoned former Prime Minister Najib Razak to his home to serve the remainder of his graft sentence under house arrest, his lawyer said.
Najib has been behind bars since August 2022, when the Kuala Lumpur High Court upheld his graft conviction linked to a multibillion-dollar looting of the state investment fund 1MDB. In September, Najib was granted royal clemency, allowing him to serve the rest of his sentence under house arrest once he pays a court-imposed fine.
Last Friday, he left prison after his political party paid the 50 million ringgit ($12.3 million) fine but he was brought back hours later after the attorney general blocked the transfer, seeking legal clarifications.
The attorney general's request sparked a public rebuke from the palace, which said that King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar’s prerogative of pardon for Najib that allowed the house arrest was clear and must be respected. It said any attempts to challenge it would amount to defying the royal order.
Najib's lawyer Muhammad Shafee Abdullah said Tuesday all was settled for the former prime minister's transfer to house arrest at his Kuala Lumpur home, where he is to remain until Aug. 23, 2028.
Najib appeared in court on Tuesday; the transfer was expected to take place later in the day. Police later sealed off the road leading to his home.
“It’s a final relief, you know, great sigh to him because he has been waiting for this,” the lawyer said.
The house arrest covers only Najib's reduced, six-year sentence in his first trial for graft and not a separate, 15-year sentence handed down last December for corruption and money laundering. That sentence followed a second major trial tied to the 1MDB scandal.
Najib is also appealing that sentence, which he is to serve after the end of his first sentence. If his appeal fails, he could return to prison after his house arrest ends.
Najib, who served as prime minister from 2009 to 2018, has denied any wrongdoing. He is Malaysia’s first former leader to be imprisoned under a sentence related to the 1MDB scandal. It marked one of the world’s largest financial scandals, rippling across global markets and triggering investigations in the United States and other countries.

Ahead of its long due IPO, adtech unicorn InMobi has bolstered its marketing by securing a naming rights for Bengaluru's Ibbaluru Metro Station for the next 30 years via a ₹65 Cr deal. The partnership will see InMobi support Namma Metro over a 30-year concession, and Ibbaluru Metro Station will be known as InMobi Ibbaluru Metro Station. "Bengaluru is one of the world’s leading technology hubs. InMobi was born here, and over the last 18 years, we’ve grown alongside the city, continuing to build from India for the world. This partnership is our way of giving back to the city that gave us our start," the company said in a statement. The deal will contribute to BMRCL's non-fare revenue, which includes income from commercial activities such as station branding and advertising, alongside its core passenger fare collections. BMRCL said the partnership would support metro infrastructure development and encourage more corporate participation in the city's public transport ecosystem. The naming-rights deal comes as InMobi continues to work towards a public listing in India, a plan first reported over two years ago. In July 2024, reports said the company was targeting a 2025 IPO at a valuation of around $10 Bn. However, the proposed timeline has since slipped, with InMobi yet to file its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP). The delay in the proposed listing has coincided with changes in InMobi's shareholding structure. In December 2025, InMobi's cofounders bought back around 25-30% stake from early investor SoftBank, bringing the latter's holding down from approximately 35% to less than 8%. The transaction was backed by $350 Mn in debt raised from Varde Partners, Elham Credit Partners and SeaTown Holdings. The reshuffle in InMobi's cap table continued in 2026, with private equity firm True North reportedly acquiring a 2-3% stake through a secondary transaction valued at around $50-60 Mn. The deal also provided partial exits to some early investors. Alongside these shareholder transactions, InMobi has been putting the banking team in place for its proposed listing. The company has appointed JPMorgan Chase, Jefferies, Kotak Mahindra Capital and Axis Capital as merchant bankers for the IPO. Earlier reports pegged the proposed issue at around $1 Bn, although subsequent valuation estimates have varied. While the IPO remains a work in progress, InMobi has continued to expand its advertising technology capabilities through acquisitions. In May 2026, the company acquired San Francisco-based mobile app marketing and analytics platform MobileAction to strengthen its capabilities in app discovery, user acquisition and advertising optimisation.

In Musan City, a decaying small town that exists only on screen, a grieving mother puts on a pair of AR glasses and spends time with her 10-year-old son. He has been gone for nine years, one of the children on a camp bus that vanished. Then the real boy comes home, grown up and a stranger, and the comfort the glasses offered starts to turn into something far more frightening.
That is the setup of “Paradise Lost,” the new psychological thriller from Yeon Sang-ho, the director of “Train to Busan” and the series “Hellbound.” It sits at the opposite end of the scale from “Colony,” which Yeon premiered in the Midnight Screenings section at Cannes earlier this year. “Paradise Lost” went on to Toronto’s Special Presentations section, where Yeon had also taken last year’s micro-budget “The Ugly,” and then screened as a Gala Presentation in Busan. Screenings sold out at both festivals.
Kim Hyun-joo, who worked with Yeon on both seasons of “Hellbound” and on “Jung_E,” plays the mother, Ryu So-young. Bae Hyeon-seong (“Hospital Playlist”) takes his first big-screen lead as Sun-woo, the son who returns. Yeon wrote the screenplay with Ryu Yong-jae, drawing on an original idea of theirs that author Oh Seong-eun turned into the novel “Black Inferno.” Wowpoint produced, and CJ ENM, which presents the film with Wowpoint, handles distribution. The film has sold to 118 countries, with Well Go USA handling North America, where it released Nov. 6.
“On one level, AI is something mechanical or technological. But when you look more closely, we can see what is beneath it. I think it is ultimately what we share as human knowledge and also collective intelligence,” Yeon tells Variety.
As he argued around “Colony,” that pooled knowledge is now beginning to threaten our individuality, he says, the very qualities that make each of us human. “The relationship between a mother and her son is perhaps one of the most deeply personal and intimate relationships we can have,” Yeon continues. “We can never truly know what lies in the depth of another person’s psyche.”
The film borrows its title from Milton’s epic poem. “Just like the story where the first of mankind are expelled from paradise, I thought that the loss of paradise is precisely where the human identity begins,” Yeon said in the film’s production notes.
He has used AI as a storytelling device before. In 2023’s “Jung_E,” an AI recreation allowed a daughter to free her mother from an idealized, self-sacrificing image, something he says would not be possible in the real world. “With ‘Paradise Lost,’ I wanted to take a much more grounded approach, using AI as a point of contrast, I would say, to explore something that is uniquely human,” he says.
AI may be built on humanity’s shared patterns, he adds, but it can also behave in very unpredictable ways, beyond our ability to fully control or comprehend. “In that sense, I think AI itself represents an uncharted territory. Something as mysterious and unknowable to us as a black hole.”
Where “The Ugly” followed a son digging into his father’s buried past, “Paradise Lost” swaps in a mother and son.
“I think the family is the very first form of society that we encounter as human beings,” Yeon says. “And because the family is our first experience of society, it plays a fundamental role in shaping much of our sense of self and also our personal identity.”
“The Ugly” was shot for KRW200 million ($150,000). “Paradise Lost” was also made lean, for KRW500 million ($374,000) over just 14 shooting sessions. Yeon leaned on Kim, whom he knew understood his directing style extremely well after several projects together. The schedule meant few takes and limited locations.
“But when you think about it, many of the most legendary films in Asian cinema were made under similar constraints,” Yeon says. “In a way I found that those limitations allowed me, and allowed us, to explore the material more creatively, and they also demanded an extraordinary level of focus and concentration from everyone involved.”
Korea’s theatrical industry is going through a major transformation, Yeon says, and some feel the market has shrunk considerably. “But I don’t necessarily see that as an obstacle to making good films. A smaller industry doesn’t automatically mean fewer great films will be made,” he says. Making “Colony” and “Paradise Lost” in the same year gave him firsthand experience of two radically different scales, which he hopes will help him lead productions of any size with greater confidence.
International sales covered the film’s net production budget ahead of release. Among Korean distributors, CJ ENM is one of the most active in working with overseas partners, Yeon says, and that experience counts. “Whether a Korean film is a box office success or not, whether it is a mainstream commercial production or something with a more niche sensibility, I believe there are audiences somewhere in the world who will appreciate it,” he says.
Making a film available everywhere is not enough on its own, he adds. “Global streaming platforms already release films simultaneously across multiple territories, using algorithms to recommend content based on individual preferences. But I don’t think we have necessarily established just how effective that approach is at helping films find their audiences.”
Yeon has two projects in post-production. The first is a Japanese-language Netflix series, based on the manga “Parasyte: Tamiya,” on which he serves as screenwriter and showrunner. It moves one of the original’s villains, Tamiya Ryoko, to the center of the story. “What I found particularly fascinating is the way Tamiya, who is a parasite rather than a human being, gradually tries to understand humanity,” he says.
The second is “Devotion,” a horror feature due next year. It grew out of the way people now put versions of their identities on display and hide behind the personas they build. Its Korean title, “Yeto,” is a Buddhist term for an imperfect world marked by suffering, the opposite of the realm of ultimate bliss.
For a filmmaker who thinks being human starts with the loss of paradise, it is a fitting next stop.

Indonesia's VP offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.
Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.
It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to "continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents," Hadi said.
As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.
"I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place," Raka said. "I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy."
The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.
Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.
The developments come amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo. The popular former president backed Prabowo's presidential bid after he chose Raka as a running mate.
The controversy over Raka's academic qualifications escalated last month after the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements.
The ruling intensified political pressure on Raka and fueled calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment.
Widodo faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, the progeny of one of America’s most famous and wealthiest families, who during three decades in the U.S. Senate sought expanded healthcare for the poor and excoriated President George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq War, died on Friday (November 6, 2026) at his home in Washington, the Washington Post reported. He was 89.
His family did not provide a cause, the newspaper added.
Mr. Rockefeller, a tall, soft-spoken Democrat with liberal views, was elected in 1984 to the first of his five six-year terms representing West Virginia in the Senate after two terms as Governor of the poor coal-mining State.
Mr. Rockefeller voted in 2002 in favour of the Republican Bush’s measure authorising the Iraq war, which began with a U.S.-led invasion in 2003. He later expressed regret over that vote and, as head of the Senate intelligence committee, accused Mr. Bush of taking the nation to war on “false premises.”
He was a great-grandson of oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller and the scion of a family that formed a political dynasty that included his uncle, New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller.
Initiatives in public office
New York-born Jay Rockefeller’s life changed direction after he graduated from Harvard and served in a national service program in impoverished rural West Virginia from 1964 to 1966.
When he was put in public office, he worked to increase healthcare access, fight poverty, provide health benefits to coal miners and assist military veterans. As a senator, he had a role in shaping the programme created in 1997 under which the U.S. government helps States provide medical coverage for millions of uninsured children.
Mr. Rockefeller backed Democratic President Bill Clinton’s failed proposal for near-universal health insurance coverage in the 1990s and then fought for Democratic President Barack Obama’s successful quest for a healthcare overhaul law, signed in 2010.
In the debate over Mr. Obama’s measure, Mr. Rockefeller unsuccessfully sought to have the federal government offer a medical insurance program to the general population — in addition to existing programs for the poor and elderly — as an alternative to private insurance plans that could be costly and exclusive.
“Championing those most in need has been my life’s calling and I will never stop fighting to make a difference for the people who mean so much to me,” Mr. Rockefeller said in 2013 when he announced at age 75 he would not seek a sixth Senate term.
On the Iraq war
Before the Iraq invasion, Mr. Bush’s administration built the case for war by touting intelligence indicating Iraq owned an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction — they actually did not exist — and alleged ties between Iraqi leaders and the al Qaeda network responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks on the U.S.
“If I had known then what I know now, I would have voted against it,” Mr. Rockefeller told the Charleston Gazette newspaper in 2004, referring to the 2002 war authorization measure.
“I think the intelligence was shaped,” he continued. “And I think the interpretation of the intelligence was shaped. You had a president who we now know was determined to go to war.”
‘Fundamentally misleading’
A report from the intelligence committee issued in 2008, when he served as its chairman, asserted that Mr. Bush, Vice President Dick Cheney and other leading officials exaggerated intelligence findings and ignored disputes within U.S. intelligence circles about Iraq’s weapons and the hotly disputed ties to al Qaeda.
The report rejected pre-war statements by Mr. Bush and Cheney that Iraq might give al Qaeda weapons of mass destruction.
“Representing to the American people that the two had an operational partnership and posed a single, indistinguishable threat was fundamentally misleading and led the nation to war on false premises,” Mr. Rockefeller said as the report was released.
During his Senate tenure, he also headed the Commerce, Science, and Transportation and Veterans Affairs committees.
Wealthy family
Mr. Rockefeller was born on June 18, 1937, weeks after the death of his great-grandfather, who had been America’s richest man.
The Rockefeller name came with high expectations. His father was a famous philanthropist. His uncle Nelson served as U.S. vice president, as well as Governor of New York. His uncle David Rockefeller headed Chase Manhattan Bank and uncle Winthrop Rockefeller was governor of Arkansas.
He was elected to West Virginia’s legislature in 1966 before age 30, then elected West Virginia’s Secretary of State in 1968.
He lost a bid to become Governor in 1972, then served as a college president before being elected Governor in 1976. Mr. Rockefeller, who became one of the wealthiest members of the U.S. Congress, spent millions of dollars of his own money to bankroll his successful campaign for the US Senate in 1984.
Mr. Rockefeller sometimes found himself overshadowed by his State’s other senator, Robert Byrd, who died in 2010 at age 92 as the longest-serving member of Congress in U.S. history.
He usually backed his State’s coal and steel industries but angered coal executives in 2012 by fighting Republican efforts to prevent regulation of emissions from coal-fired power plants.
He was married to public television executive Sharon Percy Rockefeller, with whom he had four children.

Stacy Keach, stage actor and Mike Hammer star, dead at 85
Keach died at his home in Poland, following a long battle with heart problems
Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85.
Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, "after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure," his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017.
Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favourite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.
Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating World's Most Amazing Videos on TV. He played a deranged colonel in The Ninth Configuration (also known as Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane), led the TV show Titus, had a role in Alexander Payne's Oscar-nominated drama Nebraska and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama Blue Bloods. Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney's bitter father in Jay Kelly.
"My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career," he told New York magazine in 2012. "My choices have had a cost attached to it. But I've gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything."
'One of the greats'
Actor Lou Diamond Phillips, who played Keach's son in the 2008 TV movie Lone Rider, said in a post on X that Keach was a "consummate actor, gracious, giving and incredibly kind even while he had the presence of a smoldering volcano. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him."
Keach played French painter Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries Mistral's Daughter, a Russian prince in the miniseries version of Judith Krantz's novel Princess Daisy, Barabbas in Franco Zeffirelli's Jesus of Nazareth and Maj. Jonas Steele in The Blue and the Gray. He won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, for which he gained 35 pounds.
Keach, seen in April 1984, was one of America's finest stage actors. (Daily Express/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)
Keach earned a Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Buffalo Bill in the Broadway play Indians, played Edmund opposite Lee J. Cobb in King Lear on Broadway and had other onstage roles there, including in 1993's The Kentucky Cycle, The Country Wife in 1965 and Other Desert Cities in 2011.
He also headed the national touring company cast of Frost/Nixon, portraying the fallen president, and went on tour with Sleuth with Maxwell Caulfield as his co-star. He starred in a 2006 production of King Lear at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and returned in 2017 for Pamplona, a one-man show about Hemingway, where he collapsed onstage, leading to the run's cancellation.
'Lowest moment' was prison
While he was still doing Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer (later titled The New Mike Hammer), Keach was arrested in 1984 at London's Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol shaving cream can and elsewhere in his luggage. Also arrested was his secretary.
Keach and his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, pose for a photo at a premiere in 2006. (Lucas Jackson/The Associated Press)
"As my sentence was read — nine months in prison — I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats," he wrote in his 2013 book, All in All: An Actor's Life On and Off the Stage. He added: "It was the lowest moment of my life."
He was handcuffed and taken to prison, a cell the size of a closet and where an orange plastic bucket would serve as his toilet. Before he went inside, an officer asked him to autograph a copy of the book The Blue and the Gray.
The then-44-year-old actor was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, because authorities felt a minimum-security jail would have provided too easy access for reporters. He was released after six months.
In his book, Keach wrote that while in prison he got warm letters from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He was put in charge of showing a movie one Sunday per month and recalls once picking his own, The Long Riders. He said the experience was "very lonely, very depressing, very sad. I spent a lot of my time trying to re-evaluate my own stupidity."
After prison, he narrated the TV documentary High on the Job, and testified before Congress, telling a House panel how he first became hooked on cocaine in the mid-1970s. "There is no greater imprisonment than that of being dependent on a chemical substance for one's existence," he testified.
Keach took his warnings to college campuses and rehab centres. He also married Polish actor Malgosia Tomassi, whom he met when she appeared in the Hammer series. He said he treasured the photos and letters she sent while he was behind bars.
Married 4 times
Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina.
His first role after his release was in the CBS movie, Intimate Strangers with Teri Garr, and it became the third-highest rated TV movie of the 1985-86 season. His next film, The Return of Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer, also played well, and then the Mike Hammer series, which had been on the production shelf since his arrest, was given a slot on CBS's 1986-87 schedule.
Many years later, in the TV series Prison Break that aired from 2005-2007, Keach played a prison warden and said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help inmates rehabilitate themselves.
Born in Savannah, Ga., Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art.

What do dark circles under a child’s eyes indicate?
Dark circles under a child’s eyes may not always be due to lack of sleep. Genetics, allergies and nasal congestion can also play a role. Paediatricians explain the causes and when parents should seek medical advice
Dark circles alone need not be a cause for concern if the child is otherwise healthy. Parents should, however, consult a paediatrician if the discolouration persists or is accompanied by other symptoms |Image used for representational purpose only
| Photo Credit: File Photo
A child may wake up after a full night’s sleep and still have dark circles under the eyes. For some children, this may simply be a family trait. In others, it could be associated with allergies, persistent nasal congestion or skin conditions. Dark circles, also referred to as periorbital hyperpigmentation, are not a condition in themselves. While parents may immediately associate dark circles with inadequate sleep or nutritional deficiencies, their causes can be more varied.

Jackson, Wyoming, is a pretty incredible place.
It's easy to see why it's so popular with tourists — and, having grown up there, I've seen a lot of them over the years.
If you're planning a visit to this beautiful slice of northwest Wyoming, here are a few mistakes you ought to avoid and travel tips you should try to follow.
Contrary to popular belief, Jackson isn't the only town near Grand Teton National Park and Yellowstone National Park.
The town of Jackson has become one of the most famous and crowded landing bases for people exploring Grand Teton National Park and Yellowstone National Park, but there are several other wonderful satellite communities that deserve attention, too.
Dubois, a Wyoming town located about an hour-and-a-half east of Grand Teton, is situated perfectly between the Absaroka Range and Wind River Range and offers a taste of the Old West.
Pinedale, an hour-and-a-half south of Jackson, used to be a hub for fur traders and is an exceptional place to explore central Wyoming's mountains and desert.
Victor and Driggs are two Idaho towns located just east of the Tetons that are slower-paced, cheaper, and less-crowded alternatives to Jackson.
Most travelers automatically book flights to and from the Jackson Hole Airport without checking prices at nearby airports.
Flying in and out of the Jackson Hole Airport is known to be pretty expensive. Consider booking flights to and from a nearby airport and pairing your trip with a beautiful drive through less-visited areas.
Idaho Falls, located only two hours from Jackson, offers striking views over mountain passes. Bozeman, about four hours away, allows you to drive through Yellowstone on the way.
Salt Lake City, a five-hour drive, offers a beautiful route with multiple hot springs that break up the journey.
Some tourists get so excited to see Jackson's moose, elk, and bears that they forget they're wild animals.
One of the most magical experiences that comes with exploring Jackson Hole and the surrounding national parks is the opportunity to see wildlife up close.
That said, there are close encounters, and then there are too-close-for-comfort encounters.
I've lost count of how many times I've been in utter disbelief as I watched families — with children — walk straight up to bison, moose, elk, and even bears. These are wild animals, and Jackson Hole is not a zoo where you're protected by barriers.
Every year, people are maimed, gored, and trampled because they either don't think about danger or assume that nothing bad will happen to them.
It's also worth pointing out that you should never feed wild animals. It can lead them to become habituated, dependent, aggressive, and dangerous — all things that can result in getting them killed.
Enjoy the best of Wyoming's nature, but always prioritize your safety and that of local wildlife.
People mistakenly think that Jackson is all about adventure sports, but there are other reasons to visit the town.
Many people associate Jackson Hole with adventure sports — like skiing, rafting, hiking, and mountain biking. The area is an exceptional place to partake in these activities, but they're actually relatively new to the area.
I'm disappointed that so few people know about Jackson's original attractions: ranches and cowboys.
Long before Jackson became known for its nature-based adventures, people visited to stay at ranches, ride horses, and experience a taste of the Wild West.
Today, Jackson is undoubtedly focused on tourism, but there are still plenty of cowboys and ranchers who make a living off of horses and cattle.
I always recommend visitors pay homage to Jackson's cowboy-filled history when they're in town by going to the rodeo, taking a scenic horseback ride, or staying at a traditional dude ranch.
Jackson's weather can be unpredictable and extreme, and many visitors don't pack enough warm layers.
Located along the Continental Divide, Jackson has extremely variable weather.
Summertime temperatures can swing by 70 degrees Fahrenheit between morning and afternoon, and in winter, temperatures can drop below zero degrees Fahrenheit.
Carefully research Jackson's weather right before you travel and plan for the unexpected. It may be freezing when it's supposed to be hot, rain on a day that's supposed to have blue skies, and, believe it or not, snow during any month of the year.
Regardless of what activities you're doing in Jackson, pack multiple layers to stay comfortable, no matter what the weather does.
People often cut a hike short after reaching a popular spot or vista, but the real mountain magic lies beyond the tourist crowds.
I always joke that you only have to hike one extra mile to get past Jackson's tourist crowds.
On many trails in Grand Teton and Yellowstone, I see people walk to the first main attraction or vista and then turn around, oftentimes because maps don't show anything beyond that point.
One of the great privileges of being in the mountains is being able to take a few steps beyond your comfort zone and experience unexpected wonder.
Take advantage of every opportunity — whether it's whitewater rafting for the first time, climbing to the top of the Grand Teton, or even just hiking to a point on the map that's slightly further off the popular trail.
Walk the extra mile past the crowds, take the road less traveled, and let the wilderness transform you. Just be careful while you do it.
First-timers expect Jackson to be full of wide-open spaces and walk-in restaurants, but the popular town is a tourist hot spot.
Wyoming has a reputation for having wide-open spaces and a sparse population, but over the past decade, Jackson has become more crowded than I've ever seen it.
When many families arrive in town, they're disappointed to find that hotel rooms are expensive and hard to get, restaurants are fully booked, certain campgrounds require reservations, and hiking trails are crowded.
These challenges come with being a popular tourist destination, and they're not likely to change. However, a bit of planning can help avoid travel headaches.
Be sure to book rooms and rental cars far in advance and make dinner reservations before you travel.
If you have a few nights open, there's a wonderful collection of small, authentic Mexican restaurants in town that often go unnoticed by visitors. They have brilliant menus and are well worth a visit.
Those who don't spend a night in Jackson's backcountry are missing out.
True darkness and utter silence are rare phenomena that many people in the modern world have never experienced.
Some of the country's most isolated wilderness surrounds Jackson and can provide a therapeutic escape to those who venture into the rolling pine forests. Many people visit Jackson and never have this special experience.
Fortunately, it's very easy to spend a night in nature. Experienced, intrepid travelers should backpack away from the crowds for a few nights in the remote, beautiful backcountry.
If you want a more catered experience, pack-trip providers will whisk you away on horseback to enjoy one or more nights at a backcountry camp. Usually, the companies provide comfortable tents, gear, and chef-prepared food.
People expect Jackson to have a similar feel year-round, but it offers drastically different experiences based on the season.
Unbeknownst to many, most ski towns in the Western US have off-seasons in the spring and fall, when everything comes to a grinding halt.
In an area driven by seasonal tourist activities — like skiing in the winter and rafting, fishing, and hiking in the summer — the calmer months give the hardworking staff an opportunity to relax and take time off before the next rush of visitors arrives.
In Jackson, the off-seasons usually run from October to December and from April to June. You might find fewer crowds and cheaper room rates during these times, but many businesses and restaurants have limited schedules or close.
If you're planning a fall or spring-break trip, there will still be plenty to do, but keep in mind that reservations will be tighter and fewer choices may be available.
Outsiders often get confused by the area's geography and call places the wrong names.
Even after growing up as a Jackson local, I'll be the first to admit that Wyoming geography is confusing. If you want to impress locals, calling places by their proper names is a great start.
The town of Jackson is located in a larger valley called Jackson Hole. So even though the entire region is loosely referred to as "Jackson Hole" (or "JH" for short), you should just call it "Jackson" when you're referring specifically to the town.
As for the mountains, their name is the "Teton Range," or the "Tetons," with the "Grand Teton" (note that there's no "s") as the highest peak.
I often hear people incorrectly call them the "Grand Tetons," which is an accurate description of the striking granite peaks, but not the correct name for the mountain range.

US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
- Published
An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.
A majority of the House of Representatives agreed to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky - for now.
In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".
The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.
Massie was the only Republican to vote against moving the resolution to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.
His effort failed in a 211-204 vote, with more than a dozen members, including 11 Democrats, missing the vote.
The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress before Democrats take control in January.
President Trump celebrated the vote in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort "has miserably FAILED".
"Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump said, referring to Hegseth.
After the vote, Massie said he "wasn't surprised" but "was disappointed", according to BBC's US media partner CBS.
"My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do," he added. "They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."
Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.
The Kentucky congressman also said that removing Hegseth now would give the Senate time to approve a replacement while Republicans were still in power.
Impeachment resolutions can be carried past the end of a congressional term, meaning Democrats would be able to take it up next year.
The Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January following a successful midterm election that allowed them control of both chambers.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, had predicted earlier in the day that the impeachment bid would fail.
In the eight articles of impeachment formally introduced in the House on Monday, Massie said Hegseth was "breaking the law and must be held accountable" for fighting a war in Iran for more than 90 days without lawmakers' approval.
The impeachment articles also accused Hegseth of overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the US campaign against boats alleged to be carrying drugs in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth called efforts to impeach him a political stunt by a Trump administration opponent who was "disgruntled and defeated".
Hegseth also argued Massie's resolution endangered national security, because it communicated to US adversaries "that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations".
"This is not patriotism. This is sabotage," he said.
He echoed some statements Trump had made during a surprise appearance at the White House briefing room on Monday, including touting a rise in military recruitment levels.
But Hegseth said Massie was motivated by policy differences and "not high crimes, not misdemeanours, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offences the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause".
Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year to a Trump-backed opponent, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it began in February.
He had already incurred the president's ire for demanding the Trump administration release files on deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
While Hegseth has survived politically for now, many lawmakers - including some Republicans - have questioned how long he can last in the administration.
Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican, said on Tuesday he expected Hegseth to resign or be fired by Trump.

The role of family physicians in ensuring accessible, affordable and patient-centred healthcare came into focus at the premiere of the documentary ‘The Doctor Next Door: A Legacy of Care’, screened at the Indian Heritage Academy in Bengaluru earlier this week.
Through accounts of veteran physicians, patients and young medical professionals, the film examines the decline of neighbourhood family practices and the growing fragmentation of healthcare. It highlights how long-standing doctor-patient relationships built on trust, familiarity and personal attention remain central to effective primary care.
The documentary draws attention to the rising dependence on specialised and corporate hospital-based treatment, making a case for strengthening family medicine as the foundation of India’s healthcare system.
Swetha Reddy, project manager of the documentary, said the film features perspectives from young medical students and practitioners considering careers in general practice, highlighting the need for changes in medical education and healthcare policy to encourage family medicine.
Directed by Ganesh Shankar Raj of Mindia Films and produced in collaboration with the Academy of Family Physicians of India (AFPI), the non-profit documentary explores the enduring relationship between family doctors and patients, and the importance of continuity of care in an increasingly specialised healthcare system.
The screening was followed by a panel discussion featuring scientists, medical professionals, senior family physicians, and community health advocates. The discussion centred on the challenges facing primary healthcare, the need to strengthen family medicine, and the importance of human relationships in medical practice.
Veteran family physician B.C. Rao was among the contributors to the initiative, alongside representatives of AFPI and other healthcare professionals.
The organisers said the documentary was intended to initiate wider conversations on reviving primary healthcare networks in urban and rural communities, and recognising neighbourhood doctors as an integral part of the healthcare system.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

The Child Development Centre (CDC), Thiruvananthapuram, has received an Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)-approved grant of ₹35 lakh for a three-year research project titled “Development and Validation of a Tool for Assessing Grief among Parents of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.”
The project, led by CDC director Deepa Bhaskaran, aims to develop and validate a culturally relevant tool to assess grief among parents of children with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD).
“The study will use focus group discussions and in-depth interviews involving parents of children with ASD, bereaved parents, professionals working with children with ASD, and members of the general population to understand the dimensions and cultural expressions of grief in the Indian context,” Dr. Bhaskaran said.
According to her, parents commonly experience shock, denial, fear, guilt, anger, sadness, and helplessness following their child’s diagnosis. The grief, described as chronic sorrow or non-finite grief, can recur at different stages of the child’s development, particularly when expected developmental milestones are not attained.
“The findings will help facilitate the identification of grief-related concerns among parents and support the development of appropriate grief counselling protocols and support group interventions, ultimately contributing to improved psychosocial well-being among families of children with ASD,” she said.
Inadequate social support compounds parental distress, she noted.
“There is a need for healthcare professionals to recognise and assess parents’ emotional well-being alongside the rehabilitation needs of children with autism. Early diagnosis, psychological support, and training for professionals to identify grief and help families develop coping strategies are vital,” she added.

At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of Cairo, authorities have said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles (5okm) south of the capital, when a train travelling to the south-western Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. It said one of the trains had derailed.
The health ministry said at least four people had been killed and 88 injured. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.
The president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.
A train driver and his assistant were injured in September last year when two freight trains collided in the same district.

Mohalla Tech, the parent of social media platforms ShareChat and Moj, reported a 78.5% YoY increase in its consolidated net loss to ₹1,978.4 Cr in the financial year ended March 2026 (FY26), weighed down by higher share-based payment expenses, foreign exchange losses and finance costs. The loss for the fiscal year widened despite a 40.4% jump in operating revenue to ₹1,016.3 Cr from ₹723.4 Cr in FY25. Further, the startup also reported an improvement in its operating performance. ShareChat’s management claims that it managed to narrow its FY26 EBITDA loss by 58% YoY to ₹91 Cr and recorded its first EBITDA positive quarter in Q1 FY27. The company reported an EBITDA profit of ₹9.5 Cr and a margin of 0.3% in the June quarter. Its EBITDA margin improved to over 2% in Q2 FY27, the management claimed. QuickTV Subscription Drives Revenue Growth The startup’s management said its FY26 top line growth was led by the launch of QuickTV, its subscription-based microdrama platform launched in February 2025. The subscription vertical, which accounts for subscriptions from both Quick TV and Moj (Moj+ and Moj Blue), raked in a revenue of ₹292.7 Cr in the fiscal, accounting for almost 30% of the top line in the fiscal. Mohalla Tech had counted advertising and livestreaming as its two major pillars for revenue generation since its inception over a decade ago. In the previous fiscal year, it aggressively expanded into monetising the content on its platform amid a growing fervour for microdramas in the Indian content landscape. Hailed as the "next phase of evolution for the entertainment industry", Microdrama adoption picked pace in the Indian market early in FY26. ShareChat had launched its vertical microdrama platform, QuickTV, earlier in February 2025. Since then, the app has been downloaded by over 5 Cr users from the Google Play Store. As its content monetisation took shape, the social media unicorn faced some operational turmoil for its long-set revenue driver — advertising. Advertising revenue dipped 13% YoY to ₹251.8 Cr in the fiscal year. This decline came as advertisers from the real money gaming (RMG) stopped promotional spends. To note, ShareChat had already diversified its offerings for clients across FMCG and mid-market advertisers. Hence, it managed to offset the dent anticipated from the RMG ban. On the other hand, ShareChat’s livestreaming segment grew almost by 9% YoY to ₹471.8 Cr. This segment registers revenue from paying users on both ShareChat and Moj platforms. ShareChat’s FY27 Outlook For the fiscal year FY27, Mohalla Tech is targeting an EBITDA profit of ₹25 Cr, including at least ₹15 Cr in the second half of FY27. The startup reported around ₹740 Cr in revenue in the first half of FY27, while its Q2 FY27 annualised revenue run rate reached approximately ₹1,500 Cr. It did not disclose its bottom line performance for the September half of the ongoing fiscal. To fuel this financial improvement, the startup is expecting both of its content monetisation models — subscription video on demand (SVOD) and advertising-based video on demand (AVOD) — to shoulder its next phase of growth. ShareChat is expecting its advertising to make a stronger contribution in FY27, growing by 40% YoY. While it is expecting its AVOD revenue to surpass the ₹350 Cr mark, this particular revenue stream touched ₹160 Cr in the first half. The management didn’t share any projections for revenue from SVOD in the fiscal. It believes that most Indian internet users are unlikely to pay for microdrama subscriptions, with the number of paying users for the format expected to remain below 100 Mn even as the market matures, making advertising an important monetisation opportunity. The Microdrama Dillema Mohalla Tech's push into microdrama comes as the format draws growing interest across businesses. EloElo Group, the parent of microdrama platform Story TV, recently raised $80 Mn (around ₹756 Cr) in a Series C round led by Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal. The company plans to invest in original content across Indian languages, expand Story TV internationally and strengthen its AI-powered production capabilities. Story TV has more than 5,000 microdramas across six languages, while EloElo claims over 40 Mn monthly active users across its apps. The space has also attracted startups such as Kuku TV, Flick TV, ReelSaga and Chai Shots, alongside larger platforms including JioHotstar's Tadka, Zee Entertainment's Bullet and Amazon MX Player's MX Fatafat. Businesses and platforms are utilising the short-story format to plug in marketing and products while capitalising on the rise in vertical content consumption. What's New: ShareChat parent Mohalla Tech's consolidated net loss widened 78.5% YoY to ₹1,978.4 Cr in FY26, even as operating revenue jumped 40.4% to ₹1,016.3 Cr. Why It Matters: Subscription revenue from its microdrama push helped offset declining advertising revenue, while the company narrowed its EBITDA loss by 58%. The Details: Higher ESOP expenses, forex losses and finance costs weighed on profitability, with total expenses jumping 65.6% YoY. However, rising customer acquisition costs and the difficulty of converting free viewers into paying subscribers continue to weigh on the economics of standalone microdrama platforms. For instance, Mohalla Tech said acquiring a user on its free-to-use platform Moj costs around ₹14-15 per download, while acquiring a paying subscriber for QuickTV costs hundreds of rupees, given the latter's newer brand and subscription paywall. It claimed that competing subscription platforms could be spending upwards of ₹1,000 per subscriber. Owing to this, platforms like Mohalla Tech are instead banking on advertising revenue and marketing plug-ins to increase monetisation. Where Did ShareChat Spend In FY26? Mohalla Tech’s total expenses surged 65.6% to ₹3,083 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,862.1 Cr a year earlier. During its FY26 earnings call, management said the reported loss was largely driven by non-cash and notional accounting items, including provisions for interest on hybrid debt instruments, unrealised foreign exchange losses and ESOP expenses. Employee Benefit Expenses: Expenses under this head more than doubled to ₹959.5 Cr from ₹445.8 Cr in FY25. A large part of the increase came from share-based payments, which climbed 302% to ₹739 Cr in FY26 from ₹183.8 Cr in FY25, following an expansion of the company's ESOP pool and additional grants to key employees. Foreign Exchange Losses: Owing to rupee-dollar depreciation, non-cash expenses under this head rose more than fourfold to ₹566.9 Cr from ₹128 Cr in FY25. The increase was largely driven by unrealised forex losses of ₹566 Cr. Business Development: Expenses under this head, which usually covers functions like marketing, promotions and customer acquisition, surged 7.7X to ₹334.8 Cr from ₹43.4 Cr in FY26.

The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6, 2026) termed vehicular emissions a major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR and said immediate, medium- and long-term measures were needed to curb the rising air quality index.
Hearing a suo motu case examining the regulatory framework governing air pollution, a Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana also expressed concern over “bumper-to-bumper” traffic in Delhi-NCR.
“We keep talking and sometimes make statements and suggestions, but the point is that AQI is already touching 400,” the CJI said.
The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad.
“Look at the roads in Delhi and the roads connecting Delhi with the NCR. Take a look at any road and the kind of vehicles moving on it. That is the major problem,” the CJI said.
The Bench said the poor people are the real sufferers, as they are on the roads, and moreover, the festival time is the only period when they earn a livelihood.
On stubble burning, the Bench stressed the need to educate farmers about using machines instead of resorting to farm fires.
On the plea seeking closure of schools or running them in hybrid mode for students of all age groups if the air quality index (AQI) rises above a certain mark, the bench said it will go by experts’ opinion.
Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre and other authorities, referred to the regulatory framework covering five major sectors: industrial emissions, vehicular pollution, construction and demolition dust, road dust and stubble burning.
She told the Bench that several measures had been introduced, including restrictions on the entry of certain vehicles, geo-tagging of pollution under control (PUC) certificates and action against visibly polluting vehicles through complaints received on applications and social media.
Ms. Bhati told the Bench that stubble burning accounted for 14% of Delhi’s pollution on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The Bench said it will pass some orders and take up the plea on November 16 after the court reopens following the Diwali vacation.
A thick layer of smog hung over the national capital on Friday (November 6, 2026) as the air quality deteriorated sharply and edged closer to the ‘severe’ category, with the overall AQI settling at 391.
Of the 59 monitoring stations across the city, 30 recorded ‘severe’ air quality at 9 a.m., while the remaining were in the ‘very poor’ category.
Rohini recorded the worst AQI at 475, followed by IIT Delhi at 472, official data showed.

As the Cairo Intl. Film Festival (Nov. 11-20) marks 50 years since its founding, its industry arm is looking beyond the annual event, introducing new programs to provide longer-term support for filmmakers.
“My vision is not to start very big,” says Mohamed Sayed Abdel-Rehim, head of Cairo Industry Days. “Every year, we introduce a new program, or maybe a couple of programs, but we start them small in order to make the progress steady.”
That philosophy is shaping the eighth edition of CID, which runs Nov. 14-19 during the festival’s 47th edition.
At the center of this year’s expansion is the 12th iteration of Cairo Film Connection, the festival’s co-production platform supporting Arab filmmakers. CFC is introducing a mentorship program designed to extend its relationship with selected projects beyond the industry event itself.
“We try not to make it only the four days of the Cairo Film Connection during the festival. We try to make it year-long,” Sayed Abdel-Rehim explains.
The initiative brings together five international experts covering development, pitching, budgeting and financing, festival strategy, broadcasting and legal matters. Online sessions have already begun, with mentoring continuing during the festival. CID has also partnered with the Sundance Documentary Fund to organize an online session for projects from last year’s CFC that are still seeking support.
For Sayed Abdel-Rehim, the goal is to build a pipeline in which filmmakers progress from CID workshops to CFC, before completing films that screen in CIFF’s competitions.
“We try to make our filmmakers that were selected in the Cairo Film Connection part of the alumni family,” he says, describing an ongoing commitment to supporting their careers. The relationship can eventually come full circle with directors whose films win Cairo’s Golden Pyramid, the festival’s top prize, returning as CFC jury members the following year.
There are already signs of that progression. CFC-supported films have reached major international festivals this year, including Sara Ishaq’s “The Station” at Cannes Critics’ Week, Rania Rafei’s “The Day of Wrath: Tales from Tripoli” at the Berlinale Forum and Mohanad Yaqubi’s “Revolutionaries Never Die,” which won the Special Jury Prize at Locarno. Other projects developed through CID workshops have subsequently been selected for CFC or screened in Cairo’s competitions.
“This doesn’t happen every year,” Sayed Abdel-Rehim acknowledges. “But it shows that in recent years, we’ve been selecting projects with a strong chance of reaching completion and traveling internationally.”
This year, CFC has selected 17 projects from 12 countries and will present 43 individual awards. “We initially thought we would select around 10 projects, but there were so many strong submissions that it was difficult to narrow them down,” Sayed Abdel-Rehim says.
He also emphasizes the importance of broadening opportunities for underrepresented filmmakers. “We always support women filmmakers, and we also try to support countries that don’t produce a lot of films,” he adds, pointing to Yemen, Sudan and Libya as examples.
Another new initiative, “From Book to Screen,” seeks to reconnect Egypt’s film and publishing industries. The CID director points to Egypt’s long history of literary adaptations, particularly during the 1960s and 1970s, and the subsequent decline in that tradition.
The program has selected 10 books from 10 Egyptian publishing houses, with authors and publishers receiving training ahead of pitching their works to producers. CID hopes to introduce a formal selection committee next year and open the initiative to writers across the Arab world by 2028.
The same incremental approach is visible in the Cairo Film Market, launched in 2024 with eight companies. This year’s market features 23 booths, alongside delegations from countries across Asia and Africa with which CIFF and CID are strengthening ties. CID is also expected to sign a cooperation agreement with SICA Abidjan, an audiovisual forum in Côte d’Ivoire, during this year’s edition, extending its network of African industry partners.
Beyond expanding its international network, CID is also addressing some of the longstanding challenges facing independent filmmakers. “The problem is always about financing films, about distributing the films, about marketing the films,” Sayed Abdel-Rehim says. “Some independent filmmakers, especially in their first film, don’t give a lot of attention to distribution and marketing.”
To begin addressing these longstanding gaps, CID is expanding its professional development offerings, including immersive storytelling and XR programming, as well as workshops exploring artificial intelligence in pre-production. Sayed Abdel-Rehim sees emerging technologies as particularly relevant to independent filmmakers working with limited budgets.
The wider program includes masterclasses with directors Matteo Garrone, Asif Kapadia, Abderrahmane Sissako, Óliver Laxe and Laura Wandel, as well as Egyptian screenwriter and producer Medhat El Adl. Moroccan filmmaker Nabil Ayouch, who also presides over CIFF’s international competition jury, will lead a masterclass, while Egyptian actor Asser Yassin will take part in an In Conversation session. Industry panels will explore financing for Arab films, opportunities for women directors, the challenges facing a new generation of Arab filmmakers and the future of theatrical exhibition.
Taken together, these initiatives reflect Sayed Abdel-Rehim’s ambition for CID to do more than help filmmakers get individual projects off the ground. Instead, he wants CID, as an institution, to give them the support and connections to build sustainable careers, allowing them to continue making films for years to come.
That ambition extends beyond individual filmmakers to strengthening Cairo’s ties with the international film industry.
“The vision of the Cairo film industry is to connect. To connect the North with the South, to connect the East with the West,” Sayed Abdel-Rehim concludes.

A hijack threat note was found in the washroom of a Mumbai-bound Air India flight shortly before its scheduled departure from Kolkata airport on Wednesday, PTI reported.
The airport authorities moved the aircraft to an isolation bay at the airport. The flight was scheduled to take off at 10.20 am.
The note, which warned that the aircraft would be hijacked at 11.10 am, was found in the aircraft's washroom just before departure, Kolkata airport director Vikram Singh told PTI.
All passengers who had boarded the aircraft were deboarded and the plane was moved to an isolation bay for security checks, Singh added.
Security protocols were immediately activated, with officials conducting a thorough inspection of the aircraft as a precautionary measure, he added.
